_ GENTLE INFLUENCES. Violets in tbe leafiest shade. By their odours are betrayed; Soft winch, over flower fields blown, By their fragrant breath are known. Dew, by freshened leaves confessed, Wets, unseen, Earth's slumbering breast: Rills, from out the bleak hill-side, Swell to rivers deep and wide; Rivers, flowing fast and free, Widen to the boundless sea; All-great things that move the earth To gentle issues ove their birth; And soft influence still is best, Bringing comfort, love, and rest. Sweet domestic love is strong—
Leads to right and warns ei:oni. wrong; Kindly whispers mightier rove, And to loftie. actions move, Than the fretful voice of Scorn, Of Contempt a ,d Anger born. --Chambers' Journal.

A cheerful face in nearly as good for an invalid as healthy weather. If the year is to be beautiful, Every day mast be made beautiful. The woman who undertook to sco tr the woods has aban- doned the job, on account of the sc:rcity of sand and the high price of soap. A public writer thinks that much might be gained if speakers would observe the miller's rule—always to shut the gate when the grist is out. Things of God which are marvellous are to be believed on a principle of faiths not to be pried into by reason. For it reason set them up before our eyes they would no longer be

marvellous. An Irishman wanting to buy a stove was locking over a stock in a store. The dealer, in praising a certain stove, said, "If you buy one of these stoves you will save half the coal you would otherwise use." "Faith," said Pat, "then ra better take two stoves and save all the coal." A village schoolmaster, examining a reading class, asked the head of the class: "What is artificial manure ?" "Don't know," said he, and the same reply was given by four other boys; but a precocious youngster' not yet in his teens, was equal to the occasion, and said. "Please, sir, it's trie stuff they grow artificial flowers in." A gentleman of Allpany, United States, recently married a lady reputed to be rich, who turned out to be poor and some 700 dollars in debt, which he had to liquidate. She assured him, however, for his consolation, that the debts were contracted for dress, which she bought to captivate him. Only think of a fish paying for the hook with which

he was caught! A gentlemen travelling in a railway carriage was endea- vouring, with considereole earnestness, to impress some argument upon a fello e-paesenger who was seated opposite to him, and who appeared ratner dull of comprehension. At length, being slightly irritated, he exclaimed, in a louder tone: "Why, sir, it's as plain as A B 0! " "That may be," replied the other, with alacrity, "bat I atie D E F." When Sir Charles Lyell, the geologist, was in America he had some curious advice given to him about travelling on the Mississippi steamboats. "Never pay your fare till you are compelled to," was the first piece of wisdom thrown at him. "And pray why not ?" he queried. " Because your chances are better in case of trouble." "Will you kindly explain yourself, sir ?" said Lyell, astonished beyond me:n sure. "Well," answered the American,"when I was travel- ling up the river last March somebody called out, ' Passen- ger overboard!' The caotain hurried to the office and asked, 'Has the man overboard paid his fare?' On being answered in the affirmative he turned to the pilot and said indiffer- ently, Go ahead; it's all right.' " To ALL Weleer IT MAY CoscEaN.—Don't talk too much. Learn how to be silent. There is nothing like the man or woman that can keep the mouth shut. Not that people should always keep the tongue still, it is made for use, but there are times when silence is the best and most effective reply. When a boor speaks roughly or uncivilly to you, when you are asked an impertinent question, when a sneer is conveyed under cover of an inquiry for informatien, or when, having appealed to you on a question of taste, your opinion is met with ridicule—the best answer in these or like exigencies Is masterful silence. Silence bespeaks re- serve, power, conscious strength, dignity, self-command; and nothing is at times so effective as the silence which springs from- contempt. VENTILATION.—In summer, fresh air should be obtainee, if possible, from the shaded side of the building. To effect this there shout I be a number of apertures covered with •some porous texture (so that, as we have before noticed, the air may have no sensible current), extending at intervals over a considerable space. When the windows happen to be at the shaded sides, the ventilation will be easily managed, by letting in the air at the lower part of them, by no means opening the top. In fine, these golden rules may be laid down, which have been approved by a celebrated civil en- gineer and a great authority on ventilation, that in what- ever manner fresh air is obtained, (1) it should be introduced . near the floor; (2) at various places; and (3) dispersed as much as possible to avoid currents.—Cassell's Household Guide. Wosec AND WORRY.—It is not work that kills men; it is worry. We are all agreed upon that. How to avoid worry would be a subject that would enlist a multitude of readers, if the recipe could be given. But so mach C! It anTes from causes outside our will, nnteide our very expectation, it et it would be idle to suggest tueia or that ae the way to avoid ft a:together. The subject of this paper is of a more cura- tive cheraeter then any epecinc as to avoiding causes of worry—for its aim is specially to show that the Gospel of Jesus Cei ist provides the best antidote for it. The fact is, anxiqies will come, and mast be met by some all-sufficient remtly. Let us therefore note the reasons which cur blessed Lord gives for their avoidance. "Take no anxiety for the morrow." Why? Because every day, as it brings the re- turning light of morning, brings also new mercies, new freshness of feeling, new and gracious providence% nee, np. pertueitiee ard unexpetrEd delieerencee. The pl.hrrow aleall take aexiety for the things of Itself." Do not antedate diffirql,iest because you cannot antedate their relief.—The Quiver. REMARKABLE " FtNDS "OF GOLD.—A. velume might be filled with anecdotes of remarkeble " finds" in the Vic- torian gold-fields. In inidsornoaer, 1e.39, two poor men were _ at work in a gully, when, oia digging round the roots of a tree, the pick of one of them came upon something very hard. The men exclaimed he wished it had been a nugget, even it it bad broken his pick. It proved to be a nugget, a- d one destined to be famous, for it was the "Welcome Stranger," refereed to in our notice of the Melbourne Museum. A waggoner was one day driving his team along the road, when his wheel, in turning up the soil, suddenly exposed to view a considerahle lump of shining matter. The waggoner stooped to pick it up, and by be so doing be- came the owner of a nugget which proved to be worth £1,600. In the early days of sluicing, a Scotsman was working an extensive claim, and enapleying a number of men under him. His last shilling was spent before any gold was found. He told his men he had no more funds, and could go on no longer. They had a great respect for him, and subscribed among themselves enough to carry on the works for a few weeks. Gold was Peon afterwards found in abundance. The Scot retired with £40,000, and made over the mine, while still in full yield, to the men who had so generously helped him. On 'me occasion two men who had just arrived from England sat down to rest on the outskirts of a spot to which there had been a recent rush. It was a broiling hot day, and they were glad, after their toilsome walk up the country, to rest in the shade of an old gum- tree. As they sat, one of them, rubbing up the earth with the heel of his boot, disclosed to view something hard and yellow-leoking. Palling it from the ground, they found it was a huge cake of veritable gold. Without having had to u3e pick orspecle they had realised a fortune, and speedily turning their backs on the diggings, they took the first ship home.—Cities of the World. Tun UsEs OF Haas'.—Tbe heath is applied to many useful purposes. Houses are roofed with it instead of with thatch. In Scotland a stung decoction of it is used ía tan- "— leather, and a very refreshing driek is made by brewing together tard parts of heath-top to one of malt. The he plant, too, is a good deal used for =kir.; .oroollle, and for heating ovens while the turf, full of its fibrous and matted roots, and with the plants still on it, is cut up, dried, and used as fuel by many a poor cottager. Woven into a wooden framework it makes a protective fencing. Neither horses nor cattle seem to care for it, but in some parts of the country the old heath is from time to time fired, as sheep enjoy the tender shoots which afterwards spring up. This custom is referred to in" Marmion." Its close and shelter- ing manes form a home for many a wild animal, and birds and other small creatures find a meal as well as a refuge in its umbrageous depths. Grouse thrive on it, for example, and several species of lepidoptera have the heath as the food-plant of their caterpillars. Mary Hewitt writes in on of her poems of those wastes of heath, Stretching for miles to lure the bee, Where the wild bird, on pinions strong, Wheelscreatures riouina,andpoawrsanhdiserpfirpeie.ng song' The heath-honey, however, is browner and coarser than that which is gathered in other districts, and Gerarde, we see, says, "Of these flowers bees do gather bad honey." It gains a somewnat strong and distinctive taste that is more objected to by sone persons than by others. Quite recently a new golden-yellow dye has been brought out, niade from the woody portions of the heath. The shoots and stems are crushed, and then boiled in alum-water; after cooling, filtering, and standing for some three or four days exposed to the air, the liquid assumes a rich golden tint, and in this state, says the "Textile Manufacturer," it can be used for dipping fabrics of all materials. Used alone it gives various tints of yellow and orange, with oak-bark a rich brown, with cochineal tints of scarlet; or the colouring matter may be precipitated, and then forms a fine yellow body colour for wall-papers and many other purposes. —Familiar Wild Flowers. " WRAT SHALL I DRINK ?" The Lancet says :—" We counsel the public to drink their Lime-Juice whenever and wherever they list. As a rule, Lime-Juice is, particularly during the summer, a far more wholesome drink than any form of alcohol. We have subjected the samples of the Lime-Fruit Juice' of the Montserrat Company to full analysis, with a view to test Its quality and purity. otin INTRECOURSE WITH LITTLE CHILDEEIL—If there be any good in you, middle-aged and aging folk, you know it tomes of your intercourse with little children. This in divers ways. Life is freshened. Hope revives, thinking of all the possibilities of a new start and a new career. The good which never came to you may come to your little boy or girl. Selfishness, that grows upon the solitary, is broken in upon. You are trained, naturally and pleasantly, to think of others and to work for them; you cheerfully give up your own enjoyment for the sake of the little folk, never even thinking that you are doing so. But there are great sorrows, too. I do not even suggest such a thing as one turning out ill ; that must not be. Only, with such a possi- bility for a moment in the mind, go and read Wordsworth's "Michael ;" and I think you will be aware of a homely pathos never exceeded in human writing or human speech. Ah, set beside that pages over which tears innumerable have bees shed, turning to a shallow falsetto. Ido not here sug- ' gest the parting that is made by the Great Change. Only that months slip away, and grow into years; and the time comes when they must go out from the Home, must go away and think and act for themselves, the little boys and girls who (you used to think) could not be safe out of your eight. There are things too sacred to be spoken much of; we keep them to ourselves. " Spring's delights" can only be actually realized by those who live in healthy houses, and who combine known sanitary measures for the prevention of such infectious diseases as small- ,x, scarlet fever, and measles. The remedy nctually becomes; luxury when the wash'ng of toilet, bath, and nursery is con- ducted with Wright's Coal Tar Sap. Refuse all imitations which are but dangerous counterfeits.—ildvt.

" nhe year 1843 shall be the Repeal Year," be If a war had broken out during the agitation—if the life of asserted again and again with characteristic ardour. Nor O'Connell had been prolonged ten years longer—if any worthy need we wonder at this. He had seen public opinion amone successor had assumed his mantle—if a fierce famine had his co-religionists so faint as scarcely to be perceptiole to the not broken the spirit of the people—who can say that the rulers. He had made it BO terrible that the resolution of agitation would not have been successful ?" Wellington and the ability of Peel quailed beneath it. He had seen the society of his creation unable at first to secure the attendance of ten members at its meetings, and be made It the ruler of Ireland. Looking back to such a triumph as that of 1829, it is not at all surprising that he should have entered with confidence and with cheerfulness upon the struggle. The agitation assumed its importance outside the walls of Parliament. Within the House the movement was feebly supported, but without it was supported by a public opinion which was too powerful to be ignored. In all parts of Ire- land the assemblies which O'Connell addressed were vast and enthusiastic. The greatest of all these meetings, per- haps the grandest display of the kind that has ever taken place, was held around the hid of Tara. On the great plain of Meath, not far from the Boyne river, rises a gentle emi• nence in the midst of a luxuriant farming country. . On and around its summit are still certain mouldering remains of earthen mounds and moats, the ruins of the "House of Cormac," and the "Mound of the Hostages," and the Stone of Destiny." It is the " Temora of the Kings." Here, on the 15th of August, a meeting was appointed to be held. The spot was well chosen for the purpose. Tara of the Kings, the seat of the ancient royalty of Ireland, has ever been regarded by the Irish people with something of a superstitious awe. "The vague legends that cluster around it—the poetry that has consecrated its past, and the massive relics of its ancient greatness that have been from time to time discovered, have invested it with an ineffable and a most fascinating grandeur." It was on this spot that O'Connell, standing by the stone where the Kings of Ireland were once crowned, sketched the coining glories of his country. Beneath him, like a mighty Bea, extended the throng of listeners. According to very moderate computa- tions, about a quarter of a million were there to welcome their "Heaven-sent deliverer." So vast was the assembly that thousands were unable to catch the faintest echo of the voice they loved so well; yet all remained passive, tranquil, and decorous. It was, in truth, as O'Connell called it, "an august and triumphant meeting." The scene has been well described by Balwer Lytton in his "St. Stephen's:"— Once to my sight the giant thus was given. Walled by wide air and roofed by boundless heaven. Beneath his feet the human ocean lay, And wave on wave flowed into space away. Methought no clarion could have sent its sound E'en to the centre of the hosts around; And, RB I thought, rose the sonorous swell, As from some church-tower swings the silvery bell. Aloft and clear from airy tide to tide It glided easy as a bird may glide. I To the last verge of that vest audienoe sent, • It played with each wild passion as it went Now stirred the uproar—now the murmurs stilled, And sobs or laughter answered as it willed. Then did I know what spells of infinite choice To rouse or lull has the sweet human voice. Then did I learn to seize the sudden clue To the grand trouislous life antique—to view Under the rock stand of Demosthenes • Unstable Athens heave her noney. seas. The Government at last determined to interfere. The time had. clearly come either for it to yield with good grace or to grapple with the sedition. The Government resolved upon the latter course. "Let them not dare," O'Connell had often said, "to attack 119." The challenge was now to be accepted. A great metropolitan meeting was appointed to be held on the historic shore of Clontarf, two miles from Dublin along the bey, on Sunday, the firli of October, The I place is famous in Irish history as the sc,?ne of a great vic- tory of the Irish over their Danish invaders. It was in• tended that the meeting should salvias in numbers and in earnestness tete assemblage at Tara. But late in the after. noon of Saturday, whan it was already almost dusk, a proclamation was posted on the walls of Dublin, signed by the Irish Secretary and Privy Councillors, and the Com• mender of the Forces, forbidding the meeting. Never was O'Connell's power over the people shown more effectually than in the control which at that critical moment he was still able to exercise. Long before the Proclamation was Issued, thousands of people from Meath, Kildare, and Dublin counties were already on their way to Clontarf. Why the Government delayed so long the issue of the proclamation, we cannot tell. They certainly ran a terrible risk. It was no fault of theirs that Clontarf was not the Beene of a " Peterloo Massacre." Indeed Lord Cloncurry made no scruple in designating the Government arrangements as "a projected massacre." But O'Connell was equal to the occa- sion. He issued also a proclamation—declaring that the orders of the Lord Lieutenant must be obeyed—that the meeting must not take place, and that the people must re- turn to their homes. The "Uncrowned King" was obeyed. The peasantry peaceably dispersed, and the meeting was not held. The Government prosecution followed close on the proclamation. O'Connell, his son, and five of his principal followers were arrested and held to bail on a charge of ex- citing to sedition. At length the Conspirators were brought to trial. The Government Prosecutor objected to all the Catholics who were called as Jurors. So the greatest Irish Catholics in the metropolis Of an essentially Catholic country, and at a time when sectarian ahienosity was at its height, was tried by a Jury compoftd exclusively of Proter, Waits. The trial was a long one, but its monotony was re- lieved by the brilliant oratory of Shiel and Whiteside. The trial which began on the 2nd of November, 1843, name to an end early in February, 1844. The Lord Chief Justice, in his charge to the Jury, argued the case like one of the tounsei ft the prosecution, and so far.ftlegot himself as to teren tteee traversers' counsel "the gentlemen on the other ieire:" Referring to this charge afterwards, Lord Macaulay compared it to "the display of judicial, partisanship in the State trials of Charles II." Of coulee O'Connell was found guilty, and he was sentenced to twelve months' imprison- ment, and a fine of £2,000. Against this sentence he ap- pealed to the House of Lords. Some months elapsed before the appeal could be heard, and during the early part of that time O'Connell was in great alarm lest the people should have broken into open rebellion. He despatched from his prison a most emphatic address exhorting them to tran- quillity. "Every man," said he, "who is guilty of the slightest breach of -the peace is an enemy of me and of Ire-' land." Tire Irish people took him at his word, and remained perfectly quiet. Their reception of the Government prose- cution is somewhat remarkable. While they remained per- fectly tranquil, the rent, which in the fourteen weeks before the trial had been £6,679, rose in the fourteen weeks , that followed it to £25,712. In the first week it was nearly £2,600. The appeal in the House of Lords was heard in the following September. Five law lords were present. The lay peers, on the appeal of Lord Wharncliffe, waived their right to vote, and left the matter, according to the usual course, in the hands of the landlords. The majority of these being against the judgment of the Court below, it was ac- cordingly reversed, and O'Corinell and his associates were set at liberty. Be his faults what they might, O'Connell was no more a seditious conspirator than was Richard Cob- den, and therefore, when the House of Lords cancelled the judgment, they did so amid the approbation of all impartial observers. The news of the reversal of the sentence was received in Ireland with a burst of the most enthusiastic acclamation. O'Connell passed through the streets of Dublin in a trium- phant procession. Bonfires biased on the hill tops. A per- fect delirium of excitement prevailed among his followers, yet notwithstanding these ebullitions the spell of his power was in a great measure broken. Indeed, from the moment he issued his proclamation commanding the people to dis- perse peaceably the power of the Agitator was gone. The Government accomplished far more by their proclamation than they could possibly have imagined at the time. With- out knowing it, they had compelled O'Connell to show his hand. It was now made clear that he did not intend to have resort to force. From that hour there was virtually a schism between the elder Repealera and the younger—be- tween O'Connell and Young Ireland, one of whose poets has sung : The tribune's tongue or poet's pen May sow the seed in prostrate men, But 'tis the soldier's sword alone Can reap the harvest when 'Lis grown. div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.
The Ladies' Land League, Dublin, reports the expendi- ture in the past week to hare been in grants to evicted tenants, £996; to coercion prisoners, £334; receipts since last meeting, £5,700.

. . The erection of huts by the Ladies' Land League con- tinues at Murroll, on Lord Cloncurry's estate. Large par- ties of constabulary patrol the district daily, and a hut for the accommodation of the police is in course of erection, as the intimidation of new tenants is feared. A man named Thomas IVl'Quaide, who answered the de- scription of one of the assassins, was arrested at Maynooth by the constabulary on the 14th inst. He was conveyed to Richmond Bridewell on Friday under an armed escort where he will remain awaiting the result of any evidence that may 5e forthcoming. It is stated that a difference of opinion has arisen between the Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland and Colonel Brackenbury, the new chief of the detective force, asto the reorganisation of the detective department. The latter is anxious to intro- duce the French and Belgian systems, and is said to have already brought over an eminent Belgian police-officer for this purpose. A murderous assault was cummitted at Crannagh, near Athlone, on Sunday night. Two men, named John Dolan and Martin Tracy, had a dispute about a piece of land, when Dolan struck Tracy on the head with a spade, inflict- ing a frightful wound. He was taken in an insensible con- dition to the Union Hospital, where his dying depositions were taken by the resident magistrate. On Sunday night a " Moonlight " attack was made on the house of a farmer named Walsh, residing at Ballyhahill, county Limerick. It appears that Walsh wished that tenants should pay their rents, but the others refused to do so. When the attack was made the " Moonlighters " asked Walsh if he was going to meet the agent, and an argument ensued. One of the " Moonlighters " raised his gun and shot Walsh through the neck. His life is in imminent danger.

Nit% Davitt arrived at New York on Sunday morning. He was met in the bay by delegation of Irishmen, and went almost immediately to Boston where he had a reception by the Irish societies of New England, who assembled on Satur- day to celebrate the anniversary of the battle of Bunker's Hill. The feeling among the Irish against Mr. Davitt's nationalisation scheme is said to be growing stronger. It finds no champion save the Irith Worl4, MR. PARNELL AND MR. DAVITT'S NATIONALISATION ScnEatz.—Mr. Parnell has been " interviewed " on the sub- ject of the scheme propounded by Mr. Michael Devitt for the "nationalisatien "of the soil of Ireland. As Mr. Devitt himself admitted. the hon. member for Cork does not ap- prove of this 'Acme for the final adjustment of Ireland's agrarian troubles, and Mr. Parnell, in conversation with his interviewer, was at some pains to point out in what respect lie considered Mr. Da.vitt's proposals unworkable and impos- sible. The hon. member adheres to the original Land League platform in favour of a peasant proprietary, and while admitting every one's right to formulate his own par- ticular theories, he intimates pretty clearly that Mr. Davitt's advocacy of "nationalisation" is likely at the present moment to carry division still further into the ranks of the Irish party. TRH Ngw Infsx SECIIET Poucr. Addressing a de- monstration of members of the Land League at Bermond- sey, London, at which Mr. Biggar, M.P., and some of the principal Land Leaguers of London were present, Mr. r. H. O'Donnell -slid he had to tell them of an outcome of the Coercion Bill more revolting than Russian tyranny of the worst kind. He fully took upon himself the responsibility, and it was a grave responsibility. He could tell them of his own personal knowledge that within the last few days a number of men and Women had arrived from Ireland at Euston-square terminus in charge of three Dublin detec- tives. The men were disguised as evicted tenants, labourers, or small farmers; the women (who were priuci- pally taken from the female prison warders) as their wives or other relatives. They were the first draft of a east secret detective organisation now being formed in Dublin under Colonel Brackenbury, which would extend its ramifications all over the three kingdoms. They would ingratiate them- selves into Irish families as servants or in otht capacities, and send periodical reports to Dublin Castle. They would never be brought to the front, or' ever placed in the witness box. He warned his countrymen to beware of every plaus- ible stranger, and never on any account to express their mind before them—much less join any secret organisation they might try to induce them to join. • The system was an infernal one,, worse than Talbot's, and would be the creator of crime, and bring untold misery on the Irish people. MILITARY PRECAUTIONS AGAINST A RISING IN

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

Th. Freeman's Journal of M9nday says :—" Late on Maturday orders were received at the Royal Barracks, Dub- lin, to turn out men warned for inlying pickets, and keep them under arms. Two troops of the 21st Hussars and a troop of dragoons were sent out on patrol duty with secret in- structions. The reason of these movements is kept strictly confidential at headquarters, but the military telegraph clerks are required to sleep next their instruments." A Limerick telegram states :—" Instructions have been given to commanding officers at all the great military centres in the South and West of Ireland, as well as in Dublin, as to the course which should be pursued in the event of a rising: In the present critical state of affairs it is felt that the au- thorities have done wisely ire preparing for any emergency which may arise. Numerous police and military patrols are on duty nightly in Limerick." The Press Association's Parsonstown correspondent tele- graphs :—"ln consequence of a rising being apprehended, the military authorities have received instructions prohibit- ing the admission of civilians to all military barracks throughout Ireland. The sentries have been doubled, tend the night patrols quadrupled, and the greatest precaution is being taken against any explosives being carried into mili- tary quarters." Private information has reached the Evening News to the effect that the authorities have even greater fears of a rising in the south and west than would appear from what has already been published in the newspapers. The turbulent population in the districts most disturbed, it is believed in very well informed circles, may take to arms at any moment, which would be followed by a concerted attack on every building containing rifles and ammunition, as well as on the residences of the magistrates ; and the greatest alarm is felt by those who are responsible for the disposition of both the military and civil powers, although efforts are being made to prevent the alarm from spreading. The expectation of an insurrectionary movement such as that indicated will to some extent explain the elaborate precautions recently made, and which have only just become known to the public, it is possible that the measures taken by the authorities will cause the revolutionary leaders to hesitate somewhat and reduce the number of their followers willing to enter upon a strug- gle, the prospect of success in which is so much against them. Nevertheless an early resort to the arbitrament-of arms of the advanced nationalists is anticipated by those who command the best moans of knowing what is passing in Ireland. MICHAEL DAVITT ON HIS LIVERPOOL SPEECH. A New York telegram dated Tuesday, says :—Michael Davitt, in a speech delivered last night at the Academy of Music, gave a general denial to the series of charges made against him by certain Irishmen, and defended his plan for the nationalisation of the Irish Land first announced at West- more and afterwards explained at Liverpool. He declared that he was not ashamed of this proposal, and did not regard it as conflicting with the ideas of Mr. Parnell. The charge that he was promulgating a new departure was based on a misconception of his Liverpool speech, and an unjust inter- pretation of his motives by members of the Land League, who called themselves his friends, including Mr. Parnell. The speaker denied that he was starting a new fund ; and,

Teferring to the charge that be was advocating an alliance with the English people, said he did not believe that the de- mocracy of England was blameable because the English aristocracy had wronged Ireland. Ile claimed the right to advocate the cause of any people, and if he chose to aid the working classes of England without slackening his exertions for his own people he did consider that he needed no defence.
STRANGE THEORY RE THE PHCENIX. PARK.
MURDERS.

A curious opinion is very prevalent amongst the lower classes in Dublin about the Plicenix Park murders ; and it is worth noting, perhaps, by those who look upon the whole affair as inexplicable. I have it from one who was a patient in Stevens' Hospital -when the bodies of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke were brought in ; and one of the lower classes himself says it is the belief of a very large number of the masses. When Lord Hartington was Chief Secretary to the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland in 1871, it may be remembered that the Prince of Wales visited Dublin, and that there was a very serious disturbance in the Phcenix Park. The police made a furious, and, as some say, a very unprovoked assault upon the mob, near the Wellington Memorial, and a vast number of people were badly beaten, including, I think, Me. T. D. Sullivan, M.P. Lord Harting- ton was present, and saw the whole affair, which created a tremendous sensation, and resulted in the celebrated case of " O'Beirne v. Hartington." Now, the assassination of Lord Frederick Cavendish is put down by the Dublin lower orders as an act of private revenge upon the Cavendish family. Mr. Burke's fate is believed to have been only incidental. The grudge engendered by the police batons and Lord Har- tington's presnice consenting to the occurrence, was to be at last wiped out; and directly it was heard that Lord Frederick was coming over as Chief Secretary, the private vendetta was resumed, and the account finally closed. This is common talk in the Dublin streets. Moreover,the Stevens' Hospital patient heard it first from some membersof the Royal Irish Constabulary the night of the murders ; and hence it is evident that there was an idea in that quarter that Lord Frederick was in some danger from his relationship to Lord Hartington. All this may be mere idle talk ; but it makes the affair more nearly resemble the Felton-Buckingham business.— World.

div.head: IXTRAORDINARY SCENE AT A WEDDING.
div.p: IXTRAORDINARY SCENE AT A WEDDING.
A PLUCKY BRIDE

A certain dean of Chester was called upon to perform the wedding ceremonial of a pair of happy lovers. The posi- tion of both parties was of the highest rank, and the guests who were bidden to the church were of the most fashionable aud exalted. The day arrived, and with it the hour. The edifice was packed, and all was in readiness. The dean, ex- pectant, awaited the coming of the bride, and the groom, with his best man, was in the vestry. The hour passed on, and still the bride did not arrive. After a long delay she' drove up to the church door, and with her bridesmaids swept up the large middle aisle towards the altar. In the mean- time the groom advanced to meet her, and, receiving her half-way, escorted her to the dean. After the opening words of exhortation the dean turned to the man and asked him the usual questions, whether he would have the woman for his wedded wife, kc., dm, to which he answered, "I will." The question being in turn asked of the woman, to the astonishment and amazement of all she distinctly said, looking at the groom in the face, "I will not !" The next instant she said in a low voice, "Mr. Dean, no one can more regret the words I have just uttered than myself, and if you will dismiss the congregation and take me into your vestry-room, I will apologise, and at the same time fully and satisfactorily explain what may seem to all my strange conduct." The dean, seeing that she was in earnest, in a few words dismissed the bewildered congregation and directed the britegroom to await him. The congregation having departed, and the lady and dean being together, she said, "I cannot tell you how badly I feel. I had loved my fiancée truly and devotedly, and had looked forward to a life of perfect happi- ness and joy. This morning, as you know, I was late at my marriage ceremony, bat it was not through any fault of mino. I arrived as soon as I could. Instead of receiving looks of love and words of full happiness from my future husband, he paralysed my beating heart by saying, when he met me half way up the aisle, G-- d-- you! If you expect to begin life this way, by keeping rue waiting for you, you will find out after you are my wife!' My decision was instantly made. I have been told that, sooner than suffer unhappiness through my own actions, it were better to renounce even at the altar a union that would bring misery and grief thereafter. Had I turned back he would have fol- lowed me; there would have been a scene, and he might have persuaded me to return and marry him. It also might have looked like temper, and I had fully time during your few words of prayer to make up my mind. I know that I have disappointed friends, my family, but no one more than myself. Do not ask me to reconsider his late actkn. In- ferm my would-have-been husband of my determination and let me go." The dean, seeing she was resolved, could not but approve, and gently led her through the church back to her anxious parents, not as a smiling wife, but as a woman whose present is shattered and whose future is blighted.

div.p: worst at once—Mr. Alderman POWLIIR desired to know if the Corrupt Practices Bill would take precedence over the procedure resolutions, but Mr. GLADSTONE replied that the mode of dealing with the resolutions on procedure must stand over for future consideration. He pointed out that every unnecessary speech was a contribution to obstruction, and said it was their multiplication out of which the whole of the gigantic evil arose. After further discussior. the motion was carried by 253 to 97. THE PREVENTION or CRIME BILL.—At the evening sit- ting, shortly after the resumption of Committee on the Irish Coercion Bill, an important concession was announced by the PIEMIER. Mr. Gladstone said the keenest feeling had been aroused with regard to the clause dealing. with the right of search by night. The Government were not pre- pared to give that up, but they were prepared to limit it so that there should be no search by night exc.,pt in a case where there was reasonable suspicion that a secret or illegal society was holding a meeting.—A number of the Irish members warmly thanked the Premier for this modification ; and Mr. PARMILL suggested that the right of search by night should be left out, and that a new clause should be brought up to give the police the right of entry to illegal meetings.— Mr. TRZTEIYAN, on behalf of the Government, accepted the suggestion, and further amendments were considered before progress was reported. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

THE PRETENTIOIsT OF CRIME (IRELAND) BlLL.—Almost the entire sitting was occupied by the renewed discussion on clause 11 of the Coercion Bill. Persistent efforts were made by the Irish members to further limit the right of search conferred by the clause upon the police. An undigni- fied squabble took place regarding the precise extent of Mr. Gladstone's concession announced at the previous sitting. Mr. Parnell proposed an amendment similar in tenor to the suggestions of the Prime Minister, which Sir Wm. Harcourt refused to accept, on the ground that the Government amendment would be introduced on the report. Mr. Healey, supported by several English and Irish members, thereupon ventured to make a most ill-advised attack upon the Home Secretary, with the object of demonstrating that the Premier and his subordinates in the Government were not at one in regard to this matter. The effect of this course was to elicit from both sides of the House the declaration that Mr. Glad- stone's propositions had been perfectly understood when announced lsy himself, and had been fairly and accurately repeated and acted upon by the Home Secretary. After Mr. J. Cowen had entered his protest against the clause it was agreed to by 259 to 45. The next clause, which pro- poses to apply the Alien Act of 1848 to aliens in Ireland, was under discussion when the time for adjournment arrived. _ .
HOUSE OF LORDS.—Txmisnay.

The Earl of CARNARVON asked for information as to the serious disturbances reported from Zululand.—The Earl of KIMBERLEY, in reply, read the telegrams the Government had received from Sir IL Bulwer. The latest telegram described the "situation " as " more hopeful," though the position of affairs was still serious. The question in regard to the conference of which the 'Marquis of Salisbury had given notice could not be dealt with in consequence of the absence of the Foreign Secretary.—On the motion of the PRIMATE, the Cathedral Statutes Amendment Bill was read a second time.—The inferior Courts Judgements Bill was also read a second time on the motion of Lord MONCY, after the Lord Chancellor had given his opinion that it would not be desirable that the judgments of inferior courts should be placed on the same footing as those of the superior courts. --Upon the motion for gc ing into committee on tke Inter- ments (Febo de se) Bill there was a discussion on the pre- sent barbarous mode of interring suicides, in wkich the Earl of Shaftesbury, the Lord Chancellor, and Earl Fortescue took part. The bill, which is to enable the friends of suicides to bury their dead instead of leaving it to the police, to allow of a religious service, and to allow of the interment taking place at a convenient time, passed through committee. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSMY.

EGYPTIAN AFFAIRS.—The official information on Egyp- tian affairs communicated to the House was somewhat more explicit than it has been for some time. The UNDER SECRETARY informed Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett that it was on the advice of the Austrian Consul General that the Khedive sent for Bagheb Pasha and entrusted him with the forma- tion of a Ministry. Her Majesty's Government was carry- ing out a clearly defined policy in order to secure the in- fluence of England in Egypt and the security of the lives and property of British subjects. Mr. Cookson was now nearly recovered, and the hearing of causes by the Consular Court inEgypt would be proceeded with as sood as the state of affairs would permit. Mr. CHAPLIN asked a ques- tion respecting the fresh water supply for the Suez Canal, and was told by Sir C. DILIE that means could be taken for ensuing a sufficiency of water, and he should' have no objection to inform the hon. member privately what those means were.—Mr. CHAPLIN then moved the adjournment of the House, and proceeded to attack the policy of the Government, and to argue that at this moment Ourabi Pasha was master of the situation. He wished to know what were the conditions, so far as the Canal was concerned, upon which we had entered the Con- ference. He referred to a speech made by the Prime Minister at Oxford, in which he spoke in aisparaging terms of the Canal and suggested a return to the old route to India by the Cape, and asked if that was now the opinion of the Government. He insisted upon knowing whether the Government, apart from the protection which was given by the fleet and by the Egyptian troops, had taken any measures to protect the lives and property of their fellow- countrymen in Alexandria.—The PRIME MINISTER said he thought the evident sense of the whole House was that lie should not follow the hon. member through the long list of grave questions he had raised. His hoe, friend the Under Secretary had offered togive private and personal information as to the sources of the water supply of the Suez Canal, but after the exhibition of judgment and temper they had seen he hoped his hon. friend would think himself justified in reconsidering that portion of his answer and exercising his own discretion. On the question of Egypt generally the hon.member for Mid-Lincolnshire had expressed an anxiety for papers, but he had very little need of papers, as his mind was made up without them, and the folly and in- capacity of the Government were a:ready painted on his mind in colours which could not be heightened. The right hon. gentleman then urged that nothing could be more un- wise on the part of the Government than for them at this time to indicate what were the views of the Government and what was the state of their knowledge respecting the restoration of law and order in Egypt. —Sir S. NORTHCOTE ' thought the question asked by Mr. Chaplin was a natural and reasonable one, and if the answer of Sir C. Mike had been different from what it was he should have pressed the matter to a division. By the admission of the Prime Minister the importance of the Canal had now been estab• lished, and the Government,sw tl eir way to the protection of the Canal should any attempt be made to cut off the supply of water.—Mr. M'Coarr pointed out that the Canal was no more dependent upon the fresh water supply than the Thames was upon the river Lea, and contended that the attempt to raise a scare about it was one of the wildest and most childish things he had ever heard.—Sir G. Emorr did not share the apprehensions of his friends as to the injury that would be caused to the Suez Canal by the destruction of the fresh water canal, and thought it only fair on all sides that the public mind should not be alarmed on this subject.—Sir M. HicKs-BFAcx thought the Government should make it clear how they stood as to the Conference and its power to deal with the Suez Canal.—Sir C. DUKE assured the House that the neutralisation of the Suez Canal was outside the purposes of the Conference.—Mr. NORWOOD was of opinion that with the great development of the fast•going powers of large steamers the importance of the Canal was being greatly over-rated.—Mr. Chaplin's motion was negatived without a division, the House refusing to allow its withdrawal. Re- plying to Mr. W. H. Smith, Mr. GLADSTONE said the Con- ference met that day, that in addition to the papers about to be issued there would be a batch on the 2nd of July, and that within ten days after that Supply would be brought on, so as to enable a debate to be raised.

MR. BRADLAUGH.—Mr: Bradlaugh unexpectedly pre- sented himself at the table .of the House in. the interval between private business and notices, and attempted to pre- sent a petition, but the SPZAKER ruled that as the hon. member had not been sworn he had no such right as he claimed, and called upon him to withdraw.—Mr. Bradlaugh, still asserting his right, withdrew, and took his usual seat below. the bar.
After question thne the House again went into Committee on the Prevention of Crime Bill.

Another remarkable story has to be added to the long list of curious and exciting narratives connected with the Nihilist cause. The St. Petersburg correspondent of the Paris Voltaire guarantees the authenticity of the following facts, which are said to have materially increased the anxiety felt in the Russian capital for the Czar's safety. Shortly after the opening of the Moscow Exhibition, which was recently inaugurated by the Grand Duke Vladimir, a young man demanded an audience of the chief of the police at St. Petersburg. He refused to state his errand to any of the subordinate officials, so after being carefully searched he was admitted to the presence of the general. Here he stated at once that he was sent by the Revolutionary party, and explained his mission in the following terms :—" The Emperor is prevented from going to Moscow by his fear of our schemes. His dread will cease to be justified whenever he grants a Constitution. Then he need fear no conspiracy, and can go in safety wherever he pleases, It has fallen to my lot to inform you that if the Emperor persists in his re- actionary policy nothing can save him. Neither my friends nor myself wish to murder him treacherously. Alexander 111. is warned, as was Alexander 11. 'We do not assassin- ate, but we render justice.'' At this point of the interview the police-officer seemed anxious to call in assistance, but the young Nihilist stopped him, and added :—"I do not wish to be subjected to the indignity of torture. In coming here I have sacrificed my life. I could have killed you, but we do not commit murders uselessty." With these words the youth stepped back a few paces, and knocked two large buttons, with which his cuffs were fastened, against his forehead. The buttons being full of an explosive substance, burst, and inflicted such wounds on the young man that he expired in a few moments, leaving no trace as to his identity. This sensational incident has reminded the public that the murder of Alexander 11. was preceded by similar warnings.
