div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 24, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 24, 1882.
M ISC ELLAI-NTEOUS.

At Cardiff, on Tuesday, Jeremiah Mahony was appre- hended on a charge of the manslaughter of Emma 'Magan, his paramour, whom he is alleged to have brutally ill- treated, and thus caused her death. The Rev. Canon Gibson, the oldest member of the Man- chester Cathedral body, died on Sunday. The deceased canon was born in 1802 at Newcastle-on-Tyne, and his con- nection with this city dates as far back as the year 1828. In the Probate Division, on Tuesday, on the application of Mr. Rayford, Sir James Hannen granted probate of the will of the late Mr. Walter Powell, M.P., who was last seen alive drifting to sea in the balloon Saladin, on the 1 oth of December.

Admiral Watson, superintendent of Chatham Dockyard, has received a threatening letter, warning him to prepare for death. The letter is headed with a skull and cross- bones, and is supposed to emanate from Fenians. The police have the matter in hand.

Among the inquests held by the Liverpool city coroner en Tuesday was one in which it was shown that Susannah Evans, 22 years of age, a domestic servant, had poisoned herself in consequence of a quarrel with a tinsmith named Rimmer, to whom she was engaged to be married. • The Prince of Wales paid a visit to the city of London on Saturday, and performed the ceremony of unveiling the statue at the Royal Exchange to Sir Rowland Hill. In the evening His Royal Highness was present at a banquet in the Mansion House. _ _

The cutting of grass is now being proceeded with in War- wickshire and other parts of the Midland districts. The season having been favourable to the growth of grass, mow- ing has begun somewhat earlier than in prievous years, and the crops arc found to be unusually heavy and in good con- dition.

Mr. Wm. Davies, traveller for Messrs. Davies and Sand- brook, Pontypool, has baen found dead in a lonely spot on the Montnouthshire hills. From the nature of his injuries, and the fact that there was not found upon him as much money as he is supposed to have had in his possession, there is a belief that he has been murdered. _ _ __ _

Before the Hanky magistrates, on Tuesday, Earl Gran- rille and nine colliers employed at his lordship's colliery in the district, were summoned under the Explosives Act for keeping a quantity of gunpowder in unauthorised places at the colliery. The Town Clerk prosecuted, and withdrew the summons against the Earl, but all the other defendants were fined. _ _

The body of a man was recovered on Saturday from the Wear, near the courthouse, Durham. It was recognised as that of a person who, about noon, had made an inquiry near the spot as to whether the stream was deep enough to drown him there. A letter in his possession proved him to be William Coley, of 50, High West-street, Gateshead, and it informed his wife that he had been mad for months.

Mr. George Augustus Sala, speaking at the annual dinner of the Birmingham Press Club, on Saturday, at which he was a guest, dwelt on the subject of anonymity in journalism, which he thought might well form the topic of discussion at a congress of journalists. He thought so far as the personal interests of the journalists were concerned, the balance was in the favour of their signing their names to their articles. THE DOUBLE FATAL= AT WEDDING REJOICINGS.—On Monday morning, an adjourned inquest was held on the bodies of two brothers killed by the bursting of a cannon at marriage rejoicings at Brynmally, near Wrexham. The evidence proved that the cannon was loaded with powder, hay, and clay. The explosion was believed to have occurred through a fault in the casting. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. Five other cannon, which were used when the explosion took place, are to be destroyed. We learn that in order to fernigh a definite answer to the statement of the Bishop of Peterborough that the amend- ment of the law regarding marriage with a deceased wife's sister is not needed in the interest of the poor, the Marriage Law Reform Association have instructed their secretary (Mr. Paynter Allen) to make a thorough statistical inquiry as to such marriages among the working classes in the thickly-populated districts of England and Scotland. Mr. Allen has commenced in Staffordshire, and is organising public meetings simultaneously with his inquiry. M. GLADSTONE AND SCOTTISH DisESTABLISHMENT.—At a meeting of the Free Church Disestablishment Committee in Edinburgh, on Tuesday, it was intimated that a commu- nication had been received from Mr. Gladstone, who had consented to meet a deputation, that the interview would require to stand over until there is a prospect of Mr. Peddie's resolution being discussed. The committee, acquiescing in the reasonableness of the postponement, authorised the principal secretary to take the necessary steps that the deputation may be ready to proceed to London when the state of public business and the convenience of Mr. Glad- stone will admit it. Heetunn EDUCATION IN WALES.—A deputation of peers, members of Parliament, and others representing Wales, bad an interview with Mr. Mundella on Monday, to memorialise the Government on the subject of the high education of the Welsh people. The Duke of Westminster, Lord Aberdare, Lord Penrhyn, Sir Hussey Vivian, and others present. Mr. Mundella, in reply, said Lord Spencer wished to deal with this question during the present session, and that was his own feeling, but he thought the prospects of legislation this session were small. The Department were prepared to ask the Treasury to make a reasonable loan for elementary schools, and he thought the recommendation's of the Com- mittee with respect to colleges would, sejthin certain limits, be adopted. EXTRAORDINARY SCENE.—The interment on Sunday at Kilnaboy, Ireland, of the remains of Mr. John Fitzgerald, of Roughen, whose death resulted from a fall from his horse, culminated in an extraordinary scene. The deceased, a Protestant, married a Roman Catholic lady. His mother was also a Roman Catholic. His father had teen a Protest- ant until within a few years, when he joined the Society of Friends, of which he is still a member. The Rev. John Foot, rector of Kilkeedy, when about to read the funeral service fer the dead, was interrupted by about half a dozen men, who pulled off their coats and swore that they, would let no Protestant read over the deceased, who had been baptised in the Catholic faith. A scene of indescribable confusion occurred, and the clergyman had to desist. Thereupon the father obtained the Prayer Book from Mr. Foot and read the Burial Service uninterrupted. THR TERRIBLE COLLIERY CATASTROPHE IN WARwICX- SHIRI.—Seven weeks have now elapsed since the terrible disaster at the Baxterley Colliery, whereby Si persons lost their livea. Since the pit was sealed up, with the view of extinguishing the fire, consultations have taken place amongst the mining engineers concerned, and we understand an effort will shortly be made to recover the bodies of the men and horses. Some time, however, may elapse ere the colliers can be reached, they being at a considerable dis- tance from the bottom of the shaft; and as the explosions may have done great damage in the roadways, it will be impossible for any one to get along till the debri, is removed. The work of exploration will, however, be proceeded iith as quickly as possible. After the mine has been cleared of the carbonic acid gas and rendered safe, a number of miners are ready to descend in search 'of their ill-fated comrades, eight of whom were married men. The relief fund already exceeds £5,000. and is still increasing. PRINCELY POLITENESS—The Central London Rangers (22nd Middlesex Rifle Volunteer Corps), the other day marched out for battalion drill. As the regiment was wheel- ing round Oxford Circus a carriage and pair dashed at the column, a gentleman in the carriage standing up and motioning to his coachman to go on. The sections of fours nearest the horses closed to prevent their formation being broken, but were unable to resist. An officer of the Rangers stepped up to the carriage door and asked the occupant whether he was aware of the fact that it was against the rule of the service to allow the ranks of an armed corps to be broken through. The gentleman, who appeared to be annoyed at the question, asked if the officer knew who he was, at the the same time telling his coachman to drive on, and shouting "Royal carriage.' The carriage drove through the ranks, and then it was observed for the first time that tie gentleman was his Serene Highness Prince Teck. We understand that this episode has been reported to the proper authorities as an affront to the officer, who was endeavour- ing to discharge his duty in preventing the column being broken.

CLERICAL SCANIAL.—At Clerkenwell Police Court, on Saturday, the Rev. Steward Smyth, of 18, Albion-road, Islington, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Edward-street, Liverpool-road, Islington. —Police-constable Rurnsay (279 G) said the defen- dant was in company with two other gentlemen in the locality named at about nine o'clock on Friday night, sur- rounded by a large crowd of persons. He was the worse for drink, and was flourishing a walking stick round his head, the crowd hooting him, and asking him if he belonged to the Salvation Army. He and another officer took the defen- dant, who said the people had annoyed him and he could not get away, into custcdy.—Police-sergeant Cummins said the defendant was very drunk.—The defendant, in answer to the charge, said he had not been at all intoxicated. He had only taken some claret with his brother at a restaurant. As they were walking towards home a crowd gathered round them in Edward-street—he did not know why—and com- menced calling out " Salvation Army !" He did not belong to the Salvation Army; he was a clerk in holy orders. He merely waved the stick to keep the crowd back.—Mr. Bar- stow said the case was proved to his satisfaction, and he ordered the defendant to pay a fine of 10s. A PICTURE OF Low LIFE IN LANCASHIRE.—On Mon- day, at Leigh, Alfred Gregory, 28 years of age, was charged with stealing a watch, value 455., the property of William Briggs, chimney sweeper, Redford Leigh. On the 6th of May the prisoner eloped with the prosecutor's wife, and he was apprehended a week ago at Oldham, where the pair were living together. Briggs in his evidence said prisoner had been several times at his house to tea. When his wife, who was 20 yearryounger than himself, eloped with Gregory, she took with her the watch and £2 in money. He found his wife on her return at the house of the prisoner's mother. In reply to Mr. Taylor, who appeared for the prisoner, wit- ness said that on the day his wife eloped they had been at a funeral, and at tea afterwards prisoner sat near his wife— (laughter)—and he did not see them afterwards. He made a present of the watch to his wife, but he did not intend her , to run away with it.—(Laughter.) She had been attending. the Salvation Army meetings, and prisoner made her ac- quaintance there, and afterwards continually "haunted her."—Emily Wright Briggs, wife of the prosecutor, who is a woman 28 years old, said she was a weaver. One even- ing, as they came from a Salvation Army concert, prisoner asked her if she was "spoken for," and she replied, "Yes, and paid for." (Laughter.) He then said he had fallen in love with her, and that if she would go with him he would make her a better husband than Old Billy.— (Laughter.) Afterwards he stopped her several times when she was coining from work. They ultimately eloped, and she pledged the watch in Oldham.—Withont bearing the defence the Bench dismissed the ease.

A cotton mill near Radcliffe, belonging to Messrs. Tootal, Broadhurst; Lee, and Co., was destroyed by fire on Monday night. The loss is estimated at £.5,000. About 350 opera- tives are thrown out of work. . _ _ .

The Cambridge Mathematical Tripos list roe read out en Monday, the senior wrangler being Mr. William Welsh, of Jesus College, a native of Edinburgh, who had already gained honours on both sides of the border. Another theatre has had a narrow escape from destruc- tion. Early on ,Sunday morning the stage and stage machin,ry of the Liverpool Royal Court Theatre were nearly consumed by fire. By great exertions on the part of the firemen the flames were prevented from extending to the body of the theatre. _

Miss Jessie Tanton left Bideford by the early mail train to superintend a business at rorrington, on Saturday, as was her daily custom. On the train reaching Torrin.zton, only her hat and basket were found in the compartment which slie entered at the Bideford station. Her body was subse- quently discovered in the river near the railway bridge at Handcross.

In expectation that the Prince of Wales will content to visit Preston to take part in laying the first stones of the New Free Library and Museum, a special committee has been appointed by the Corporation to visit Bradford this week to see the nature of the arrangements there. It is stated that if the Prince comes there will be a great gathering of Freemasons. The Guild festivities will last a week. On Tuesday morning a house in Cunliffe-street,Chorley, was demolished, and several others were damaged, through an explosion of gas, which is supposed to have escaped from the mains in front of the premises. There were several persons in the houses at the time, all of whom escaped injury in a marvellous manner except one man, and he was not very seriously hurt. At Halesowen, oa Monday, Henry Hall, blacksmith, was committed for trial for poisoning trout in a stream in the Manor Abbey. Large quantities of fish have been poisoned in streams in tie Worcestershire district Isy chloride of limo being thrown into the waters. Prisoner and two others were seen to throw chloride of lime in the stream, and the fish then came to the sarface and were netted.

The Town Council of Bury St. Edmunds having re- quested the borough coroner to hold an inquiry respecting the fire which occurred in the town on Friday, that official called a jury together without formal summons on Saturday afternoon, and said he had no power to hold an inquiry on oath, nor to crlnpel any one to give evidence, no lives 'hav- ing been lost. The jary, however, requested him to go on with the inquiry privately. The town-clerk observed that £35,000 worth of property had been destroyed in Bury by fire within the last six months.

DANGEROUS POACHERS.—At Burslem, on Tuesday, James Pillington, who had been handed over to the Burs!ern police authorities by the Wigan police, was committed to the Staffordshire assizes on a charge of night poaching and threatening to shoot a keeper named Pass, on the estate of Sir Lionel Pilkington, near Trentham, with five other poachers. Pass discovered them poaching with guns, and they threatened to blow a hole through him if he advanced. To save his life he therefore bad to let them go, but the prisoner was afterwards identified. ANNIVERSARY OF WATERLOO—Sunday being the anni- versary of the battle of Waterloo, which was fought on June 18, 1815, the usual ceremony of decking the colours with laurel was observed in every regiment throughout the British army which took part in the memorable battle. Only one survivor of Waterloo remains in Chelsea College as an in-pensioner. His name is John Mackie, and he served in the 42nd Highlanders (the Black Watch). He is 97 years of age, and, notwithstanding his great age, retains all his faculties. There are, however, several other survivors, out- pensioners, in various parts of the country. SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDENT.—A shocking accident has •occurred at Horwich, near Bolton. It having been de- cided by Mr. Adam Mason to recommence the working of the cealpit in Green-lane, which had long been stopped through flooding, two men named Henry Harrison and Wm. Worall were engaged on Monday in putting new connecting rods in the pit shaft. Whilst being lowered the engine gear- ing got out of order, and the cage descended with fearful velocity, dashing the unfortunate men to death. They were both married, and Worall leaves a large family. MARRIAGE OF THE EARL OF SHRERSBURY.—A long ex- pected matrimonial ceremony was (says the Derby Tele- graph) celebrated on Sunday. Charles Henry John Talbot, twentieth Earl of Shrewsbury, and fifth Earl Talbot (pre- mier English Earl) has conferred a name and title upon the divorced wife of Mr. A. E. Millar Mundy, of Shipley Hall. The marriage was conducted by special license, the officia- ting clergyman being a relative of the bridegroom's. It is said that the earl's rent audit (which, in the ordinary course of events, would have taken place in a few days) has been postponed, in order to facilitate a large gathering of tenants from the whole of the Shrewsbury estates. This occasion will be marked by what may be called wedding" festivities!'

NEW MARKET HALL FOR DARNVEN. A new market- house, which includes also offices for the Corporation; was opened at Darwen on Wednesday by Mr. F. W. Grafton, M.P. The buildings, which are very commodious and of handsome exterior, have been erected at a cost of about £25,000. The Marquis of Hartington had promised to per- form the inaugural ceremony, but, to the great regret of all interested, his Lordship was prevented, in consequence of baying to attend a meeting of the Cabinet, from fulfilling his engagement. The proceedings, which were marred by an incessant downpour of rain, included a procession, in which the local authorities and the various trade and friendly societies of the town took part; and hi the evening here was a binauet in the Co-operative DASTARDLY OUTRAGE.—The Press Association Carlisle correspondent reports that early OR Tuesday morning a dastardly outrsge was perpetrated at the village of Dalston, about five miles from Carlisle. Three sisters named Brown occupy a house in the village, and at an early hour one of them was awakened by a crash, and a smell of burning. She perceived a lighted fuse on the floor, and called to her nephew, who threw the dangerous objeet over the balus- trade, when it exploded in the lobby. Great damage was done to the walls, windows, and -doors by the explosion. The missile consisted of some tubing filled, it is supposed, with dynamite. It is surmised that. Miss Brown's window was mistaken for that of a neighbour, who had frequently been threatened.

CLEVER CAPTURE OF A HOUSEBREAYER.—At Bromley, on Monday, Mr. R. B. Berens had before him a daring case of housebreaking by a ticket-of-leave man, named George Miles. It appeared,that at an early hour on Saturday morning James Divall, who lives at Sheepcote Farm, left the house on business, and locked up the premises. Returning about half-past ten, he unlocked the door, and on going into his bedroom he saw the prisoner, who was wearing a suit of his clothes, and his silver watch, chain, and pencil case. The prisoner, with the greatest nonchalance, said, " Good morn- ing; I suppose you did not expect to see me ? " Divall replied that he did not, and requested the prisoner t 9 take off the clothes. This he did, and when he was undressed, the prosecutor called for assistance at the door, and the pri- soner was captured. He was committed for trial.

EXTRAORDINARY DRATH OF A GENTLEMAN AT SOUTHPORT. —On Saturday evening an extraordinary occurrence took place at Southport. It appears that between five and six o'clock a young gentleman, named Giles Thurnher, residing in Virginia-street, was partaking of a glass of refreshment in Our House beerkonse, Queen street, in company with a young man named Sutcliffe, when he rose from his seat for the purpose of crossing the room to speak to a frienJ, when he caught Sutcliffe's leg and fell. He cried out, and on an examination being made it was found that he had dislo- cated his ankle. He was at once removed home, and Dr. Smith and the house surgeon from the infirmary called in. Steps were immediately taken to set the injured limb, but from some cause or other the young man died between seven and eight o'clock. ANNIVERSARY OF THE BATTLE OF WATERLOO.—SIMday being the anniversary of the battle of Waterloo, which was fought on June 18, 1815, the usual custom of decking the colours with laurel was observed in every regiment through- out the British army which took part in the memorable battle. The subaltern doing duty with the detachment of the Ist battalion of the Coldstream Guards which mounted the "Queen's Guard " at St. James's Palace in the morning carried the laurel-decked colours from Chelsea Barracks to the guardroom at St. James's. The anniversary falling on a Sunday, the band of the regiment played a selection from the oratorios in place of the usual operatic selections performed during the changing of the guard. Very few survivors of the engagement remain, and only two pen- sioners who served under the Iron Duke are at present in Chelsea Hospital. The hearse which conveyed the remains of the Duke of Wellington from Apsley House to their last resting place in St. Paul's Cathedral was decorated with laurel and irnmortelles. Tha LORD MAYOR OF LONDON AND TUE PROVINCIAL MAYORS—On Saturday evening the Lord Mayor of London entertained at a banquet in the Mansion House the mayors of England and Ireland and the provosts of the principal cities and towns in Scotland, to the number of over 360. The Prince of Wales was present, and in replying to the toast of his health His Royal Highness expressed his grati- fication at meeting so many of the representatives of the cities and towns of the kingdom, and took the opportunity of asking them to use their influence in furthering the scheme for the establishment of the Royal College of Music, a subject in which he felt the greatest interest. The Lord Provost of Fdinburgh, the Lord Mayor of Dublin, and the Mayor of Liverpool, in responding for the Scotch, Irish, and English municipal representatives, expressed their entire approval of His Royal Highness's scheme for the better cultivation of musical art. On Monday there was a ball at the Mansion House. THE limn CHURCH SURPLUS AND THE ARREADS BILL. —A Treasury minute, dated June 16th, was issued on Tues- day with the Parliamentary papers. To it Mr. Gladstone gives an outline of the financial measure required by the Arrears Bill. The permanent income of the Irish Church Fund is estimated at £293,000, en which the present annual charge amounts to £515,000. There are besides additional charges and repayments to consider, but Mr. Gladstone pro- poses to make certain alterations, spreading the instalments over longer periods. Mr. Gladstone reminds the board that, in preparing his Arrears Bill, he estimated the cost to the Government at £2,000,000, of which £1,500,000 might pro- bably be defrayed out of the Irish Church Fund. Careful examination encourages the expectation that the fund, care- fully administered, may suffice to meet the.whole demand. The Consolidated Fund must only be drawn upon, under the Arrears Bill, when the board is satisfied that the Church Fund cannot afford further aid. Mr. Gladstone promises to ask Pailiament in the forthcoming Public Works Loan Bill to empower the Treasury to borrow £2,000,000 for the pur- pose of the Arrears Act, issuing bonds secured on the Church Fund and guaranteed by the Treasury ; the arrangement to commence NOM the next financial year, Their lordships have accepted the scheme.
It is announced that the contributions to the Wesleyan Methodist Thanksir,iying Fund amount to £30`3„590 103. 61._

On Thursday night, George Stewart, aged 24, a g,,oods guard on the Glasgow and South-Western Railway, while crossing, the line at Eglinton-street station, Glasgow, was knocked down by an engine and killed on the spot. At the Circuit Court of Justiciary, at Glasgow, on Wed- nesday, Andrew Kerr was s.entenccd to 15 months' imprison- ment for having stolen sums amounting to £505 while he acted as sub-agent for the branch of the Commercial Bank of Scotland in Trongate, Glasgow. On Wednesday Margaret Tate, the wife of a Bradford fish- monger, murdered her youngest child, a girl a year and a half old, by cutting her throat with a large fish knife, and then made a desperate attempt to destroy her own life with the same weapon. The woman was removed to the infir- mary, where she lies in a precarious condition. It is stated that for three months she has been in a despondent state of mind.

THE EGYPTIAN CRISIS AND THE PEACE SOCIETY.—The -committee of the Peace Society on Wednesday issued an address to its members deprecating the policy of intervention in Egypt, and alleging that the presence of European ships of war at Alexandria, by aroysing the jealousy of the native population, has led to the outbreak of violence, during which many lives have been sacrificed and panis spread throughout the country. Early on Thursday morning, a large portion of the shuttle and bobbin works of Messrs. Irvin and Sellers, Preston, was destroyed by fire. The flames were seen shortly after twelve o'clock, and the brigade was soon on the spot, but the fire spread very rapidly, and considerable damage was done before it could be extinguished. FATHER AND SON DROWNED.—lnformation reached Glas- gow on Thurday of the drowning in Loch Indaal, Islay, of a man named James Munro and his son, a lad of 17. The Munros, who were visitors from Glasgow, went out on the loch in a small boat to lift their fishing lines, and the boat seems to have capsized, as it was afterwards discovered floating bottom up. The bodies have not yet been recovered. Mr. Munro is described as a wood merchant.

A divorce case, which came before Sir James Hannen on Thursday, resulted in the injured husband not only obtain- ing a decree nisi with costs, but also damages to the extent of £5,500. The case was one in which the co-respondent, Dr. Hoare, was the leading medical man of the district, and was a personal friend of Mr. Stenning, a solicitor practising in Maidstone, whose wife -he attended professionally. The doctor's wife died in 1881, and in October of the same —nr an improper intimacy was formed between him and Mrs. Stenning, with whom he ultimately eloped. The lady by a post-nuptial settlement had an income of £2OO a year, so that considering all the circumstances of the case the damages are not excessive. THE HOME SECRETARY AND THE LICENSING BILL.— An influential deputation, including many members of Parliament, had an interview with Sir W. Harcourt on Wednesday to urge the desirability of introducing at the ' end of the session a Suspensory Licensing Bill, to prohibit the granting of any additioral licences for the sale of iutosi- eating liquors until the Government were able to bring for- I ward a general measure dealing with the whole subject I Sir JOSEPH N. PEASE, M.P., introduced the deputation; and in reply the HOME SECRETARY stated that he fully ap- preciated the importance of the subject. He would care- fully consider the representation which bad been made to him, and would on a future day communicate to SIR J. PEASE and the members present as to the course which the Government might determine upon. Considerable commotion was created at Accrington, on Wednesday, on the news becoming known that an elopement had taken place. The parties were a young woman of about twenty, of prepossessing appearance, and a marricd man of about thirty. It appears that the man has been separated from his wife for some years, has one child, and worked at a printworks at Church, near Accrington; while the woman followed the occupation of a weaver in the same locality. The elopement took place from the house of the female run- away's parents, at Antley, an outlying portion of Accring- ton, and both departed with their luggage hr a back en- trance, and took train to Manchester on Wednesday. The male absconder put in an appearance on Saturday to effect the elopement, but the final arrangements not being com- plete, it was postponed. A SEVERE CRITICISM OF MR. COWEN, M.P.—The following appear gin the paper -Outlook:—" Joseph Cowen, M.P. for Newcastle is a good popular speaker, but shows the very poorest political judgment, and is rapidly becoming a public nuisance. On Sunday, the 11th inst., he orated in Hyde Park to a crowd of the lowest of the people, assailing the powers that be, and taking the part of the incorrigibles in Ireland. Not one even of those Radical members who have been trying to enfeeble the Government measure for the prevention of crime stood by Mr. Cowen. But he probably persuade shimself that he, with his Sunday mob, knows much better what ought to be done than all the men of position and education in the empire. He must have some fine qualities to have won the favour of the Newcastle con- stituency, bat he is a dead failure in the political arena, and has killed himself by self-conceit, and by peevish be- haviour to the Prime Minister." Loss OF A LIVERPOOL STEAMER AND 20 HANDS.—On Tuesday the owners of the screw steamer Escambia, of Liverpool, received a cable message from San Francisco announcing the total loss of that vessel. The first telegram was quickly succeeded by another to the effect that all hands were lost. The Escambia was a vessel of 21.50 tons register, and left San Francisco en her voyage for England. She foundered suddenly outside the Heads, and about five I miles only from port. The Escambia was under the corn- mand of Captain Purvis, and had a crew of 30 hands. The wreck is also reported of the steamer Virago on her voyage from Hull to Constantinople. Her crew of 40 hands are all lost. The cargo was valued at .540,000. The Liverpool .owners of the steamer Escambia received a cablegram on Wednesday morning from San Francisco, an- nouncing the safety of the captain, engineer, cook, and steward of the vessel. The steamer was literally engulfed by the gigantic breakers, and taleen bodily down. It is be-', believed that over 20 persons perished by the disaster,includ- ing one passenger. The British and African Steam Navigation Company's Royal mail steamer Malemba, Captain F. H. Herbert, has arrived at Havre from the West Coast of Africa. She brings information of an encounter between a party of blue jackets and other British troops and the natives in the vicinity of Sherbro, resulting in, it is said, the killing of some 200 natives and the wounding of some of the British. The advices brought by the last arriving West African mail steamer at Liverpool stated that Governor •Havelock, in the Colonial steamer Prince of Wales, accompanied by Her Majesty's ship Foam, had gene up to Sherbro for the purpose of punishing some offending natives. It now appears that owing to the shallow watet the Foam could only proceed as far as York Island, some ten miles from Marti°, where the offending natives lived. A detachment of 50 blue jackets from the Foam, together with 25 Sierra Leone armed police, and 15 of the Bonthe people, proceeded to Martio in steam launches, having with them the rocket apparatus for operating against the enemy. The natives had evidently got word of the attack, and on the arrival of the British troops the natives were lying waiting in the Purro Bush. As soon as the British troops got within 50 yards of the spot the natives opened fire upon them, wounding several. The fire was re- turned, and in a short time a general engagement took place. The natives ultimately fled, but not, it is said, before about 200 of their comrades had been killed. MR. GLADSTONE AND THE SCOTCH FARMER'S ALLIANCE. —On Wednesday, a deputation from the Scottish Farmers Alliance waited upon Mr. Gladstone to present a memorial setting forth the demands of the Scotch farmers with respect to land legislation. Mr. Barclay, M.P., who introductd the deputation, said tho Alliance consisted of 7,000 members, and among the deputation were representatives from nearly all the counties in Scotland. The Alliance had arisen spon- taneously among the farmers owing to the extremity of the position in which they found themselves. This extremity was due partly to the bad seasons of recent years, to low prices' and to a great extent to the absurd conditions under which the farmers endeavoured to carry on the cultivation of the land. They urged upon the Government the extreme desirability of proceeding at once with the reforms required, not only in the interest of the farmers, but the landlords and the community at larg.e. Mr. Gladstone, in reply, said throughout the whole body of farmers in Scotland as well as in England there prevailed a strong conviction, which was shared by the Government, ot the necessity of legislation, but the condition of the House of Commons at the present moment was such that it was impossible under present cir- cumstances to do justice to the farmers or anybody else. He should be deceiving them if be told them that he saw his way to Government legislation this year. The country was addressing its mind to the settlement of procedure, and that was the main ground of his hopes that the House of Com- mons would be led to deal with it effectually. A "CONFESSION" OF THE HARPURTIEY MURDER.—LatO on Tuesday night a man, under the influence of drink, gave himself in custody at Leeds, stating that he was the mur- derer of Sarah Jane Roberts, a domestic servant, who was killed at Harpurhey in January, 1880. The self-accused prisoner gave the name of William Nightingale Thomas, and described himself as a native of Manchester, where, he said, his friends resided. On Wednesday morning he was in- formed of his confession, and he then said he remembered nothing of it. He was taken before a magistrate, however, and as the police naturally wished to make inquiry into the , matter a remand was asked for and granted. A description of the prisoner, with a statement of his confession," was prepared and transmitted to the police at Manchester. Mr. Superintendent Bent, of the county constabulary—who after the murder directed the efforts which were made to trace

the criminal—had not, down to Wednesday evening, re- ceived any communication from Leeds. Information of the arrest had, however, been brought under his notice through the medium of the evening newspapers, but the facts de- tailed do not create the impression that Roberts's murderer has at length been found. The man now under arrest is altogether unknown to the police of Manchester, and the officers having the best knowledge of the case do not attach any weight to his statement, which, according to the pub- lished accounts, betrays no such knowledge of detail as would be possessed by the murderer. Further information will no doubt be forthcoming, but there is ample reason to believe that the " confession" will be akin to similar state- ments made from time to time since the _murder by indi- _ . . .

viduals seeking cheap notoriety. From further inquiries which have been made, we learn that no importance what- ever is attached by the Manchester county police authorities to the " confession " made to the Leeds police on Tuesday evening. The man in custody does not appear to know even the name of the murdered girl, and ether circumstances he related are not in accordance with the ascertained facts. The prisoner, William Nightingale Thomas, has since stated I that he does not know where Harpurhey is. In the course of a few days he will probably be released‘

BROKEN-HEARTED CETEWAYO.—k HI u e boo k on South African affairs was issued on Tuesday. Sir Henry Bulwer, writing to Lord Kimberley on May 13,h, points out that the permission given for Cetewayo to visit England has given rise to intrigues for his reetorat ion, and produced an uneasy feeling throughout Zu:uland. In consequence of the Governor's representations, Cetewayo was informed that his visit was indefinitely pestponed. The ex-King thereupon wrote to Sir Hercules Robinson asking that his letter might be shown to the Queen. lie says he is at a loss to know why this pain is caused him. He has done no harm. He will never trust white men again, as their promises have all been broken. The large deputation recently des,patched from Zululand convinces bim teat the majority of hi S people wish him back. "If he is found dead" he says, " they will know he died of a broken heart." DEATH OF A FRENCH MILITARY VETERAN.—The death is announced of General de Cissey, a well-known veteran in • the military service of France, and a soldier who succeeded in corning out of the Franco-German war with an un- tarnished name and reputation. General de Cissey was in his seventy-second year, having been born at Paris in 1810. He worked his way up from the grade of lieutenant, and he put in 30 years laborious service before he received the rank of general, seeing during that period much fighting in Algeria and the Crimea. 'ln 1870 the late general had the misfortune bo be with the besieged Metz army, whose capitu- lation formed such a disgraceful chapter in the history of that epoch. De Cissey, however, did not suffer in name from this fact, as he strongly opposed the capitulation, and fought with distinctien at the Battles of Borney, Bezonville, and St. Privet. He was sent after the capitulation as a prison& of war to Germany' and on returning to France he was made Minister of War by M. niers. He resigned in 1873 along with his fellow Ministers, but was again in office in 1874 and 1875, during a portion of which time lie was nominally Premier. A few months ago the aged soldier's name was dragged into the law courts in connection with what was known as the Jung scandal., Though super- annuated at the time, the general subsequently succeeded in clearing his name of the base charges imputed to him. TERRIBLE SCENE IN MINNESOTA. The New fork Herald of the 10th inst. reports a terrible scene at Perham, Minnesota, on the previous day. A lad named Tribbets was in custody on two charges of murder, and in regard to which he had made a full confession. The youthful mis- creant appears to have been much given to reading the "trashy literature with which Western homes are flooded," and be had waylaid and murdered two men in the woods near Perbarn, having a "good time " afterwards with the booty he obtained. He seems to have been an irreclaimable villain, although only 15 years of age, and when he was arrested and taken to Perha:n a crown of men determined that he should be lynched at once. They broke into his cell, dragged him out, and hanged him on a telegraph pole on the railway. The lynching was witnessed by a consider- able crowd, who were of the opinion that Tribbets had been justly done to death, and there is no probability that the persons who committed the lawless act will be punished. THE FINANCIAL POSITION OF NEW ZEALAND.—A tele- gram from Wellington states that the Hon. A. Atkinson, Colonial Treasurer, made his financial statement in the Legislative Assemby on Saturday. The revenue for the last financial year amounted to £3.800,000, or £174,500 above the estimates. The actual expenditure was £3,610,000, or £77,000 below the estimate. The customs realised £125,000, stamp duty £ll,OOO, and the depasturiog license £56,750 above the estimates. The sut plus at the close of the finan- cial year was £215,000. The Treasurer estimates the revenue for the current year at £3.900.000, and the expen- diture at £3,700,010, including temporary charges amount- ing to £lOO,OOO, thus leaving a sui plus, including balance for last year, of £258,000. Of this sum £170,000, derived from the sales of land, will be appropriated to local public works. The gross revenue from railways last year was £884,000, and the net revenue £368,500, yielding nearly four per cent. on the capital expended. The railway revenue for next year is estimated at £940,000. There is a large increase in savings' bank deposits and in the number of de- positors. The total deposits amount to over £1,500,000, and the unexpected balance of former loans to £024,000. It is proposed to borrow £3.000 000, which is to be raised at the rate of not more than £1,000,000 per annum, and to be expended on specific railways and other works, which will be decided upon before the money is borrowed. The public debt on March 31 amounted to £31,400,000, and the annual sinking fund was fixed at £2,260,000. SERIOUS STATE OF ZULULAND. COMMENCEMENT OF CIVIL WAR. Serious disturbances have occurred in Zululand. The Abarpalusti tribe who were attacked by Oham some months since have made two raids in retaliation. Several lives were lost and cattle carried off. Undabuku, Cotewayo's brother, has also attacked the appointed chief Urribibu, with the assis- tance of the other membeie of the ex-King's family. In consequence of these disturbances the other appointed chiefs are arming, and the people generally are alarmed. It is not known yet whether these raids are part of an organised demonstration in favour of Cetewayo, though it is suspected. The last communication from the British Resident, dated the 13th, expressed some hope of preventing a general out- break. The situation, however, is very serious. A correspondent says :—"lf the English Itovernment relaxes its grasp en Zululand, by restoring Cetewayo or recognising Undabuku, it may expect to encounter worse trouble than ever in South Africa. The more it gives up, the more the Zulus will demand. Nothing short of a firm hold upon the country will save bloodshed and avert disaster." The Bishop of Natal, in a recent letter, says:—" I am sure that if the constant prayer of the Zulus for the restora- tion of their King is trifled with there will be bloodshedding on a large scale in Zululand. I think I mentioned that the recent deputation came without arms, having left, their asse- gais and knobkerries of their own accord in Zululand. I have sent by the Zulus £2O for the famine, which it is feared will be very bad in Zululand. This brings the Zululand Relief Fund almost to an end." , A Standard Durban telegram save :—The reports giving an account of the disturbances in Zululand are greatly ex- aggerated. Of course affairs are in an unquiet condition there. Nobody doubts that. Everybody who is in the least degree acquainted with the country snows, and has long known, that it is inevitable that such disturbances must result from a settlement like that which was carried into effect by Sir Garnet IVolseley. It is but natural that some one or two of the strongest chiefs should strive for predomi- nance. DRAMATIC SUICIDE OF TWO YOUNG LADIES NEAR .VIENNA. It is understood that at Wednesday's Cabinet Council important decisions were arrived at in regard to the Egypt- ian question, but it is hoped that it may not be necessary to take any active steps before the result of the Conference becomes known. Further pressure was brought to bear upon the Sultan, on Wednesday, to induce him to nominate a Turkish representative, but without avail; and the meeting will accordingly take place without the Porte being repre- sented. In Egypt the situation is practically unaltered. A new ministry has, however, been formed as follows : Raglaeb Pasha, President of the Council of Ministers and Minister for Foreign Affairs • Ahmed Rashid Pasha, Minister of the Interior •, Arabi Pasha, Minister of War ; Abi Ibrahim Pasha, Minister of Justice ; Mahrnud Falaki Pasha, Minister of Public Works; Sulieman ' Pasha Abaza, Minister of Instruction ; and Hassan Pasha Cheree, Minister of Worship. The chief features of the programme of the new ministry have been foreshadowed. It promises that the Sultan's fir- mans shall be upheld, and respect shown to all international • engagements. A general amnesty is to be granted to all excepting those actually concerned in the recent distur- bances at Alexandria, who are to be judged according to the laws of the country. All communications between the Con- suls-General and the Government are henceforth to be made through the Minister for Foreign Affairs only. A corres- pondent telegraphing from Alexandria early on Wednesday morning, gives cerrency to a report that at least five of the new Ministers are not favourable to the military rigime created by Arabi Pasha. No confidence is felt in the pro- fessions of the New Ministry, and the flight of foreigners consequently continues. From Cairo we have the same reports of the "continued flight" of Europeans from the city and the adjacent country, and thousands are being carried away from Alex- andria in any shipping that can be provided. At Cairo it is said that the National party are showing hostility to , Dervish Pasha, and that they will fight to the last against any "occupation," whether Turkish or European. From Alexandria it is reported that 32,000 Europeans have fled from the Nile Valley, and that as many more are awaiting the means of transport. Sonut alarm has been caused at Ismailia by the appearance of large numbers of Bedouins near the Canal. which is quite unguarded. Dervish Pasha has urged the Khedive to return to Cairo with the view of reassuring the panic-stricken population, but it is extremely unlikely that Tewfik will voluntarily withdraw himself from such protection as the combined fleets can afford. There has been no fresh outbreak, but Mr. Cookson is urging all British subjects to leave the country. Only 300 remain, of whom one-third are Englishmen. A telegram from Constantinople which gives the latest news from the Turkish capital with reference to Egypt reads like a grim jest. It states that Dervish Pasha reports to the Sultan that the state of things in Egypt is quite satis- factory, that Ourabi Pasha diligently obeys the orders of the Khedive, and that a conference is therefore unnecessary. In view of the despatches from Cairo and Alexandria this despatch is intelligible only on the supposition that Turkey has determined to prevent the meeting of the Con- ference by any means. The rejection of the Conference by the Sultan was placed beyond question by the remarks of Said Pasha to an English interviewer. The Turkish Premier complained strongly of the intervention of the Western Powers, and said they would crown the edifice of error if they landed a force in Egypt. At Portsmouth there are evidences of preparation for the conveyance of troops to Egypt, though no doubt the points that would be occupied would be for the protection of the Suez Canal only. Sir E. Malet is suffering at Alexandria from fever and dysentery, and Sir A. Colvin is acting temporarily as Consul-General in Egypt. Mr. Cookson has recovered from the injuries he received in the riot, but is still confined to the house.

From Alexandria it is now explicitly stated that the out- break was organised by the Prefect of Police, a "creature " of Ourabi's, and it is added, as showing the extent of the slaughter, that already the bodies of 310 Europeans have been cast up by the sea, into which they were thrown after the massacre. . . .

The Lord Mayor of London has received the following telegram from Dr. Mackie, consular surgeon at Alexandria: —"Thousands and thousands of poor Christian families are fleeing from Egypt, leaving all, and will be destitute. Would you think proper to organise a small fund for present help and future need of every nationality and Jews ? ' The Lord Mayor says the news from the at only too fully confirms the state of distress among European and other fugitives, and it will be for the English people to say whether any and what steps should be taken to meet the emergency. Any practical suggestion that may be made by those acfplainted with the East and with the emergencies of the situation will be acted upon. On receipt of a letter from Earl Granville offering a subscription of MOO, and enclosing a telegram from Sir E. Malet, the Lord Mayor has opened a subscription for the relief of refugees arriving at British or Maltese ports, and has himself given a donation of fifty guineas. In all probability the movement thus liberally begun will be continued in the same spirit. Unfortunately, Sir E. Malet's telegram leaves no doubt as to the necessity for the fund. He says the flight continues, and there is not only a necessity of immediate help, but also in the future of aid to recommence life for the poorer classes who have been ruined. The Khedive has expressed complete confidence in the goodwill and the power of England to protect him and restore order in the country. After all that has occurred in Egypt there are still persons who doubt whether there is any real reason for panic. Dr. Schweinfurtb, who knows Egypt well, and has just returned ,from a visit to Upper Egypt. writes to say that he every. where heard satisfaction expressed at the condition of things that has been brought about within the last two years. The people said, "We are now contented ; the Government is ten times better than it formerly was." As to what was pas- sing at Cairo, that was a matter with which they did not trouble themselves ; hence his belief is that Europeans would have done better to have gone into Upper Egypt than to Alexandria or abroad. He admits, however, that intel- ligent members of the Egyptian Chamber with whom he conversed were full of Socialistic ideas, that they all dreamed of a republic, and that they were partisans of Arabi Pasha. This materially weakens what he says as to the opinions of the common people in Upper Egypt. RUMOURED "SECRET CONVENTION."

The dambettist Paris gives " additional particulars" of a I secret Convention which it stated the other day had been I concluded between England and Turkey, according to I which British troops would, undercertain conditions, occupy the Suez Canal. The Paris says:—" This Convention was signed on Friday last by Lord Granville and Musurus Pasha. It was drawn up on June 8, and had since been shown to the German Government, which expressed its approval. The Convention is preceded by a protocol, of which the following is an analysis :—The English Cabinet starts from the theory that events may occur which may compel England to have recourse to an armed intervention, not only for the protection of the Suez Canal and of the lives and property of Her Majesty's subjects, but also with a view to restoring the prestige of the British flag. It therefore appears to the English Cabinet that as this neces- sity for an armed intervention on its part may arise at any moment, it is advisable to take the precaution of accu- rately defining it without loss of time, and, if it is pos- sible to arrive at a previous understanding on this point before the fait accompli. This entente would facilitate the ulterior negotiations. If the necessity for an intervention by arms does not arise, the Convention will be considered null and void." THE ATTITUDE OF THE SULTAN. -

There was no sitting of the Conference on Thursday at Constantinople, the German and Austrian representatives not being in possession of their instructions. The Sultan has ordered Dervish Pasha to inform Ourabi Pasha that he is perfectly satisfied with his attitude and the same com- mendation is bestowed upon the Khedive, who also receives an assurance that everything that is possible will be done to strengthen his authority. The English and French repre- sentatives in Egypt will hold no intercourse with Ragheb Pasha, who has issued -a kind of manifesto on assuming office as the ostensible Premier. The exodus of Europeans is decreasing, but there are no signs of a more assured feel- ing among the bankers and commercial men at Alexandria and Cairo. The banks are sending their specie out of the country, and some are forlifying their places of business in order to guard against a sudden assault. Bitter complaints are made of the constant insults to which Englishmen are subjected within sight of the fleet.

- - " ef June for the chief of the Executive to make a statement as to the views of the Government with respect to the, measures promised, and this, Mr. Glad. atone did on Tuesday evening. From it we learn definitely that the County Government Bill, the London Corporation Reform Bill, the Bankruptcy 4,134 and the Criminal Code Bill are to be abandoned ier the present. The Irish Sunday Closing Bill is not allowed to expire, and if nothing more s;:e done with that measure it will at least included in the Expiring Acts Con- Bill. The important bills relating "" agriculture, introduced by Sir T. D. Acland, Mr. • Chaplin, and Mr. J. Howard, it is proposed to refer t° a Grand Committee of the House; and it has been finggeeted that the same course should be adopted *ith respect to the Scotch Bills en Entail and Educe.- ti°nal Endowments. The suggestion is a good one, alad will. doubtless be acted upon, at least we judge so the manner in which it has been received. If so tnay be useful as showing how the system of having egnlar standing committees as proposed by Getvern- 44ent in their reform of procedure will wcrk. We Ste glad to learn it is the intention of the Government t° Persevere with the Corrupt Practices Bill; but with roegatd to the other two bills of a cognate character— Which has for its object the partial diefranehise- iblkent of certain boroughs, and the other relating to amendment and continuance of the Ballot- Act- -4° final decision has been arrived at. We may be however, that the Ballot Act Continuance Bill 'VII become law. It is hoped, too, that the Floods revention Bill, which was only opposed on the reading by 18 members—erowing that its rnai plaell provisions are generally approved—may be -•es upon the statute book, though that is another of the ,Ineaeures upon which the Government have not at a definite decision. the work would be as great, it was estimated to entail an expenditure of but £622. But Mr. Kershaw thinks the Board will this year, or, at least, ought, to get more work done for £6OO than was performed last year for £l,OOO. If this is so, it judicates gross management by tke former Board, and shows that the ratepayers are not likely to be the losers by the infusion into it of a little "new blood." The Gas Committee has also made a reduction in their stiff. But it was, in my opinion, incontroyertily demonstrated by Mr. Thos. Handley, that these reductions will not cause a corresponding diminution in the rate. The total estimates amounted to £8,706 14s. 2d., £1,613 7s. 4d. below the year previous. So far this looks well. Last year, however, a 2s. 6d. rate, in consequence of empty property, kc., produced over £l,OOO less than was expended, and nearly £2,000 less than it should have realised. 1n face of these facts, and that since the estimates had been drawn up, a bill for £7OO had been received, Mr. Handley could not do less than ask again for a 2s. 6d. rate. Disagreeable duties are never easy to perform, and the Board at last decided to discuss the laying of a rate at a special meeting, when they will endeavour to make a reduction. The rates, truly, are heavy, and if they accomplish their purpose, consistently with a due regard for efficiency, they will earn the thanks of the overburdened ratepayers.

Like many other persons who are neither sportsmen nor betters, I travelled to Farnworth on Saturday to witness the athletic sports, and, I think, had my fair share of enjoy- ment. Were I a Dickens, or a Thackery, I might, for the edification of your readers, Mr. Editor, describe some of the peculiar characters of the "many sided" crowd which there assembled, but being myself, I shall not attmpt it. I wish simply to ask the use of issuing a prohibition against betting, when men, who are possessed of particularly rubicund countenances, were allowed to cry such intelligible phrases as "30 to 10 bar one "on the ground and "3 to 2 bar one." I feel constrained to admit that the officials, with this exception, conducted the sports in such a way as to leave no cause of complaint; but these practices, if per- mitted to continue, are likely to have a degrading influence. Englishmen are born with an innate love of out-door exer- cises, and do not wish athletic exhibitions to be lowered to the level of a mere betting ring. Many persons admit that they never saw betting so prevalent at Farnworth as it was on Saturday, and I trust the committee will, in future years, "put their foot on it." The inhabitants of Runcorn, after encountering some obstacles, have secured for themselves the means of attain- ing a higher intellectual development ; and having the means, they have only themselves to blame if they do not use them. The two thousand volumes which the Free Library will contain have no doubt been judiciously selected by the committee, who, in that comparatively small number, will have succeeded in covering a wide field of literature; and whatever may be the bent of an individual he will, I opine, find something to satisfy it. Much is heard now-a- days of counter attractions to the public-house, and many schemes are tried, but I cannot conceive of one more power- ful than a healthy taste for reading. And the way to culti- vate that taste is to provide ''good books, which one eminent writer has described as " the true Elysian fields where the spirits of the dead converse." I hope, therefore, that the in- auguration of the Free Litrary will mark the commence- ment of an era of intellectual and temporal advancement for the.people of Runcorn. Lawyers bills are so enigmatical that people who are so unfortunate as to receive them have given up trying to find a solution. Mr. Weller's knowledge of the law was confined principally to the proving of an "alley bi " ; but the mem- bers of the Wines Local Board have a fuller insight into the intricacies of the law. At the last meeting, Mr. Midwood, who evidently intends to act on Ingoldsby's capital'advice, to " take care of the rhino," brought to light something quite as extraordinary as lawyer's bills; and that was the taxing of theta. From Mr. Oppenheim the Boallbd received a bill for £635 tla. 4d. ; an in order to get a reduction on that amount, the Board forwarded the bill to the taxing master. That gentleman did tax the bill, which he reduced by es,, and called upon the Board to pay a fee of £5 for tin uenefits thus derived I Mr. Midwood thought this a great hardship upon the rateplyers, and no one will be inclined to disagree with him. The taxing master was certainly entitled to his fee for hi s services, htit upon the Board rested the responsibility ef Huang out to him what charges in the hill they deemed excessive. This they would seem to he:ee neglected, and Mr. Midwood sug- gested that - future a deputation should take the bills to the registrar to explain their objections to the charges. Some means ought decidedly to be adopted by which the ratepayers will not be caused to pay such a sum for such aft insignificant return.

A subject deeply affecting Mr. Jonea, the master of Dutton Workhouse, was brought before the Runcorn Guardians at their last meeting by Mr. Dansey, the Local Government Inspector. Regret that it should have been, broached is now unavailing; but it shows that the ikcal Government Board have on their orders rules which outrage all the feelings of a parent. Mr. Jones, who has a large 'family, is required to keep outside the house his children who have reached the age of 14, a request which, Mr. Norman observed, accom- panied by exclamations of approval, would not he tolerated by a single guardian or a member of the Local Government Board in the case of their own offspring ; while Mr. Rigby expressed his opinion of the matter in his usual facetious way by the remark that the Local Government Board were "tittle-tattling at every verse end." The reason for this extraordinary regulation is because certain irregularities have occurred in one or two instances, and the Local Government Board on the principle, I suppose, that "pre- vention is better than cure," make the rule apply to inno- cent and guilty alike. But in my opinion it is makins, the many suffer for the iniquities of the few, and I, with Mr. Hazlehurst, trust the Guardians will resist the proposal without regard to the money question. The telegraphic reports of Thursday's proceedings in Parliament show that Mr. Bradlaugh has not yet relin- quished his claim to take part in the proceedings at St. Stephen's. On the evening of the day stated he advanced towards the table with the view of presenting to the House a petition. The Speaker, amid a few cries of "Order," 'requested the bon. member to withdraw. The hon. member claimed the right to present a petition, but the Speaker held that as the hon. member had not been sworn he had no such right, and insisted upon his withdrawal. This the hon. member did. At the same time he again claimed his right. The incident did not occupy above a couple of minutes; but it may be this is only a prelude of what is to follow. Mr. Gladstone, in his statement as to the course of business, has made no allowance for another Bradlaugh debate; but I am inclined to think Mr. Bradlaugh is not likely to allow members to separate for their holidays without again remind- ing them of his presence, and again demanding that he be permitted to take the oath and his seat as the thrice chosen of Northampton. Mr. Parnell has been " interviewed " upon Mr. Davitt's scheme of "nationalisation of the land," and from the account of the interview which has been published I arrive at the conclusion that though Mr. Davitt claims Mr. Parnell and himself are at one on the land question, Mr. Parnell entertains a very different opinion. Mr. Parnell advocates a system of occupying ownership, which he argues was the original programme of the Land League. Mr. Davitt goes beyond the Land League programme, and urges a scheme of nationalisation of the land, which has been described as "barefaced robbery." Explain it away as Mr. Davitt may, there is a wide difference between Mr. Parnell and himself. Since his famous Liverpool speech, Mr. Davitt has not received the same consideration at the hands of his friends in Ireland, for the reason it is felt that he has gone too far. A Mr. Matthew Harris, a prominent Land Leaguer, writing to the Dublin Freeman, says :—" Mr. Davitt has done more damage to the cause of Ireland than a dozen Forsters with a dozen Coercion Acts at their backs could accomplish. At the very outset he struck a blow at the Nationalists in his letter to the Standard, and his answer to Mr. Forster's pamphlet was in the same strain. Mr. Davitt is misleading English public op- inion and outraging the feelings of Irish Nationalists through- out the world. His actions since his release are such as to cause discord and disunion throughout the whole Irish race." , Mr. Harris declares Irish landlordism compares favourably with the scheme of Mr. Davitt, and in denouncing Mr. Davitt's project the writer observes:—" If the six hundred thousand farmers (who with their families number over three millions of human beings) were to become tenants of the British Government Ireland might bid farewell for ever to her long cherished hope of becoming an independent nation. Our yoke is a heavy one. England can tax us at her pleasure, can disarm us at her pleasure, can imprison us ,at her pleasure- but if, in addition to this, we take Mr. Davitt's advice, and give her, through her Government, ab- solute ownership in the land, power over the poor man's turf bank, cabbage garden, potato field, why then we may I say, as they say when entering the abode ca the damned, 'Farewell hope.'" It is evident there is not the same unanimity in Home Rule or Land League circles now than there once was. .

In the House of Commons, on Monday, Colonel I. Blackbarne presented petitions in favour of the repeal of the Contagious Diseases Act from Warrington, Latchford, St. Helens, and Huyton Quarry. BRUNSWICK SUNLIT SCHOOL ANNIVERSA.RT, RUN- CORN.—On Sunday last, the annual school sermons were preached by the Rev. E. Lloyd Jones, of Rhyl. There were crowded congregations at each servic.-, especially in the evening, and the collections realised £4l 4s. sd. Special hymns and chants were sung by the choir and scholars in a manner highly gratifying to those who had undertaken their training. A service was also held in St. Paul's Chapel, on Tuesday evening, when the Rev. C. Garrett, of Liverpool, was the preacher. From the words " Thou, Lord, art a God ready to pardon," taken from the 17th verse of the 9th chapter of Nehemiah, the rev, gentleman preached one of his characterittic and soul-stirring sermons, drawing forth frequent exclamations from the large congregation which again filled the .sacred edifice. The scholars sang a number of hymns and chants so tastefully and creditably, that Mr. CI irratt desired to have the hymn, "Strike the harp of Zion," given on Sunday, repeated. His desire was acceded to, and also in two other instances. Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst officiated at the piano. The collectionq, including those made on Sunday, amounted to £6O.

UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES —Mr. James Bramwell, of Liverpool, preached the anniversary sermons of the Zion Sunday school, in the above church, on Sunday last, and there was a good congregation at each service. In the afternoon the Rev. Billington, of Run- corn, delivered an address to th a scholars on "Sunday school work," which contained many excellent suggesti ons. The singing of the scholars was an attractive part of the day's services. Besides special hymns, the scholars in the after- noon rendered in good style Fawcett's anthem "Infancy ;" and in the evening Handel's splendid chorus" And the glory of the Lord," with orchestral accompaniment. Mr. John Betney was the conductor. On Monday evening a miscel- laneous entertainment was given to a large audience. The Chairman, Mr. Warne, and the Rev. J. Billingtbn delivered short addresses, and a number of hymns and solos were sung by the choir. An interesting item in the evening's pro- gramme was a composition by Mr. James Walters, entitled "Changes since our last anniversary," which was recited by Miss Esther Robinson. Recitations were also given as follows :—" Little Katie's dream," Jane Summerbell ; "The child's first grief," Julia Springett ; "The voice of spring," Catherine Beasley; "Do what you can," Charles Perrin ; "The widow of Main," Wm. Warne; "Difficulties," Mar- garet Ann Forest; "Say your prayers in fine weather," Walter Mellor; "23rd Psalm," Francis R. Warne; " Early blest," Jessie Betney ; "The two crossing sweepers," William Warne; "A mother's love," Jane Warne; "If papa were ready," Thomas Perrin; "The voice of the stars," Ellen Perrin ;" On the death of a sister," Jessie Hughes. The total collections amounted to £2O is. 6d.

A WIDNES BIGAMY CARL—At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs. W. W. Pilkington and A Bright, Eliza Kerr, apparently about 40 years of age, who resided at Widnes, was charged on remand with feloniously marrying and taking to husband one John Horbinson, her lawful husband, John Kerr, being then alive.—Mr. Beesley appeared for the prisoner.—Thomas Thomson, tailor, 41, Westfield-street, St. Helens said he knew the prisoner, and her husband, John Kerr, Who was now in court. He was present at St. Simon's Church, Liverpool, on the 23rd Sep- tember, 1867, when John Kerr was married. The prisoner's maiden name was Eliza Roberts. Witness put up the banns at prisoner's and John Kerr's request. The marriage cere- mony was gone through in his presence.—John Jessop said be was parish clerk at St. Mary's Parish Church, Widnes, and resided at 26, Church•etrOt, in that town, 11e knew the prisoner, and a man named John Horbinson. On the 91st November, 1881, he was present at St. Mary's Parish Church, Widnes, when the prisoner was married to John Horbinson. Witness subscribed his name to the marriage register as one of the witnesses, and at the same time he gave a copy of the marriage certificate to the prisoner. The ceremony was ner- formed by the Rev. W. H. Duggan,--john Clarkson said he was a police sergeant stationed at Widnes. At half-past three o'clock on the morning of the 14th June he apprehen- .. • ,• dea toe prisoner at John Horhinson's residence, No. 5, Eleanor_ street, Widnes. When witness got in, prisoner said, "It is all right; I have been expecting you; am quite prepared. My husband turned me out, I am obliged to do something." Witness had a warrant for her apprehension, and he read over to her. Prisoner then produced the certificate (tnerked "A ") of her marriage to Horbinson, and gave it io him, re- marking that she was married to Horbinson. Witness had seen the certificate (mafged "B ") pro:luced, and on the 16th instant he WCht to the Padilla Church, where he com- pared it with the entry in thee register, and found it was a 'Jo copy of the marliage register recording the marriage between her and icerr in 1867. On the same day he com- pared certificate marked "A," and found that it was a true copy of the marriage certificate of a marriage having taken place between her and Horbinson. After witness had read the warrant over to the prisoner, she replied "It is all right." Prisoner, on being formally charged, said "I reserve my defence." She was then committed for trial at Liverpool, bail being accepted in one surety of £4O, or two of £2O. A WIDNES CHEMICAL MANUFACTURER T. TUB SHEFFIELD AND lel ID LAND RAILWAY COMPANY. —On Friday, at the St. Helens County Court, before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, judge, the case of Francis Dickson, chemical manufacturer, Widnes, against the Sheffield and Midland Railway Company, was re-heard. Mr. A. L Riley, St. Helens, appeared for the plaintiff ; and Mr. Hamp, from the solicitors' office of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- shire Company, London-road, Manchester, represented the defendant committee. Plaintiff claimed £3 9s. 2d., the price of some speller dross, which he alleged had been lost on de- fendants' lines while being conveyed to his works at Widnes. Defendant had been served with notice to appear before the court some time since, but as they were unrepresented judg- ment for the amount claimed went in default, and costs were *added. An application had, however, Aince been made for a new trial, which his Honour granted. The claim was made up of two items. On the arrival of a consignment made on the 27th December, 1381, from Warrington to Widnes, by the Cheshire Lines Committee, it was found that 3cwt. 3qrs. 41bs. of the speller dross was missing • and on the 2ul January, 1882, in a consignment from Tinsley in Yorkshire, the weight was lcwt. 171bs. less than stated in the advice note. Plaintiff said he always settled his accounts for delivery of goods with the Sheffield and Midland Railway' Companies Committee, whom he now sued. Mr. Hemp contended that the wrong parties had been sued. In the one, case the contract was made with the Cheshire Lines Com- mittee,.which consisted of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshie Railway, the Midland Railway, and the Great Northern Railway, who were responsible for the whole journey; and in the other, the consignment from Tinsley was alone received by the• Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Company. The defendant committee was a distinct corporation, and not the receivers of the goods.— His Honour nonsuited, with leave to sue again. SERIOUS CHARGE AGA.INST A BEERHOUSE KEEPER.— A FATAL OBJECTION.—On Monday, at the Runcorn Petty Sessions, before Messrs. John Brundrit (chairman) and , Charles Reynolds, Sarah Abrams, keeper of the Blue Ball Inn, Friar-street, was charged that on the 7th inst., she did unlawfully permit her hotese to be the habitual resort of women of bad repute, allowing them to remain there a longer time than was necessary for the purposes of reason- able refreshment.—Mr. W. H. Linaker defended.—Superin- tendent Williamson said that in consequence of what took place at that court, he, on the 7th inst., directed P.S. Walley and P.C. Noden to watch the defendant's house. The Bench would hear from the evidence of the officers that during the time they were watching they saw no less than 10 women of bad character in the house, where they re- mained for a considerable period. Of course the Bench were aware the police had their duty to perform, and if such characters were allowed to remain in beerhouses for such a length of time, they might expect what would follow. Mrs. Abrams, he believed, was about to leave the house, but it was not the first time these had characters had assembled there, and she had been previously warned that she could not keep them there au unreasonable time • so that she could not plead ignorance of the law.—P.. Walley and P.C. Noden gave evidence of what they saw during their watch of two hours, and Inspector Hollingworth stated that abeut 9-30 he was informed of a disturbance at the Blue Ball. He proceeded there, and in the vault found five women of bad character, while in a room behind were three musicians, two other men and a woman. One woman seized a man's glass and drank the beer which it contained. —Mr. Linaker submitted that there was no case against the defendant. There had not been one word of evidence given referring to any other day but the 7th inst. The onus of proving that this was a house for the resort of women of bad character was upon the prosecution. They should have shown to the Bench that this house had on several previous occasions been an open resort for these women, to justify them in a conviction. Whether from forgetfulness he could not say, but the prosecution had neglected to prove this.— Superintendent Williamson said he must acknowledge that he had omitted to call evidence to prove his opening state- ment that the defendant had been several times eautioned about keeping these womeu.—Mr. Linaker remarked that the prosecution having closed the case could not now re- open it. —Superintendent Williamson: I never asked for that. I leave it with their worships.—After several minutes consultation with the clerk, the Chairman said the Bench had carefully considered the case, and they thought the ob- jection Mr. Linaker had taken was fatal to it, that the police had not shown that it was the habitual resort of women of bad character, although they had plenty of opportunity of doing so. The Bench thought Mr. Linaker quite right in taking the objection, and dismissed the case. I the House of Commons, on Wednesday, Colonel Ireland I3lackburne presented a petition in favour of the Vagrancy Bill from the Prescot Board of Guardians.

NEWTOWN 11lissiox eaußail, Rracconx.—On. Sunday last at this church two adults and five children, com- municants and workers in connection with the mission, were baptised. Formerly they were members of the Salvation Army. A CHILD SCALDED AT WIDNES.—A child named Jas. Tobin, two years of age, and whose parents reside at 26, Water-street, Widnes, was severely scalded on Tuesday. Whilst its mother was abseat from the kitchen, the child overturned upon its neck and shoulders a tin of boiling water. Under the care of Dr. McLennan, the child is now recovering.

GOOD TEMPLARY IT WIDNES.—The Samaritan Lodge, 1.0.G.T. paid a fratermil visit to the Star Lodge on Wed- nesday evening ; Bro. C. Webbe, W.C.T. presiding. Ad- dresses on temperance were delivered, and a number of songs and recitations contributed to the pleasure of the evening.

It will be seen from our advertising columns that the annual sermons on behalf of the Holy Trinity day schools, Runcorn, will be preached to-morrow in Holy Trinity Church, by the Rev. G. Bennett, who was formerly incumbent of the parish. VPIT OF STUDENTS FROM OWEN'S COLLEGE TO WIDNES.—The Tharsis Copper Works, Widnes, were on Tuesday visited by a number of students from Owen's College, Manchester. The different processes of the manu- ture were explained to them, and subsequently they lunched at the Central Hotel, returning to Manchester in the course of the afternoon.

FLAT SUNK NEAR WESTON POINT.-At midnight on Saturday, the fiat " True Briton," belonging to Messrs. Hill and Grundy, of Sankey Bridges, collided with the steam tug Gladiator, whilst sailing up the Mersey near Weston Point. Being laden with sand, the flat quickly sunk after being struck, but the men were taken on board a steamer. On Wednesday the flat was raised by chains, and was towed up the river to Sankey Bridges to be repaired. The bow had been stove in.

SINKING OF A FLAT AT IVlDNEs.—During the strong wind on Wednesday morning, a flat belonging to Mr. Thos Snape was overturned in the river at Widnes, and a hole being made in the bottom by some of, the caustic bottles, with which she was laden, the boat quickly sank. The young man who was in charge of the boat in the absence of the captAn, escaped from, drowning by means of a small boat attached to a flat. The owners succeeded in raising the vessel on Thursday. MAN FOUND DROWNED IN THE Loma AT RUNCORN. —On Wednesday, a lock tenter named Samuel Lewis found the body of a man floating in the Top Locks, Runcorn. The body was much decomposed, and apparently that of a man 40 years of age. He had dark hair, and " billygoat " whiskers. The dress he was wearing points to the conclu- sion that he was a boatman; but he had nothing in his pockets which furnishes any clue to his identity. He had on corduroy tronsers, dark vest, blue striped cotton shirt, and clogs. The inquest on the body was held at the Cemetery yesterday, and evidence in accordance with the above facts having been given, the jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned."

ACCOUNTS OF THE RUNCORN C AndiSSIONERS.—In another column is published the abstracts of the accounts of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners for the year end- ing the 25tb March last, from which it will be seen the Commissioners halm a b.tlance of £lB5 2s. 21. in their favour on the year's working. The general district rate of is. 91. in the £ realised £3,493 Bs' lid.; the market tolls £384 18s. 94., private imptovetherit tale £2l, and other receipts £256 Os. 7d.; the total income being £4,155 85. 3d."
