CAfiridi bE IN LANCA.SHIRB AND CHESHIRE.— Portions oi the townships of Edgeworth and Westhoughton, 10 ibis county, which have for some time been "infected places" within the mealVg of the Contag:ous Diseases (Animals) Act, are now declared by a Privy Council Order to be free from disease. The following places are, however, declared by an Order, dated the 20th inst., to be infected with foot-and-mouth disease, namely, the townships or por- tions of the townships of Worsley, Walmersley-cum-Shut- tleworth, Higher Booths, Royton, Crompton, Spotland, Castleton, Ashton-under-Lyne, and Birtle-cum-Bamford. The disease has appeared at Bredbury and Eaton (near Macclesfield) in the county of Chester, and those places are likewise proclaimed by an Order of the Privy Council. AN OLD WOMAN A SSILITLIND AT ASTON-BY-SUTTON.-- Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. S. B. Chadwick were on Wed- nesday engaged at the Runcoin Police Court, hearing a serious charge of assault against a teamsman named James Clarke, employed by Mr. Percival, farmer, Aston-by-Sntton It was alleged that the prisoner on Tuesday went to an old woman named Ann Rutter, and asked her why she was not with a gang employed in the fields. He was informed she was working in another part of the farm, when, with curses on his lips, he struck the poor woman on the head and face, and knocked her to the ground.—Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared for the prisoner, who pleaded guilt, and in suhmitting that a small penalty would meet the merits of the case, stated the prisoner had received great provocation from the old woman. Mr. Reynolds observed that the prisoner had pleaded guilty to a most serious charge, and would be fined 40s. and us. 6d. costs.

DITTON CATHOLIC COLLEOE.—Ditton Hall, former- ly the residence of Lady Bretherton, Stapleton, but for a number of years a Jesuit College, has lately undergone ex- tensive alterations. Early last year, the accaramodation being insufficient, it was decided to make an addition to the building, which it was decided should take the form of a dwelling-house for the students. The erection of the new portion was commenced last summer, and with the excep- tion of the furnishing is now completed. It consists of two storeys; is about 110 feet long by 52 feet broad; and the front of the building is ornamented with stone facings. The entrance hall, which is on the north side, opens into a cor- ridor which runs the entire length of the building, along which are the rooms for the students,-13 in all—each measuring 12 by 18 feet' On the second floor is another coiridor similarly fitted up. The skylights and windows are filled with stained glass. It will probably be autum before the students can take possession of the new building. RUNCORN AND THE SALT TRADR.—From the report of this company, which will be submitted to a meeting of shareholders in London, on Wednesday next, we learn that the works are making highly satisfactory progress. It is the intention of the company to convey brine from Mar- bury, near Northwich, to Runcorn Heath. At the latter place the reservoir to hold the brine is drawing near com- pletion; and the brine shaft at Marbury has been driven about three-fourths down, with every prospect when the ground has been penetrated to the requisite depth, of an abundant supply of brine. To convey the brine pipes are being laid from Marbury to Runcorn, and the tunnel under Beacon Hill, which is to con- vey the 9-inch pipes from the reservoir to Weston, is about half-done. The building for the forcing station at Marbury only requires the roof, and the cottages for the workpeople there are finished. As these works are likely to give a great Impetus to the trade of Runcorn, and promote in no small degree its commercial prosperity, it is pleasing to know that the whole of the work between Marbury and Weston will probably be finished in three or four months; when the works for the manufacture of salt will only remain to be constructed. These are being designed, and every means adopted for economical manufacture. Negotiations have already been commenced for the disposal of the brine. Wider developments of the scheme have been mooted, and there is some probability, we understand, of pipes being con- veyed under- the Mersey to Widnes, to supply with brine the chemical works there. The statement of accounts shows that 7,198 £lO shares have been issued, and £5 called up, realising, less £9.575 arrears of calls, £35,990. There have also been issued 2.250 shares fully paid up to vendor amounting to £22,500, and 416 shares paid up to contrac- tors amounting to £4,160; making with interest, &c., £53,259 95.2 d. Against this is to be placed purchase money under agreements £40,000; works, machinery. &c. £16,640; and other charges; amounting in all to £65,881 18s. 2c1.; leaving a balance of £12,622 9s. to be carried to the credit side of the balance sheet.

WIPE DESERTERS IN THE PEES= UNION.—At the Whines Petty Sessions on Monday—before Messrs. Hol- rook Gaskell, senr., and Holbrook Gaskell, junr.—Thos. Dudley, lately of St. Helens, was charged, in custody, with having on the 24th September last left his wife and four children chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union. On being taken into custody, prisoner gave a false name, but afterwards acknowledged be was the woman's husband. The total cost of the relief paid by the guardians in this case was £B, and they preferred to sacrifice the money and have the prisoner sent to gaol, so that his fate might be a warning to the many husbands in that neigh- bourhood who were inclined to adopt a similar course. The man was sent to gaol one month, with hard labour.—Henry Mizen was charged with a like offence. Mr. Hartley said that the prisoner deserted his wife and family on the 10th May. He had formerly worked at Messrs. Gaskell and Dea- con's, and earned 455. per week for a long time. The man and his wife had lived very unhappily together, but that was no reason why the Guardians should maintain his wife. Mr. Scannel, relieving-officer, was called to prove the case. The sum of £5 Bs. 6J. WAS owing by the prisoner, who said he was unable to pays the money, and was sent to gaol for one month.

;MEETING OF THE WIDNES SCHOOL
BOARD.

The monthly meeting of the members of the Widnes School Board was held in the Board Room, Victoria-road, on Thursday afternoon, when there were present : Mr. T. Sutton-Timms (in the chair), the Rev. T. Clarke, and Messrs. R. H. Davies, Robert Shaw, H. W. Deacon, W. Hart- land, and G. 11. Danby (clerk). TILE EDUCATION COMMITTEE. Mr. DEACON, on behalf of the District Education Com- mittee, r.,ported that during the month of May the number of cases summoned before the committee were 275, 70 of which were applications for payment of fees, and 205 for contravention of the Education Act. Fees were recom- mended to be paid in Gd cases. There had been 30 prosecu- tions before the magistrates, and a conviction was obtained in each case.

A BUTCHER'S ACTION AGAINST A RAILWAY COMPANY. Yesterday afternoon Mr. Hulton, judge of the Haslingden County Court, gave judgment in a case brought by the Accrington Butchers' Association against the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company for the recovery of the value of a sheep. The animal, with some others, escaped from a pen at Accrington just as it was unloaded from a truck. A butcher followed it with his dog, and the sheep ran down an embankment into a watercourse and was drowned.
The railway company contended that it was the
The CHAIRMAN: Certainly. Mr. Deecox: There are a great many questions I should ike to ask.
plaintiff's negligence that caused the lass of his sheep. His Honour held that the plaintiff was only trying to recover his property, and gave a verdict against the company for £2.

Mr. DAVIES was proceeding to explain some of the points of the proposed scheme, when Mr. SIIAW remarked that they could not carry it all in theit mind. He thought the committee ought to print the recommendation and scheme in the next notice of motions and then each member of the Board would have them be- fore him. Mr. DEAcoV said there was another point that might be taiga Would the denominational schools use the classes? The CHAIRMAN: Some may and some may not. The CLERK : That would he left open. Mr. DEACON Our own schools would not keep the classes going. The CLERK: The committee think they would, sir. The CHAIRMAN remarked that he thought the committee ought to have the scheme printed and laid before the mem- bers of the Board. If all the matter was read now they could not sufficiently remember all the details. Mr. DAVIES: The subject is a most important one. Would it be better for the whole Board to resolve itself into come tnittee ? The CHAIRMAN replied that he was going to suggest that it should when the scheme was brought before them. Mr. DEACON: I should like the school management to be able to tell us whether the denominational schools will use them or not, as it will make a great difference. The CHAIRMAN: We might consult with the managers of the denominational schools. If all the pupil teachers could be collected in one central school and taught together it would be much better than the present system. There is no doubt about it. _ _ _

A HOAX. Yesterday morning, about ten o'clock, two working men discovered a brown paper parcel which they believed to con- tain gunpowder within the railings surrounding the Ken- nington Vestry Hall, a large building in the south of London. They gave it to a policeman, who found that in- side the parcel there were several old cartridges, but no powder. The matter caused some excitement in the district, but the authorities declare the discovery to be a hoax. THE RUSSIAN GOVERNMENT AND THE OUTRAGES ON I'HE JEWS. A circular addressed by the Minister of the Interior to the Governors General is officially published, in which the latter are reminded of the Imperial order of May 3rd, relative to outrages against Jews. The Governors are enjoined in the strongest terms to take all possible measures against the re- currence of outrages, and intimates that the whole responsi- bility in such cases will fall upon Governors and officials under them charged with the prevention of outrages. The penalty of immediate dismissal from the public service with- out respect of persons or admission of extenuating circum- stances, will be incurred by any officials guilty of any negligence in the matter. On the suggestion of the CHAIRMAN the recommendation was withdrawn it being understood that it could be again brought forward at the next meeting of the Board. , • FINANCE. Mr SHAW reported, on behalf of the Finance Committee, that accounts amounting to £354 Os. 3,1. had been recom- mended for payment. Since their last report the sum of £2643 14s. sd. had been paid into the bank, including £l5O from the overseers on account of precept. He remarked that he was afraid they would have to ask for a mandamus if they could not get more money from the overseers. They had endeavoured to meet them in every way possible, and they had only asked for a sum sufficient to carry them over without any large surplus. He was sorry to say that the overseers had left them almost entirely without anything, and if they did not hand more over they would have to ask for a mandamus to compel them to let them have it. MEETINGS OF THE BOARD. In the absence of the Vice-Chairman, the CHAIRMAN moved—" That in order to meet the convenience of the mem- bers of the Board who wish to be away during the summer months, regulation 8 be suspended, so as to allow of the ordinary meetings of the Board being held in July on the first Thursday in the month, and in August on the last." The motion was seconded by Mr. Sneve, and carried. THE GOVERNORS OF FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL. The CLERK read the following communication :—" Mace- brook, Widnes, sth June, 1882.—Sir,—A vacency having occurred among the governors of Farnworth Grammar School, the filling up of which rests with your Board, I have to request that you will forward their nomination to me as soon as possible.—Your obedient servant, JAMES CROSS (chairman)." The CHAIRMAN briefly explained that they were entitled to appoint two governors of the Grammar School in ques- tion. They were at present represented by Mr. Brock. He intimated that it devolved upon the Board to appoint another member, and he proposed to bring forward a resolu- tion at the next meeting of the Board. ANOTHER KIND OFFER. The following letter was then read :—" Widnes, June 22, 1882.—My dear Sir,—Following your good example I shall be obliged if you will make it known to your Board that I shall be willing to pay half the school fees of those children who do not miss more than five of the total number of attendances possible during the present and next succeed- ing school years. The payments to be appropriated in the same way as defined in your letter.—Yours very truly, FRED. H. GOSSAGE.—T. S. Sutton-Timmies, Esq., Chairman of the School Board, Widnes." The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Gossage is very anxious to do what he can for education in Widnes, and that is what he pro- poses to do No doubt you will accept the favour. Mr. SHAW: I have great pleasure in moving that the best thanks of the Board be given to Mr. Gossage for his kind offer, and that it be accepted. The Rev. T. CLARKE : I second it. The motion was then passed, and the Clerk instructed to convey the thanks of the Board to Mr. Gossage. The CHAIRMAN remarked: He proposes to follow the same cgurse as I did as regards the payment of the fees, that is, give the parents half, and invest the ether half in accordance with the rules of the Board, so that the parents cannot withdraw the money. This concluded the business, and the Board adjourned.

The British and French diplomatic agents are stated to '.e3 opposed to the appoint- ment of any court of inquiry into the late massacre during the present disturbed state of things. Meanwhile, however, the foreign Consuls will take evidence of such of their com- patsiots as still remain here. REPORTED DESPATCH OF BRITISH TROOPS. A London correspondent telegraphs:—A rumour is afloat on the London Stock Exchange that troops have been ordered for Egypt. The report has not yet been confirmed, and has probably been originated for purely speculative purposes. Yesterday morning the Supply, tank vessel of 250 tons, left Portsmouth in pursuance of imperative ordets to juin the Mediterranean fleet. Originally the vessel was intended for service at Bermuda. The Supply was used as a vessel for condensing water during lhe Crimean war, and as a tank ship will be of immense seruice to the fleet, as her engines are capable of pumping about 100 tons of water an hour. SHOCKING SUICIDE NEAR LIVERPOOL. Mr. James M. Arnold, residing at Antield, Liverpool, has committed suicide by shooting himself through the head with a revolver. The deceased had been unfortunate in business, and had also recently lost his wife, and these and other domestic troubles seem to have overthrown his reason. The deceased was only thirty years of age. COURT-MARTIAL AT DEVONPORT. The court-martial on Oliver Jew, late ship's steward of the Cambridge, assembled at Devonport yesterday morning, Mr. Lovne, solicitor for the defence, explained the ert ors in the prisoner's accounts, contending that they were solely the result of carelessness and lack of proper assistance in his work. The charge of embezzlement of meat, he submitted was not proved, as the prisoner never had the beef house under his control. Jew was found guilty of falsifying the ship's books. He was sentenced to eighteen month's im- prisonment with hard labour, and dismissed Her Majesty's service with disgrace. THE UNDERGROUND FIRE AT SOUTH SHIELDS. The underground fire at South Shields, which has smouldefed for six or seven years past and has defied all efforts for its extinction, has again broken out. The Crown and Canon public-house, Laygate-street, has fallen into ruins, and other property adjoining is being gradually demolished. Since the outbreak of the fire, nearly two streets of houses have been demolished. The Corporation officials have trenched several places without effect, and further destruction of property is inevitable. POLICE PROTECTION IN DUBLIN. Mr. John Curran, one of the Dublin police magistrates, is the latest addition to the number of officials who have been forced to accept police protection, and two =stables are now stationed at his residence. Mr. Curran was very popular previous to his appointmrnt to his present posi- tion, which took place only a short time ago. Several ether gentlemen holding Government positions in Dublin, especially in the Castle, are daily followed for their safety by policemen in plain clothes, and this, with the conse- quent restrictive regulations forced upon them, make their lives exceedingly irksome. HORRIBLE OUTRAGE UPON A BOY. Ahoy named William Kirk died yesterday morning in the Glasgow Infirmary from injuries received under the follow- ing circumstances :—While playing in a court in Glassford- street, Glasgow, the night before last, he sat down, when some one from the adjoining premises below thrust, it is said, a red-hot iron idto the lower part of his body. He lingered in great agony till death ended his sufferings yes- terday Morning. Two boys, named Hamilton and Boswell are in custody on suspicion. THE " ALIEN " DIVISION IN PARLIAMENT. The most important division en Thursday night was on Mr. Morgan Lloyd's amendment to extend the operation of the 12th clause, -dealing with aliens, to the United Kingdom. Amongst those in the minority of 51 were Messrs. Jacob Bright, Hopwood, and Rylands. The majority of 228 in- cluded Sir R. A. Cross, Lord Hertington, Messrs. Hibbert, Hugh Mason, Colonel Stanley, E. L. Stanley, and Summers, Messrs. Slagg, Arnold, Armitage, Agnew, and Le.ake did not vote. IMPORTANT TO ALKALI MANUFACTURERS. A case of considerable interest to manufacturers of alkalies, was heard the other week in the Chancery Court, Liver- pool, before Mr. Vice-Chancellor Bristowe, at Sr. George's Hall. The action was brought by Mr. E. W. Parnell and Mr. James Simpson, of Widnes and Liverpool, against Messrs. More, Liddell, and Co of Widnes, for an infringe-1 ment of a patent, No. 4,188, of the year 1878, granted to Mr. E. W. Parnell for improvements in the manufacture of alkalies. Evidence was given at great length to show that many attempts had been made from time to time to purify crude alkaline solutions, by removing sulphurets. sulphites, I and hyposulphites from those solutions. Mr. Parnell, one of the plaintiffs, succeeded in doing this by two alternative pro. cesses, one by adding metallic zinc to the solution and subse- quently treating with heat anti agitation. This process causes the sulphur to combine with the zinc and to be .pre- cipitated, and at the same time that that reaction took place the sulphites and .hypesulphites were, what the evidence went to show, all pewerfully reduced to sulphuret of zinc. The other process consisted in makinz solution of zinc in a caustic alkali, making in fact zincate of soda, and adding this to the mass of crude alkaline solution. A third and subsidiary part of the patent was for the recovery of the zinc used as oxide of zinc and the re-use of it in caustic alkali as a zincate of soda. The point which occupied the court so long was whether some prior specifications did not disclose the invention sufficiently to enable manu- facturers to obtain the same results. Messrs. E. K. Mos- pratt, Brunner, Joynson, M'llvvain, and others were called

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

THE EGYPTIAN QUESIION.-Sir C. IteeKE, replying to questions relative to Egypt, seid that the date when inform- ation was received of the loss of life at Alexandria, was the 20th June. The number of killed varied from 50 to 200 Europeans, but not British subjects. It was intended to demand reparation for six British and two Maltese subjects, known to be killed. It was impossible to say with exact- ness, the number of Europeans killed.—Mr. CHAPLIN ex- pressed dissitisfaction at the answer of the Government, and gave notice that on an early day, he would move a resolution stating it to be the duty of the British Government to take prompt steps to protect the lives and property of British subjects in Egypt.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Sir S. Northcote, said at the present moment the Sultan still ob- jected to the Conference. The meeting did not take place on Thursdly, as representatives of some of the Powers had not received definitive instructions. ' England, France, and Italy were ready ; Germany and Russia were prepared, and the representative of Austria would shortly receive instructions. It was not expected Austria would take an isolated position. It was still the intention of the powers to hold a Conference as to reparation for British losses, and the maintenance of peace. Directiens had been given Her Majesty's representative to meet the cases of failure. The neutralization of the Suez Canal was outside the Conference.—Sir C. DILKE, with respect to the provision in Egypt for carrying on the control and punctual service of the public debt, said as regarded legality the same provision or guarantee existed now as hitherto. As regarded the tem- porary position, the view of the Controller was that there presence at the meeting of the Council would give strength to the military party by seeming to sanction their preten- tions, and would lower the influents and control. For these reasons the Controllers would abstain from presenting them- selves at the Council. PREVENTION OF CRIBIE (IRELAND) BILL.—The HOUSB went into committee on the prevention ef Crime (Ireland) Bill. Clause 12 which re-enacted the Alien Act for three Years, and was last night made applicable to the United 'Kingdom, was further considered. Dr. Comeners moved a provision making it necessary that an order for departure of person under the Clause, whould only be made on sworn information. A long discussion ensued, and the provision was withdrawn.—The O'CONNOR moved a provision enact:nc that the Clause should not be operative against foreigneis provided with a passport. The provision was negatived.— Mr. SEXTON moved to add to the clause "Provided nothing in thj said Act should affect any alien who should at the passing of the Act have been residing within the section for one year." A discussion ensued.—Sir W. Heneouter said he was anxiouslto shorten the discussion as much as possible. He would undertake to consult the Irish Government with a view of ascertaining whether it was possible to shorten the period for which the Act was to be renewed for less than three years.—Mr. Parnell expressed satisfaction at such an announcement, and Mr. SEXTON withdrew the addition he had moved. Mr. Par- nell then moved the addition of words to the clause to give an alien the right of appeal against an order made for his depertation.—On a discussion, the amendment was withdrawn.—Mr. HEALY moved an amend- ment providing that aliens ordered to leave the country should be given means for °complying with the order.—Sir W. 11/atom:lx opposed.—Progress was reported, and the • sittibg suspended.

EXTRAORDINARY ELOPIIMENT.—A correspondent writes:— An extraordinary elopement has just taken place from this quiet village. The parties could not perhaps, be correctly described as May and December, but there is a remarkable disparity in the ages which makes the affair more ludicrously absurd than such cases usually are. Another curious feature is that appearances point to the the presumption that the woman has run away with the man rather than vice versa as is usually the case. The woman appears to have been unusually fickle. She hai been married three times, and three times had worn the widow's weeds, hut though she was encumbered with three children she did not prove a drug in the matrimonial market. She was very soon united, at the age of 40, to a 4th husband, who had himself two chil- dren. 2:03D after this last marriage the woman commenced to carry on an intrigue with a 'youth of seventeen, who lived in the adjacent village of Rush Green. This came to the knowledge of the neighbours, and remarks of a very complimentary character were made. Eventually the place became too warm for the ill assorted couple, and they eloped together, the woman leaving behind her the five cnildren. MEANNESS VERSUS MAGNANIMITY. Sir —I wish to say a word about a little circumstance,' in connection with the athletic sports now being held at Tarn- worth. To commemorate this event, the railings and the railway bridge pillars in the immediate vicinity are copiously immersed in a dark solution bearin,,, an unquestionable affinity to tar. If I had not previously observed the same thing on similar occasions I should have set it down as being a freak on the part of some hireling more zealous than dis- greet ; but as the daring operation has beeen practised before, I am led to conclude that it simply fulils the deliberate mandate of some one high in authority. It is not easy to conjecture any reason of sufficient waiuht to account for the issuing of such an order. To say nothing of the illegality of disfiguring other peoples' property, such a proceeding is in my opinion gross'T indecent. No lady could conve- niently pass the place in question without soiling het gar- ments. What real purpose, therefore, is sought to be serval by this daubing process? Doubtless the imaginary one is that of preventing people €btaining for nothing that for 'which they ought to pay something in return;* but I ask 'What person with any self-respect would be inclined to brook the discomfort and risk of witnessing an exhibition from the top of a brick column—l mean, of course, when free from tar? The improbability of such an occurrence is such as to preclude its consideration for a single moment. There is only one class for whom the trick can be designed, namely, , those who have a natural desire to see the sports, but who have not the means wherewith to gain admission to the in- terior; but only to fancy the incredible paltriness of seeking to deprive one or two waifs and strays of the pleasure of having a gratuitous glimpse at a game of romp! Thatmen- tal littleness is by some perverse instrumentality the in- variable counterpart of physical prowess I refuse to believe, but a society would enjoy no less a share of popular esteem by instructing its agents to pay reasonable regard to etiquette in the execution of their duties.—' am, sir, your obedient servant, J. SMITH. Upton Rocks, Widnes, June 17th, 1882.

WANTED, AN IRISH POLICY. (LETTER. IV.) Sir,—Continuing my remarks on the character of Irish industries, it is scarcely requisite to repeat that agriculture, from modest potato growing to more important operations, takes the lead in the business of Irish life. There was a time when Ireland boasted of extensive woollen and cotton trades. At the beginning of the obtaining century she kept thousands of hands employed at the loom' at wool-combing, and in her flannel manufactures. Now, however, she has Comparatively few, for since the union—thanks to the assis- tance of English capital !—her manufacturing industries have declined as any one may learn by consulting the report of the late Mr. T. M. Ray 9n this subject. It is an admitted fact that Ireland is now more than ever dependent upon her soil for the sustenance of her people. How neces- sary it is, therefore, that the land be unfettered by any legal restraints such as unfortunately exist, not in Ireland alone, but all over the United Kingdom. No rural population can develope into an intelligent, independent, self-governing Community so long as the ground they cultivate is hampered by laws of an inimical rather than a benefactory nature. such taws are net merely hostile to individual enrichment, bat exercise a curse upon the soil, by condemning each "tiller of the ground" to "hard labour for life." This is too true to be simply a witticism. Land crippled by arbi- trary laws is a sore possession ;• while yielding to importu- nate toil—providing the weather be favourable—a hearty harvest, it not infrequently incites its real owner to give another twist to the wrench of penurious landlordism. In our own country we have seen farming decline in accor- dance with this view, for, as noted previously, commerce and other pursuits offered more remunerative scope than agriculture. Bat in Ireland—as in some parts of Scotland —landlordism has swayed the destinies of thousands, by rack-renting, by abuse of tenant rights, by taking unfair advantage of successful tenants, and by exaction not the least formidable weapon handy to the knavishly disposed of kaacilords. If Irish landlords as a class represented the honourable sbrewclnee illtra,;!ed in the instance alluded to through the limes by Mr. McMinnies, you. sir, qtwted last week—the existent disturbances in Ireland would have no justification, but would justly incur our con- - tempt and disapprobation. Unhappily for Ireland, they do not represent anything so conducive to good feeling between landlord and tenant. They are more frequently unjust, pitiless, and blindly selfish than not; while the middlemen —those who lease and re-lease farms—are perhaps even worse than the landowners themselves. Without entering into extensive details, the primary cause of Irish defection is the poverty and ignorance of the industrial classes. These in their turn are attributable to the crashing effects of the Irish land laws. Incapable of self-deliverance from oppression, Ireland has fretted over her humiliating pos- ition, made tenfold more hideous and unbearable by the • wrongs ;which she is aware have humbled her. The • outcome is chronic distractioa ; and every fresh batch of • evicted tenants only increases her misery over her conscious degradation. The Government Arrears Bill is of course in- tended to mitigate 'the; evils attending eviction. While believing it will do some good, I doubt its general result will net be so happy as Mr. Gladstone hopefully expects. I concur with Mr. W. H. Smith's view of of the matter, viz., that it will create dissatisfaction amongst the small shop- keepers and those tradespeople who have given credit, and who may legitimately consider themselves entitled to share the benevolence of our Government. However, it will afford relief where it is much needed, and this is a satisfac- tory feature of the Arrears of Rent Bill. Still we are far from a solution of the Irish qucstion. Mr. Gladstone's dual rolicy—a bit of sugar in one hand and a whip in the other—is not the way to Irish reform. Depend upon it, Ireland will not it either in morals or behaviour if the Premier insists upon practising on Ireland with English ideas. Nothing short of treating the Irish question from an Irish standpoint will satisfy Ireland. We cannot stop the mouths of such men as Davit:, Parnell, and other advo- cates of land-law reform ; yet while these agitators speak they add feel to the flames of the agitation. None the less they will speak, as our pioneers of reform spoke, on bshalf of the people. Where will it end ? Where? We frequently hear people deploring the animosity Irishmen show towards England. While it is deplorable, it is not astonishing, at least not to those familiar with Irish history. 'fifth hatred (for it amounts to it) of England is accountable for on perfectly sane grounds. If the tables were turned, we should hate Ireland with precisely the same fervour, I have no doubt. If ever history pirpe'uated the truism that Man's Inhumanity to man Makes countless thousands mourn," it has done so in Ireland. After the lapse of two centuries —it is not desirable to revive a remoter and possibly more repulsive phase of English intermedding in Irish affairs than "The Black Act" era—we find Ireland still presenting ' the spectacle of a badly-governed revolting people. Why is this ? History repeats itself ; it also furnishes the key to prudent and efficient legislation. In the case of Ireland, it supplies an Irish view of a difficulty that can neverbe settled by conformirg to an Irish policy of English manufacture Out of English material. Few who read Irish history will. deny that Ireland has grievances, something to nationaliz discontent, and renler her irritable and anarchial. "Th BI tck Act" era refer el to was an epoch of infamy and disgrace to England. lam an Englishman, sir, bat I con- fess that my blood tingles when I peruse the records of that period of our history. From "Ireland, industrial, political and social" (Longman's publication) we glean some of the following figures, which will help us to understand Irish petulance. The year 1665 produced the "Act of Settle- ment," justly termed "The Black Act," by which the land of Ireland was re-settled as follows :—The profitable lands were estimated at 12,500,000 statute acres. Observe how they were distributed—
Statute acres.

Granted to English Protestants of profitable land forfeited under the Oommonw e^.lth Previously possessed by English colonists of the Protestant faith and Church,--pr( di able land Granted or disposed of to the Irish—profitable 600,000 824,391
land Previously possessed by " good affection" men of
the Irish Remaining still unappropriated

12,208,237 Thus English and Scotch settlers obtained by forfeiture front the rightful owners 8,400,037 out of the 12,500,000 acres of profitable land belonging to Ireland. Again, "After the Treaty of Limerick, A.D. 191, William 111., though bound by its articles to confirm the Irish in their estates, escheated 1,723,763 statute acres for the benefit chiefly of De Ginkle, Keppel, Bentinck, and other foreigners." Within fifty years confiscation " reduced the property of the Catholic Irish to about 2,000,000 statute acres of profitable land, against-10,000,000 held by those in whose favour they were dispossessed." Here then is the starting point, so to speak, of Irish grievances. Robbed of their patrimony by English monarchs of doubtful morals—for William apart from his faithlessness to the Treaty of Limerick, proved his looseness of character by giving to a "favourite lady" an Irish estate valued at £25,000 per annnutn—the Irish people from that date to this have actually declined. It is true they rallied at the period of the Irish Parliament, and even succeeded in their commercial and other enter- prises. But that Parliament was too feeble, owing to the laws of the time, to last long, and the Union struck the death blow at home government for Ireland. The Irish people are still prostrated, still under the finger and thumb of Anglo-Irish landlordism. And after all, how can a people rise to the realisation of their hopes if fettered by tyrranons, law-supported monopoly? It is this- wise with Ireland. At the feet of a land monopoly, which owns England's historic sharve as its birthright, taxed to support military and police qces em- ployed to protect the soil, which othersYossess, at her ex- pense, struggling for very existence, it is no exaggeration to say that Ireland is browbeaten to the very dust. We English people do not understand what it is to be tied & own by laws of feudal origin. Heaven knows both our land and people are taxed heavily enough. But we have the consk '- lotion of educational and constitutional freedom. Somehow or other, Ireland does not participate in these blessings. and her abnegation must be a terrible incentive to rancour, if not to crime. In my humble, but sincere opinion, Ireland must have a free soil before she will smoke the pipe of peace. How this can be accomplishen dare not pretend to say. Mr. Davitt's scheme, if moderated, might do. it, although doubtful. Personally, I should delight to see the land brought under State control, either by purchase or otherwise. A free soil is essential to the happiness of a people ; and no nation can be truly free and self-governing so long as the land is the possession of a few. The nationalization of the soil, so far from being a chimerical idea, is one that will gather popularity with the fruit of years, and will some day destroy the truculent power exercised by some English as

SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley and Alderman Burgess. REFUSING TO BREAK STONES AT THE WORKHOUSE.— Jobn Hall, a tramp, and a casual inmate of the Workhouse, was charged with refusing to work as a stone-breaker, on Saturday morning.—Prisoner stated that he was in the Workhouse 10 years ago, and when working as a stone- breaker he lost the sight of one eye and his other eye was now in a very bad state.—He was sent to prison for? days _

with hard labour. MONDAY.—Before Major Cartwright and Mr. Ziba Armitage. CHARGED ON SINPICION.—A boy named Job Longson, aged 12 year., hailing from Buthworth, was charged on suspicion with having stolen £l, the property of some person unknown.— Prisoner was remanded for further . .

inquiries. Rumex AND DISORDERLY. Thomas Hornsby was charged with being drunk and guilty of disorderly behaviour in the Market, on Saturday evening. It appeared that whilst drunk he assaulted a woman named Mary Ann Phillips, and threw her to the ground. He was ordered to pay 20s. and costs, or in default undergo one month's im- prisonment with hard labour.—Richard Weaver, for being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street on Saturday night, vas fined 10s. and costs, with the alternative of 14 days' imprisonment with hard labour.—Mark Casey, a farm labourer, of Bold, for a like offence in Percival's- Fold on Sunday morning, was mulcted in the sum of 10s. and costs, or in default 14 days in gaol with hard labour. —A young man named John Baguley, aged 20, made his 15th appearance on a charge of drunkenness, in Horse- market-st. on the 10th inst., and he was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment with hard labour.—Thos. Kenny, who made his 16th appearance, for being drunk and disor- derly in Horsemarket-street on the 10th inst., was ordered to pay 10s. and costs or go to prison for 14 days.—John Kelly a carter, for a like offence in the same street and on the same day, was fined ss. and costs, or in default seven days' imprisonment.—William Toole was summoned for drunkenness in Wilson-Patten-street on Sunday. Fined 58. and costs, or seven days with hard labour.—Ellen Burke, a married woman, was fined in the sum of 10s. and costs, or ordered to undergo 14 days' hard labour, for being drunk and creating a disturbance in Buttermarket-street on the 10th inst. REFUSINGJO Qurr LICENSED PREMISES.—John Stolter, ' fer refusing to quit the premises of John Hindley, landlord of the Horse and Jockey, Winwick-road, on the 12th inst., was fined 20s, including costs, or in default 14 days' im- prisonment with hard labour. ABUSIVE LANGUAGE.--:A youth named Richard Jefferson, of no settled residence, was mulcted in the sum of 103, including costs, with the alternative of seven days' impri- sonment with hard labour, for using obscene language to a woman named Mrs. Stringer, of Culcheth, in the market, on Saturday. ALLEGED ROBBERY BY YOUTHS.—A youth named Wm. Woods was brought up on remand, charged with having etelen.from Mersey mills a sack, value is., and 281bs. seek- ing, worth about 2s 61, the property of James Fairclongh and Sons; with stealing from the premises of Michael McCoy, Market-street, one bag, value about is, his property; and from the premises of William French, confectioner, Golborne-street, two sacks, of the value of is. He was also charged, with another youth named Thomas' Hardy, with entering an outbuilding at the Eagle and Child Inn, Bridge-street, Warrington, between the ith and 9th inst., and stealing two shewle, two pairs of men's trousers, a vest, one dozen electro-plated teaspoons, a silver caddy spoon, and a quantity of books, altogether of the value of £1 lOs , the property of Mrs. Holloway, for- merly landlady of the Green Dragon.—The prisoner Woods nleaded guilty to the whole of the charges, and after hear- ing the evidence, reported in our last issue, be was committed for three months with hard labour.—No evidence was forth- coming to prove that Hardy was connected with the last robbery, and he was accordingly discharged. A CAUTION TO BuTcssEns.—John Mynekvne, butcher, Priestley-street, was charged with cruelly ill-using a sheep on the 13th inst., on Liverpool-road.—Mr. Wm. Greenwell, of Altrincham, appeared to prosecute on behalf of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals.— From the evidence of Robert Hunter, it appeared that about one o'clock on the afternoon of Tuesday, the 13th inst., when passing near Messrs. Cartwright's works, Bank Quay, he saw defendant driving a flock of sheep. One sheep left the flock and ran into an openingclose by. Thedefenslant ran after it, and dealt it about 20 blows on the head and face with a stout ash plant, causing blood to flow very profusely. Mr. E. Bolton, of Orford-lane Glass Works, appeared shortly after the occurrence, and having learned the facts of the case from the last witness, followed the defendant along Liverpool-road. He had proceeded some distance when he saw defendant strike a sheep first on one side of the road and then on the other with what appeared to be a very heavy stick. He then caught up to defendant and asked him for his name, which he gave correctly. On being spoken to by Mr. Bolton as to his cruelty, defendant stated that he had had a great deal of trouble with the sheep which was enough to make him illuse it. Mr. Bolton replied that such a reason was no justification whatever for his cruet usage of the poor sheep. Witness said on retracing the steps he saw marks of blood which had fallen from the sheep's head for about 1000 yards, and when he crot near to Messrs. Crosfield's gateway he saw a large pool of blood. He had taken the matter up on the ground of humanity, irrespective of person.—Defendant stated that he brought the sheep from Beeston Castle, and the one which the witness stated he had illused, had been bitten by a lot of togs before he bought the flock. He also said that it had been amongst some wire in the Whitecross Wire Company's yard, and whilst jumping among the wire had cut itself.— Major Cartwright said he could not understand how butchers could be so cruel. It was a question with the Bench as to whether they should commit the defendant to prison with- out the option of a fine. They were of opinion that that would meet the case admirably; but by way of example, and as a preventative against further abuses they would fine defendant £3 and costs, with the alternative of two months' imprisonment.
TlJEBDAY.—Before Councillor Monks.

Dar Nit AND DISORDERLY.—John Cu'keen, a farm labourer, of Altrinchana, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Knutsford-road on the previous thy', and was fined 7s. 63., including costs, or, in default, seven days im- prisonment. ROBBING A. FATHEB.—Job Longson, a lad, 12 years of age, was brought up, on remand, charged with stealing £2 in gold and £1 in silver, the property of his father, John Longson, a fiatman. It appeared that whilst at Runcorn on Wednesday morning, the prisoner got up early and took the money from a cupboard in the cabin of the flat. He made his way to Warrington and purchased a toy steam engine, two boats, a bird and cage, and a rabbit. He took the above to a house occupied by Mrs. Hall in Golden Grove-street, and she, perceiving that the lad seemed to have a good deal of money, gave him into the oust( dv of P.C. Evans. The prisoner, who' said a flatman had given him £l, was remanded to the Runcorn police. ASSAULT.—Joseph Bibby, a young man, was charged with assaulting Elizabeth Blease, in Haydock-strect, on the I 19th inst., and was fined in the costs 4s. 6d. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley (in the chair) and Councillor Fairclough. There were no cases of public interest.

TECTRSIDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds (chairman), Captain Litton, and Alderman Webster. A JEA.LOIIS WIF)I.—A married woman named Lucy Bluck was charged with having made use of language towards Mary Ellen Ellison calculated to provoke a breach of the peace on the 17th inst—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the defendant. —The evidence showed that defendant's husband had been in the habit, during the whole of his married life, of paying visits to the complainant, and it was this inti• macy which provoked defendant.—The Bench considered the case not proved, and accordingly dismissed it. THREiTENING A WIFE —J. E. Brown was charged with threatening his wife Mary Ann Brown, on the 10th inst.— Defendant came home in a drunken state on Saturday night, the 10th inst., and told his wife she would never live to go out of the house again.—Complainant stated that her hus- band was not a bad man when he was sober.—Defendant promised the magistrates he would not get drunk again, and he was fined 4s. 6d. costs. A CONSCIENCE-STRICKEN TEttF.F.—James Davenport, a cab-driver, was charged with stealing £1 103. from the Swan public-house, Bridge-st, the property of Hy. Gittens on the night of the 6th instant. —From the statement of the Chief Constable that between the hours of five and six o'clock on the night in question the landlady, Mrs. Gittens, recollected putting underneath a glass on one of the shelves in the bar one sovereign and one half-sovereign. She went to her tea, and on returning to the bar found the glass which the coins had been placed under broken to pieces OR the floor. Mrs. Gittens remembered seeing prisoner in the house at the time she secreted the coins.—Prisoner that morning went to the police office and gave himself up. and when charged with stealing the money replied, "That's right; I have done it." When before the magistrates he stated that after he had stolen the money he could not rest, and that was the reason be had given himself up.—Prisoner was sent to imprison- ment for two months with hard labour. STEALING A FAMILY BIBLE.—A young man named John Donlan, of no settled residence and a native of Glasgow' was charged with stealing from the dwelling-house of Ed. Bur- rows, Golborne-street, on Wednesday night, a family Bible and a musical album, his property.—Prosecutor's wife, Mary Ann Burrows' bad opened a window in the front of the house and had forgotten about it until she was informed by a person who was passing the house that the window was open. She then went to close it, and found that the articles above stated were missing. About eleven o'clock informa- t, on was given to the police and enquiries were made at va rims lodging-houses.—P.C. Rowbotbam found the priso- ner at Mrs.Mularky's, with the stolen articles in his posses- sion.a When charged prisoner replied, "I know nothing about them, only that a man gave them me to keep for -Prisoner now pleaded guilty, and be was committel to gaol or two months with hard labour. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess. •

A yotrr, TIFUL VA.GRANT.—Patrick Cornelia (15), charged with being Knowles Coa Ifound on the premises of the Pearson and and Iron Co. He was scnt to prison for 14 days, and on iered to find surety to be of good behaviour.

CLARE proposed. and Mr. Lomas seconded, that the following resolution be forwarded to the Commissioners: viz.: "That this meeting disapproves of the site selected for a cemetery, and thinks that a cheaper and more suitable one cal be selected, and that the probable cost be laid before the ratepayers prior to any scheme being proceeded with."—The resolution was carried. Mr. PRESOOTT then proposed, and Mr. ELLISON seconded, the following resolution, which was carried: "That if a cemetery be required for this district, the Commissioners be requested to negotiate with Mr. Legh to secure the common fur that purpose." It was also resolved that a petition be prepared for signa- ture by the ratepayers, and that the same be presented to the Commissioners; also that the ratepayers be instructed to select a suitable candidate for the next election. The meeting terminated.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

_ The Ratepayers' Association will deserve well of their compatriots and of their country if they succeed in saving ' the community the cost, or the greater part of the cost, of a 1 new burial ground. The parish churchyard, according to the very best authority, is nearly full, and so is St. Peter's. The Roman Catholics have not much ground to spare, neither have the Congregationalists, and other churches and chapels have none whatever. The wish no doubt was father ' to the thought when speakers at the meeting on Monday night said that Mr. Legh would let the inhabitants have that part of the common favoured by their scheme for next to nothing. Supposing this to be an accomplished fact, and that the site is moved from east to occident, will not this in- volve the making of a new road that shall rival the making of the nine arches opposite, and swallow up much of the public money? Is litigation even hinted at that may cost quite as much or more? The soil is clayey after turning the first or second sod, and so in that respect it is no great im- provement on Wargrave ground. Perhaps it was rather cheap generosity to talk of buying an extension of War- grave churchyard to give to that church at the public ex- pense. We freely admit there is something romantic in the idea of being buried on the edge of the desert by the banks of the Sankey (with one solitary exception the only river of that name in Europe or perhaps the world) and enough to make an ancient Druid turn in his grave to think that the inhabitants of Newton and Earlestown had chosen to sleep beside its "magical or miraculous waters." On rising some fine morning the Druid may fancy himself in wild Wales if it is filled with slate slabs, as many burial grounds are, and if a Briton, he may think the people here had taken to talk- ing French and that women have been " employed " at iron foundries. Any way, we have no partiality for site C, which is just as bleak as the common is barren, and about as far removed and inconvenient. A and B are much more central and nearer civilization than the other two situations, and for that reason, if for no other, we prefer the Commissioners' scheme if it can be accomplished at any reasonable cost. But we are struck dumb when we begin to think how easily twenty thousand pounds can be saved. The new bridge over the railway at Earlestown only waits the formal or informal opening, as it is finished, and the granite sets grouted. It is sowbacked and steep enough on the Earlestown side, hut gentle enough on the other gradient, and will do away with a very dangerous level crossing a little nearer, the railway station, which will then be a elrl de sac like the road under one of the arches of the new bridge. Now that we have done so well, would it be impracticable to do the same by level crossing in Railway-street over the Haydock line, on which, however, the traffic is much less. The trip to Moreca:nbe is a united effort of the Noncon- formist schools to provide for their Sunday school scholars a pleasant day's run and recreation at the sea-side, to which the general public have this year given good support, as the fare is abnormally low and the half-crown so spent will not be grudged by those whose desire it is to rusticate in real pic-nic fashion. There are many places within easy reach, if its attractions should prove insufficient, to satisfy the in- dividual taste. Th 3 school treats began on Wednesday with the Ptimitive Methodists, and on Thursday the WeBleyans went tb Burtouwood to spend the afternoon at Bradley Hall, the Congregationalists to a field generously lent to them by Mr. Pardv, in Newton, the one with the Earlestown brass band, and the latter with the Warrington Workhouse band,

div.head: NEWTON RACES. INTERESTING REMINISCENCES.
div.p: NEWTON RACES. INTERESTING REMINISCENCES.

Newton is so centrally situated between Liverpool and Manchester that it has ever been attractive as a race meeting to the busy sons of toil in those hives of industry; not to mention those of Wigan, Preston, and Warrington. Salmon and new potatoes' ducks and green peas, have had, however, quite as much to do with the attractions of Newton races as its sports. It was a huge picnic before the iron road ran to within a couple of hundred yards of the grand stand, and there Are few pleasanter drives now than to Newton. Many, even yet, prefer that mode of journeying thither, forithe last year, owing to some fear of their safety, the lines from the main line to the Common were not used, and Earlestown Junction was made the point to which the special trains journeyed to and fro. A pleasant walk through the fields is far preferable to the drive through the black coal dust which abounds in the neighbourhood of the course, which, when once reached no longer presents the vernal appearance it did a score of years ago. The " march ef improvement "—that is the correct phrase, whatever it may mein-has long since des'royed the vegetation which used to form such a dis- tinguishing character in the attractive features of Newton Common. Neither tall chimneys nor modern science has checked the noxious vapours emitted from the numerous works in the vicinity from blasting large ttacts of the race- course in places; yet such is the elasticity of its turf that It is always good aoing in the driest weather; whilst the recent rains give it a fresher appearance than it has possessed in many previous years. Few of ciir readers can call to mind, we ex- pect, that via Newton station was once one of the orthodox ways to get to Snuthport, yet the writer of this article re- members it well, for he was (serried thither by train fully forty years eel) from the old station in Liverpool-road, Man- chester, and found on his arrival a stage coach which car- ried him to Southport by way of Ormskirk, and a grand drive it was, quite worthy of being repeated. Newton as a race meeting has had varying fortunes. In the days of that good cross-country horse Trent, we had steeplechases at Newton, but they decayed for want of patronage; and until Mr. Parity, Mr. Legh's present steward, came to Ince, the races looked like going out altogether. During his steward- ship they have improved considerably, the added money has been increased, and now to strengthen the locality in a sporting sense Haydock Park has been purchased from Mr. Leah for a coursing meeting, and the first brace of dogs are to be slipped "on the new principle" next November. The "new principle" is not open coursing as at Waterloo, Ash- down, or Newmarket. The hares are confined in a large space prepared for them, are driven out one at a time to be coursed. Good law is then given be- fore the dogs are slipped, and escapes are made for the hares, if they beat the dogs for speed, to get away. Care is always taken that no bare shalt be coursed twice in one day. Hayclock Park is over 400 acres in ex- tent, and one straight run can be given of 1,100 yards, which is 400 more than the longest run at Gosforth, near Nowcastle-on-Tyne, where the finest "enclosed coursing" aver seen was witnessed this year. In addition to the longer course at Haydocle Park, there are two shorter ones of 600 yards each; so that the slipping can be varied to suit either puppies or elder greyhounds. The family seat of the Leghs, of Lyme, is not at Newton, but at Disley Hall, near Man- chester. • The Leghs are sportsmen tried and true, and the present owner of his ancestral home had the honour of winning the-Waterloo Cup with Lobelia, one of the most beautiful bitches ever seen; so beautiful that her likeness was transferred to canvas, and, associated as she was with those mig•hty greyhounds Master M‘Grath and Bab at the Bowster, the three combined gave a trio of caniaae excel- lence the coursing world may never know again. The pic- ture was afterwards engraved, and is to be found on the walls of nearly all the coursing homes in the kingdom. It was in the devs of the late Lord Derby, Sir John Gerrard, James Meiklam, and other good men and true that Newton races were at the best. It was Sir John's pride to reserve his best horses for Newton and ride them himself ; and if he could only ride them and heat the late Lord Wilton, either at Newton or Heaton Park, his ambition was satisfied, his cup of iey full. Lord Wilton's, however, wanted beating As "Mr. Clarke" he was the best amateur horseman of his day. Pantosa was one of the best horses Sir John ever had. If our memory serves us rightly, Sir John Gerrard's horses were trained!in the neighbourhood of Newton. Many good horses were so trained in the olden time. Maid of Lyme was prepared there before she won the Goodwood Stakes, so was Persuasion, a recent Portland Plate winner at Doncaster. Both her owner and trainer however have now gone over "to the majority," hut "old Joe" Peace still lives in his son James, who (rains for Mr. Townley-Parker at Newton ; but James Clarke, who used to train for Mr. Leah, has given up training hors'es for farming, and Mr. Edwin Weever, the famous trainer of Emblem and Emblematic, has the care of Mr. Legh's horses at Bourton-in-the-Marsh. Sir John Gerrard was a good all-round sportsman; he was fated of racing, hunting, and shooting; and he at one time kept a pack of hounds. Prince Louis Napoleon was his guest for a long time. The late Emperor was always understood to have a large share in the confederacy managed by Count Lagrange; but now the 'sinews of war" are conspicuous by their absence. "Its money that makes the mare to go," and for the want of it the Lagrange stud, which has not paid for some years, is to be sold off at the end of the present summer. The present Baron Gerard (who was raised to the peerage by Lord Beaconsfield) is not a racing man, but his son is; and his horse Sweetbread won the Royal Hunt Cup at Ascot this year. The "blue and white stripes" of Mr. Meiklam were always opposing the "stripes " of Sir John; and Mr. Meiklam's horse Aristotle did what no other horse ever ac-
Mr. Mr. Mr. Mr.

complishel, by winning the Manchester, Newton, and Liver- pool cups in one year; and they wanted winning at that time (1843), for some good horses were running. "Dan- gerous Dawson" was Aristotle's trainer, and it is not a little singular that his son Tom, in conjunction with Mr. R, Johnson, jun., is now clerk of the course at Newton. Young Tom was for a time trainer at Tupgill to the lat.e John Jackson, and others, whilst his father trained privately for the late Lord Glasgow ; but, eventually, the father returned to Tup- gill, to train for the wealthy China merchant, Mr. Jardine, for whom be won the Two Thousand and Derby. He died there, and now Tupgill is tenanted by his son-in-law Fred. Bates, who is as dangerous in handicaps as his father-in-law was. Lord Derby never did much at Newton. His ambi- tion led him further afield o.• else to Liverpool July, when Knowsley used to rival Croxteth in the extent of its house party "for th' races." We could fill quite a little history of Newton, had we time to search our bookshelves and their records. But it was never a high-class 'ace meeting for the last quarter of a century. Up to that time it was held as a sacred duty to visit Newton on " th' Cup day." div.head: CUSTOMS REORGANISATION.
div.p: THE CUSTOMS REORGANISATION.

Several weeks ago we printed an article under the heading of "The impending Customs changes." It was there stated that the long-expected assimilation of Customs and Excise would be effected on June Ist; and that the amalgamation

of the two departments would follow, should the new scheme prove as excellent in a practical sense as it certainly is theoretically considered. Before proceeding to describe how in a few hours one system was abandoned for another entirely different in principle, we will glance over some of the extraordinary difficulties against which the Treasury and the Board of Customs have had to contend in order to prevent the necessity of further postponing the assimilation. Most of these difficulties have arisen since the appearance of iur first article on this subject. The revealed intentions of the Treasury regarding officials were then only of a general nature, and in some instances expressed in rather vague an.: uncertain language. Questions put to the Treasury at tlsat period in Parliament rarely elicited more than was previ- ously known, though probably their frequent repetition impelled that high official body to a more rapid consum- mation of things. We stated that retirement of the older members of the service, both indoor and outdoor, was invited, and that the Treasury could grant terms only in accordance with the Superannuation Act of 1859, which provides an allowance not exceeding two-thirds of the salary and emoluments of office. Rejecting the plea that circumstances were very extraordinary "my lords" refused the exceptional terms which were held out to the War Once and Admiralty officials by the late Government, and granted, as a means of conciliation, six months' leave of absence on full pay, commencing on the let April, the original date of assimilation. The postponement of the assimilation, however, reduces the leave to three months. With it the members concerned seem tolerably well satisfied, and many on their last day of office looked forward with great satisfaction to a long and pleasant summer holiday. Many of these retirements, however, must be coneidered not as voluntary, but in a degree as compulsory. In these pir- tieular cases, owing to peculiar circumstance of official position, a transfer to the outdoor department meant a posi- tive reduction of salary. For example, there were several clerks, who, in addition to their ordinary salary, were granted (as compensation for the exceptionally onerous aetteeih nerfarmed) what is known in Dr. Pleyfeir'e celebrated scheme as "duty pay." This "duty pay,' amounting in the maximum to £lOO per annum, has been enjoyed so long as to be looked upon by many as a per- manent addition. It ceased all round on the Ist *June; and retiring officials formerly in receipt of it reasonably expected that their superannuation would be calculated on their gross salaries. The spirit of the Superannuation Act would appear to intend this; and the refueal of the Treasury to nice these claims, as well as their previous rejection of the idea of exceptionality in the assimilation scheme, indi- cate too close an adherence to the letter of an Act which was passed more than 20 years ago. The retirements, not- withstanding, were so numerous as to considerably embarrass the Treasury in their arrangements for the classi- fication of the new outdoor department, the Treasury evidently expecting many of them to accept the newly- created positions. It was at this conjuncture that Mr. Herbert Murray (lately holding an important position in Ireland) was appointed by Mr. Gladstone secretary to the Board of Customs, the gentleman who previously held that office having resigned from ill-health. In making this appointment the Treasury was, evidently desirous of having a convenient mouthpiece on the actual secene of operations, and in this sense the appointment can be most strongly defended. It created much discussion in the House of Commons, the prevailing system of nominating Treasury favourites to places of trust and responsibility being much eondemned in some quarters, but vigorously defended by the late Lord Frederick Cavendish. In this case, though without precedent in the Customs since 1672, the appoint- ment has been an excellent one, Mr. Murray having proved himself throughout as a gentleman of great tact, energy, and business capacity. To the new secretary, then, was entrusted the task of offering the outdoor positions to those who had been selected for them, a task requiring something more than mere departmental skill, which, valuable and indispensable on ordinary occasions, is alone scarcely suffi- cient to cope with great changes involving wholesale retire- ment. Most of these appointments were accepted by the members of the higher division, who will henceforth be known as Ist, 2nd, and 3rd class surveyors. The redundant class (which in very department of the Civil Service since its unavoidable introduction by the Playfair scheme has been a difficult class to deal with) proved in this instance a veritable thorn in the flesh. It must not be supposed for a moment that the services of this body are in any way redundant. Their status places a bar tolheir promotion to the rank and privileges of the" higher division," though they perform almost exactly similar duties; on the other hand, from length and value df service they cannot be reduced to a level with the" lower division," the members of which are mostly very riling men. The " Playfair scheme" recognises two great divisions in the clerical eitaff and " redundant " is presumably the fittest term which can be applied to the mean existing between " upper" and "lower." The terms offered to the members of this class were so utterly inadequate for the extra duties and in- creased responsibilities required from them, that they we. indignantly and unanimously refused. The resistance was effectual, for almost instantly their demands were acceded to. Probably the long list of retirements, and the possible loss of the valuable services of experienced men had much to do with this sudden recognition of reasonable claims. Had the claims been even more strongly pressed, it can scarcely be doubted that "my lords" would as readily have submitted. At all events, the " reclundants" were keen enough to see their opportunity and sufficiently strong and courageous to push it to the front. In the classification several seniors were made 3rd class surveyors, and the re- mainder Ist class examining officers, a few from delicate health and other causes preferring to be transferred to other departments or be retained on the new indoor classification if required. As regards the members of the lower division the whole of those who offered themselves for out-door employment were accepted. Nat a single exception was made, and con- sequently much amusement his been caused by the non- effect of a Treasury minute which stated that from those who offered themselves only a certain number would be selected. It is not too much to say that the ultimate suc- cess of the new scheme depends to a very large extent upon the late lower division clerks, now 2nd class examining officers. They are certainly young, and cannot he said to have had as much practical experience as the older officials. But in this charge, their very youth tells greatly in their favour, for they can more readily adapt themselves to altered circumstances, their new duties will be more quickly learned, and will weigh less heavily upon them than upon those who have for years worked in one groove, fitting the groove so closely as to render withdrawal a matter of labour and dila- malty. Owing to the unexpected desire for retirement on the part of so many, aact the determination of others to remain on in- door employment, it was found that a sufficient number of competent officials coald not be obtained in the Port of Lon- don alone to permanently undertake the new duties. This is one of the greatest difficulties which the Treasury has encountered, and it cannot be said that the difficulty has been fairly overcome. A scarcity of men to fill all the posi- tions created by the new classification is certainly a striking incident in a department which, in London alone, numbers its members by the thousand. A closer inspection, however, will reveal the true causes of this temporary scarcity. It must be recollected that the new scheme practically provides for the keeping of accounts at all the legal quays, sufferance wharves, uptown warehouses, vaults, and docks, instead of as formerly at one central office; and that the work being purely clerical can be per- formed only by those previously engaged in somewhat similar clerical labour. It has been :asserted that the further vacancies should have been filled by appointments from the old and strictly out-door department. But the members of the latter, though well acquainted with the actual movements and operations of dutiable goods, are not capable of immediately taking up a system of book-keeping which is marvellously intricate, and which would almost be as foreign to them as to complete outsiders. Besides, the particular department to which they belong is scarcely in a condition to suffer a loss of men without serious detriment to the Crown interests. It was therefore a wise movement on the part of the Treasury to call in the temporary aid of experienced clerks from such ports as Liverpool, Glasgow, Bristol, Leith, Belfast, Dublin, and Cork. These clerks, for several days before the actual date of assimilation; were re- quired to attend at the Custom House to make themselves familiar with the books of which they would soon be in com- plete charge at the various stations. It must be mentioned, however, that there are some instances of out-doer officials being intrusted with the carrying out of the new scheme at certain stations. These may be considered as "all round men," who are quite capable of carrying out the trust com- mitted to their care. One more instance may be given of the straits which this scarcity has caused. Many of the re- tired officials, and most of those who will ultimately be trans- ferred to other departments, have been requested to give temporary aid. The out-port clerks are engaged for a period of about three months. It may therefore be supposed that the Treasury has had the two ends in view of providing for the scarcity, and also of enabling the cleric to carry away well-earned experience to the out-ports reae"y for the assimi- lation there, should it prove successful In London,
