div.head: WIDNES AT i I LETIC CLUB SPORTS.
div.p: WIDNES AT i I LETIC CLUB SPORTS.

These porta, which were command f d on Friday, the 16th inst., were continued on Saturday afternoon, the weather, in Idle meantime, having changed for the worse. At two o'clock, when the first event took place, there was a cold strong wind blowing across the ground, and the sky was darkened by, passing clouds, which, about four o'clock, gave unmistake- able evidence of what was to be expected, rain falling heavily from about half-past five to the conclusion of the sports. Notwithstanding these unfavourable conditions, the celebrity which this annual event has obtained in the north of England, drew together a large concourse of people, numbeiing, at a rough computation, about 6,000. In striking ciontraet to it deserted appearance on the previous evening, the grand stand was well filled, many of the elite of the Reighbourbnod being present. From this excellent point of observatien, a goodly nutnber of ladies, watched with interest the various trials of endurance and speed, themselves form- ing a conspicuous and pleasing picture in the day's scene. various events were contested with commendable regu- larity, and there were some good displays. In only one instance was there any dispute or unpleasantness, the cora- znittee fa the first event (two miles walking handicap) find- ing it r;:ze-],itry to disqualify R. Davies, of Wrexham. Ex- oludic which took place on Friday, the programme contained 22 events, for each of which the entries were numerous, and some of the prizes were valuable. The arrangements were carried out by the following officials : Judges, Messrs. F. H. Gossage, E. Bolton, J. IL Crossley, E. A. Chorlton, Major Cross, and Dr. Booth; clerks of the curse, Messrs. C. E. Barlow, R. W. Whalley, D. Forster, A. W. Mcllwaine, and A. Speakman ; handicapper, official timekeeper and judge of walking, Mr. Walter Platt; pro- isesional starter, Mr. T. Wilkinson, Sheffield; hon. treasurer, Mr James Hurst; hon. secretary, Mr. C. E. Barlow; Secre- tary, Mr. Jae. W. Davies; representatives of the Northern Counties Athletio Association. The Star of Temperance Brass Band, under the conductorship of Mr. Kay, played selections II music during the afternoon. Refreshments were supplied by Mr. Doe, of Liverpool. Inspector Barnett, with aposse of policemen, was on the ground to preserve order, but the spectators were on the whole well behaved. The following is• a hat of the various events Two MILES WALKING HANDICAP (300 yards limit).—lst prizes silver sugar basin and sifter, value Os.; 2nd, silver oup ; 3rd, silver bladed knife. There were ten entries, and with one exception, all put in an appearance. J. Worrell, of Liverpool AC., started from scratch, while C. W. Lloyd tad 230 yards start. Lloyd, who had rather a heavy asp, walked well, but was the 6th man at the conclusion. Worrell made several efforts to secure a place, but he was too heavily handicapped, R. Davies, Wrexham (100 yards start), taking the first position at the end of the 3rd lap. This he maintained until he had half finished the last lap, when he suddenly stopped and stooped down, as if some- thing were amiss with his shoe. J. Jervis, Liverpool (40 yards start), who had been showing good form, then passed him. He kept the lead for some distance, but Davies again Starting " on the track" drew level, but again dropped off, and did not regain his position, coming in second. He was received with groans from the people round the winning post, and the committee asked him for an explanation. He stated he had stopped in consequence of a pain in his side, but quickly recovering himself, had endeavoured to win the rue. The committee, after considerable deliberation, came be the conclusion that he had wilfully lost the race, and disqualified him, while the public showed their view of the ratter by hissing him off the course. The result of the race was declared :-1, J. Jervis; 2, R. Parry. Liverpool (80 yds start); 3, R. Howard, Thornton Hough (120 yds start). Time 14 mine. 23 secs. HIGH LEAPING (running).—lst -prize, silver and pla- tinum goblet, value £4 45.; 2nd, silver cup; 3rd, silver bladed knife. Ten entered for this contest, but only three competed. Some good jumping was shown, the winner, R. F. Houghton, Newport F.C., clearing 5 feet 9 inches. D.' A. Brownfield, Trentham Park C.C. took the second place; and Tom Ray, of Ulverston, the third. 100 YARDS FLAT RACE. Ist prize, the club's gold medal, value £lO 10e.; 2nd, silver cup, value £3 3e.; 3rd, silver pencil case. Four ran, and the contest was exceed- ingly keen, the distance separating each man at the finish being very small. Ist, C. S. Johnstone, Moseley Harriers; 2, C. Cunliffe, St Helens R.F.C.; 3, J. Saxton, Broughton F.C. Time 11 and two-fifths secs.

120 YARDS FLAT RACE HANDICAP. - First prize, silver- mounted fias'r, value £5 55.; 2nd, silver cup; 3rd, silver fusee box. For this race there were 20 entries, and it was run in 3 heats, all of which were keenly contested. First heat, 1, A. Barlow, Rusholme F.C. (61) ; 2, W. Jackson, Litherland F.C. (11k). Won by 3 yards. Time 12 and two-firths sees. Second heat, 1, G. W. Rowley, Liverpool (6); 2, R.. r, Boughton, Newport F.C. (7). Won by half a yard. Tima 13 secs. Third heat, 1, J. Hancox, Waver- tree F.C. (10k); 2, J. Saxton, Broughton F.C. (6i). Won on the tape. Time 12 and four-fifths secs. Deciding heat, 1, A. Barlow; 2, J. Saxton; 3, W. Jackson. Won by a yard, one foot between second and third. Time 12 and one- fifth secs. .

- PCTTING THE SHOT (16033.) HANDICAP. - First prize, silver tongs, sifter, and butter knife, value £4 45.; 2nd, sil- ver cup; 3rd, silver fusee box. Out of the 20 who had en- tered, only 10 competed. let, R. hmall, Famwerth (7(t.) ; 2, J. Small, Farnworth (7) ; 3, N. Ford, Widnes (6). The distances were 38ft. llin., 37ft. ein , and 37ft. Sin. re- spectively. ONE MILE FLAT RACE. - First prize, timepiece and busts, value 30 guineas; 2nd, case of silver salt cellars and spoons, value £6 65.; 3rd, silver cup. Great interest was manifested in this race in consequence of W. G. George, of tdoseley Harriers, being a competitor. Only three ran, and George at once took the lead, closely followed by T. Crellin, Liverpool; while S. Hunt, Birkenhead, was 3rd. George, who-was evidently in "condition," ran in grand style, and easily maintained his lead. At the fifth lap, however, he was only about four yards in advance of Crellin, who was making a brave effort. Hunt bad fallen about 100 yards behind an 4 exhibited signs of fatigue. When the last lap was commenced, George put on a slight spurt, and increased his lead 10 yards, quickly making it 20. Crellin pluckily followed, but it was of no use, and George, ap- parently quite fresh, won easily by 50 yards, while Hunt was about half a lap behind Crellin. Ist, W. G. George ; 2nd, T. Crellin; 3rd, S. Hunt. Time 4 mine. 40 3-5 secs. Two MILES BICYCLE RACE HANDICAP.-First prize, case of silver salt cellars and spoons, value X 8 Bs.; 2nd, silver cup ; 3rd, silver pencil case. Of the 14 who entered, 10 ran, and the race was decided in three heats. In the first heat four competed, A. Fowler, Liverpool, taking the lead with 300 yard., W. Doming, Widnes F.C., coming next, with 170 yards, while 40 yards behind, G. A. Pennington, W.L.8.0 ,took up his position. C. W. Bayes, Anfield 8.C., was last, 80 yards from scratch. When about seven laps had been run, Hayes, who had been riding splendidly, had overtaken Pennington and Doming, but all his efforts tol overhaul Fowler were futile. Some good racing took place between Doming and Pennington, but eventually Doming drew ahead. 1, Fowler; 2, Bayes: 3, Doming. Won by two lengths. Time 7 MiDS. 44 secs. Six competitors took part in the second heat. When about six laps were to be run, F. Bate, Runcorn A 8.C., with 300 yards start, who had been leading, and riding steadily, had to take second place to T. A. Edge, Broughton A.B.C. (240 yards). In three more laps he was outrun by T. H. Overton, Liverpool (190), and G. 11. Illston, Royal Mail B.C. (160), who had been putting in some good speed. A contest then took place be- tween Illston and Overton for second place, the result being: Ist, T A. Edge; 2nd, G. H. Illston; 3rd, T. H. Overton. Seven minutes 431 secs. Only five yards separated the second and third men. Bate occupied the fifth place. Some good riding was exhibited in the concluding heat, but Edge won easily in 7 mins. 34 secs. Bayes, who was second in the first heat, had a nasty fall ' over his machine when making good headway. He slightly injured his band, and had to leave the course. Ist, T. A. Edge; 2nd, G. H. Iliston ; 3, T. H. Overton, ONlil MILE FLAT RACE HANDICAP.-First prize, carriage timepiece, value £lO 10e. ; 2nd, case of silver fish carvers, value £5 55.; 3rd, silver cup. Eleven ran. J. Wright, Widnes W.F.C. (75 yards), started in good style, and in three laps bad distanced S. Heat, Birkenhead (75), Bayes, Liver- pool (g 0 and Lloyd, Ellesmere (100). The lead thus gained he maintained till the finish, his good running calling forth plaudits from the spectators. The last man, Shay, Bootle (30), showed some exceedingly fine running, and came in second, Lloyd, with steady pace, taking the third position. Time 4 mins. and 35 secs. THREE-QUARTER MILE STEEPT.ECHASE HANDICAP.-First prize, marble timepiece, value £7 7s. ; 2nd, silver mustard pot, value £3 as. ; 3rd, silver bladed knife. For this event there were eight entries, and six competed. A slight accident occurrril to G. W. Wathen, Liverpool L.C.C,, in this race. When jumping the pit, which was about 12 feet wide, he alighted on the edge, and gave his leg a severe wrench. It was thought the limb was broken, but Wathen was afterwards able to walk about the grounds with the aid of a stick. let, W. Houghton, Widnes E.F.C. ; 2nd, T. Crellin; 3rd, W. Peters. Crellin was the only competitor who successfully leaped the pi', and he ran hard for the first place, only three-quarters of a yard dividing him from Houghton. Time 4 mine, and 26 2-5 secs. ONE MILE TRICYCLE RACE.-First prize, carriage time- piece, value £5 55.; 2nd, silver cup; 3rd silver pencil case. 1, W. Doming, Widnes F.C. ; 2, G. H. Illston, Royal Mail D.C.; 3, J. M. Fawke, Southport. Time 5 mine. 171-5 secs This was a splendid race. On the start Dorning at once took the first position with a lead of three yards, which by the end of the first lap he had increased to six. He, how- ever had a stiff opponent in Illston, and on one or two occasions they almost rode level; then Doming, putting on a spurt, would draw away again. Fawke showed some good riding.

HALF MILE FLAT 11/CE. —let prize (shield, presented by Messrs. Elkington acd Co.), W. G. George; 2nd (silver mustard pot and spoon, value £5 55.), D. McDonald, New Brighton, F.C. ; 3rd (silver cup), S. J. Hewitt, Newton. George won easily by several yards in t mine. 4 2-5 secs. QUARTER Mau FLAT BACE.-ISt priza, Club., gold medal, value £lO lOs ; 2nd prize, silver butter, preserve, and pickle spades, value £5 55.; 3rl, silver cup. There were AUX entries, and three ran, C. S. Johnstone, Moseley Harriers, winning very easily; F. SS'. Schofield, Liverpool, WdP second; and D. Davies, Bootle, third. lime, 56 secs. TUG OF WAR.—The heats for this event were contested on Friday, and the struggle for supremacy was between Messrs. N. Mathieson and Co.'s team of six men, and six employ6i of the Widnes Alkali Company, Limited. In the first pull Messrs. Mathieson's team proved the strongest, but in the sccond and third the men from the Alkali Company, although of slighter build than their opponents, were suc- cessful. The firs: pr:ze was six cases of spoons and tongs, value 15s. each ; and the second, six electro te3pots, value Is, 64 each.

silver mounted meat and fowl carvers, value £5 55.; 2nd, silver cup, value .E 3 31.; 3rd, silver fusee box. In this race, for which there were ten entries and nine competed, the jumping was very good, each hurdle being cleared in ex- cellent style, while the time in which it was run, 1 name. 4-5 secs., showed that there was no lack of speed. HALF MILE FLAT RACE HiNDICAP.—Ist prize, silver watch, value £5 55.; 2nd, silver cup; 3rd, silver pencil case. The feature of this race was the splendid running of J. Wright, Widnes W.F.C., who won easily in 2 mins. 2-5 sec., and he was heartily applauded. Ist, J. Wright (50) ; 2nd, N. G. Woodyat (45), Over W.F.C.; 3, T. Fitzpatrick (70), Widnes. Th( re were 20 entries, and 15 ran. POLE LEAPING.-15t prize (silver cup, value £4 45.), Tom Ray, Ulverston ; 2nd (silver cup), R. F. Houghton, Newport F.C.; 3+d (silver bladed knife), no competitor. So equal were the two competitors that it was with great difficulty the judges came to a decision, and their skilful leaping was universally admired. Two MILES FLAT RACE HANDICA?.—Ist prise, silver , cigar, cigarette, and match cases, value:£lo 10s.; 2nd, silver ' tankard, value £5 51.; 3,d, silver cup. This, the last event, was contested in a heavy fall of rain. Of the eight who entered to compete, si e ran, the in- , terest concentrating upon the running of W. G. George, I who was the scratchman. W. Honghton, Widnes (190 yds.) retired before he had concluded the first lap. At the 4th lap, George overhauled P. Shay, Bootle (100 yds.); while, with his swinging easy pace, he in the next lap placed him- elf in front of F. Crowth6r, Wakefield Trinity F.C. (130), and R. Beveridge, Black Heath Harriers (180), who had previously been passed by E. McCabe, Bootle (120). When there were two laps to run, McCabe had to give way to George, and then an exciting contest took place between the former and Shay for second place. Ist, W. G. George, 2nd, P. Shay; 3rd, E. div.head: FARNWORTH GENTLEMAN AND
div.p: THE FARNWORTH GENTLEMAN AND
THE CABMAN.

On Monday, at the Widnes Police Court, before Messrs. Ho'brook Gasket!, sen., and Holbrook Gaskell, jun., Mr. George Walker, cab proprietor, Liverpool, was brought up on remand from Friday, charged with stealing a watch, worth 305., and a waistcoat, worth 155., the property of Mr. Robt. Foster, of Farnworth.—Mr. G. B. Horner, of Liverpool, ap- peared for the defendant.—The prosecutor repeated the evi- dence of Frday, and in cross-examination by Mr. Horner, said he had a drink in Runcorn-street and in Clayton-square, Liverpool, during the afternoon of Thursday. Before he went to the latter place he paid £1 to another cab driver for a watch.
Mr. Horner : Which I presume you had pledged before for fares.—Witness : Yes.

Mr. Horner : How often have you ridden from Liverpool to Farnworth without paying P—Once or twice, and on two occasions perhaps he had pledged articles with the cabman for his fare. He did not know the prisoner before Thursdag, but he knew the driver, from whom he borrowed 2s. 4d. on the way ts Farnworth. He, however, returned the money whilst he was in the cab. Sometimes he stood drinks to the cabmen when going home, and on Thursday night they had two or three drinks together. Mr. Homer: Why didn't you pay the fare this night? Because I hadn't the money. When I arrived at Farnworth I had only 214. In answer to further questions, prosecutor alleged that the prisoner entered the ;al:, on purpose to rob him, and denied that he had deposited his waistcoat with the prisoner as security for his fare. He was not aware that he was called " cracleed Foster" in the neighbourhood. The prisoner's brother, the cabman, had on Saturday offered to give him his own watch to keen the thing quiet. The Chairman : What did the watch cost you ?—I have not paid for it yet. (Laughter). The Clerk: Have you paid for the vest yet P—No; I can get these things without paying for them ; which is more than everybody can do any way. Jane Clare, wife of John Clare, landlord of the Ring O'Bells, Farnworth, deposed that the prosecutor had lived at their house 12 days. About 9 o'clock on Thursday the proseeutor, the prisoner, and the cabman entered the house together, going into the kitchen. The prosecutor " stood " drinks for all three. In the absence of the prisoner and the cabman she saw the prosecutor pull his coat and waistcoat of and place them on the table. SubsEquently she was told the waistcoat was missing, but no mention was made of the watch.

P.C. Ross stated that about nine o'clock on Timrsday night he went to the Ring-o'-Bells, Farnworth, where a cab driver complained of the windows of his cab being broken, and afterwards the prosecutor informed him that his vest and watch were missing. Subsequently the prisoner was taken into custody. He was then wearing the vest produced over his own, and was in a state of intoxicttion. The watch could not be found. When charged the prisoner said, "I did not steal the vest; I gave him 2s. 4d. for it. The watch I know nothing about." Mr. HoaNER, in addressing the Bench for the defence, laid stress upon the fact that the prisoder had lent the pro- secutor 2s. 4d. in the cab, and though the prosecutor alleged he had returned the money, there was good reason to doubt that at ttement. From what the prosecutor had admitted in evidence, it was reasonable to suppose the prosecutor had given the waistcoat to the prisoner in pledge. He believed the charge was a trumped-up one, concocted in consequence of the policeman being sent for when the cab windows were broken.
The Chairman observed that as the waistcoat was found in the prisoner's possession, it was clear there was a case for a jury to decide, and the prisoner would be committed to trial.
The prisoner was then committed in the usual manner. He was admitted to bail, himself in 50 and two sureties of a 5 each.

div.head: CONFERENCE OF THE UNITED FREE GOSPEL CHURCHES.
div.p: CONFERENCE OF THE UNITED FREE GOSPEL CHURCHES.

On Monday, the 77th annual meeting of the United Free Gospel Churches was commenced in Salem Chapel, Nelson under the chairmanship of Mr. William Oxley (president). There was a good attendance of delegates, amongst whom were representatives from Warrington, Grappenhall, Lymm, Present, Wigan and other places.—The PRESIDENT said he thought there was much consolation in the fact that, taking the churches all round, they had an increase this year of 332 members. (Applause.) It was further gratifying te find that, besides an increase of 332 members, there was an in- crease of 194 members on trial, making a total increase of 526. (Hear, hear.) After urging them to cultivate a larger connexional spirit, he appealed to the churches for support and symp %thy, remarking they could not do the work they wished them to do thoroughly and efficiently without sub- stantial assistance.

Tbere were three gentlemen nominated for the position of president—Mr. William Oxley, of Manchester; Mr. M. Ken- nedy, of Southport; and Mr. W. Sanderson, of Liverpool. On a vote being taken. Mr. Kennedy was elected by a large majority, and he briefly returned tharks.—Messrs. W. Bri- melow and J. Hudlass, of Bolton, Were nominated for the office of vice-president, and Mr. Brimelow was elected. Mr. A. Roscoe, of Pemberton, was elected secretary, and Mr. J. Wild, of Oldham, vice-secretary. The connexional treasurer, Mr. E. Twiss, of Warrington, was re-appointed; and the editor of the magazine, Mr. W. Brimelow, was re-elected. Applications for admission into the Union had been received from two churches—Grappenhall, near Warrington, and Silksworth, Sunderland, and they were accepted. The re- port on the state of the churches showed that the number of churches was 90, a decrease of one, and other preaching places, 11. a decrease of two; number of members, 4,921, in- crease 32; number of ministers. 274, increase 13; number of teachers, 812, increase 81; number of scholars, 15,027, increase 717.

• On the proposition of the Vice-President the following resolution was submitted :—" That this annual meeting desires to place on record a profound expression of gratitude to Almighty God for the success which has crowned the labours of the church during the past year, as shown in the good spiritual condition of the churches, and especially in the largo addition to our membership; and urges the churches to renewed consecration of full service to the Master, in order that still more glorious results may be attained than those achieved during the past year." (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Wm. Sanderson seconded the motion, and, after being suppo;ted by several speakers it was carried.—During the year one rrinister, Mr. James Trickett, of Ince, had died, and a vote of condolence was passed. Votes of thanks were accorded to the officers during the past year, and the meeting was adjourned.—ln the evening a largely attended tea meeting was held in the schoolroom, and several addresses were delivered.

Business was resumed on Tuesday under the chairman- ship of the president (Mr. M. Kennedy). The Connexional Committee was appointed as follows :—Messrs. J. Knowles (nominated by the Warrington circuit), T. Pennington (Manchester), W. Crumblehulme (Bolton), J. Taylor (Wigan), A. Spencer (Cleckheaton), W. Bradshaw (Coins), J. Hudlass (Oldham), and W. Sanderson (Liverpool). Mr. Silas Cooke was appointed Connexional accountant and auditor. After considerable discussion the following resolu- tion was carried :—" That no members of the Connexional Committee who may be in receipt of moneys from the Ministers' Assistance Fund shall be allowed to vote on affairs of that fund." The following resolution was unani- mously paseed without discussion, on the proposition of Mr. Cook, seconded by Mr. Sanderson :—" That this asaem- blv. having regard to the hindranbes caused to the spread of the Gospel by the drink traffic on the Lord's Day, earnes'ly desires the Houses of Parliament to pass the Sunday Clcs- ing Bill forthwith, and thus accord to England the blessing of closed public-houses on the Sabbath, already enjoyed by Scoland and Ireland, and which is shortly to be enjoyed by the Principality of Wales. That a copy of this resolution, aimed by •the Presirlunt and secretary on behalf of the annual meeting, be forwarded to Mr. Gladeone and Earl Granville." It was agreed, on the proposition of Mr. Sanderson, that the next annual meeting be held at Sunder- land.

The PRESIDENT rend a paper on "How can we utilise the hest features of the Salvation Army Movement?" He remarhed that there were many lessons which they might learn from the strong faith of the "Army." The faith which animated its lenders was not an empty notion, but a living principle. It demonstrated the genuineness of the "Army's" character by the etececv of its influence; the *ld truths of the linle bad lost none of their freshness or

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 24,: 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 24,: 1882.

vigour; they never adopted any expedient such as penny readinga or sacred dramas to attract the people and get then' to their meetings; however low and degraded the people might be, they believed the Gospel could reach them, and showed. their faith by the efforts they put forth to rescue the perishing. If they meant to profit by the example of the "Army," they mast go and do likewise. They needed more of the faith that the Salvationists had. Speaking upon their aggressive work, the President said that in 17 years they had Galled out between 400 asd 500 evangelists, and in addition to this they had 14,000 "soldiers" ready to speak at any time. They had established themselves in most of the principal towns of the kingdom, and had also sent "c iptains " to America and Australia. Instead of talking so long about doing a certain thing, they got it done. If they intended to utilise this feature of the movement, they tnus.t lay aside their crotches respecting mission work, and pursue it with more faith and energy. They believed that the men who had beed trained up in their denomination were as pious, as well educated, as fit to be trusted, and as well adapted to do evangelistic labour as the " captains " of the Salvaticn Army movement. They did not repose the same confidence in their men as General Booth reposed in his "captains," or allow them the same privileges respecting the conducting of their services. The money feature of this movement was an impottant one, and one they needed to utilise, if ever they must make their principles known extensively. If they were raising £l,OOO a year—which was a small sum in comparison to their number—for evangelistic purposes, they would be capable of doing much more work than they were doing; and if the Salvation Army could raise £50,000 or £60,000 per year, and it had only been before the public 17 years, and they could not raise £l,OOO after 70 years of existence, it was time that there should be a reaction. If their people would respond more favourably to the appeals of the Evangelistic Secretary they would be able to do more aggressive work; and he felt convinced that if the leaders of their churches were favourable to this department of their labour, all opposition on the part of the people would dis- appear, and they would be in a position to storm every town in the kingdom. (Applause.)—An interesting dis- cussion followed, and a vote of thanks having been accorded to the President for kis paper, the meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the church for their hospitality. In the evening a temperance meeting was held in the school, and addresses were delivered by the President and others.

Truairs AND THEIR LODGINGS—CharIes Bowles, who made his second appearance, was charged with sleeping out on the previous night.—P.C. Pitt had discovered the priso- ner asleep in a chemical works.—Prisoner was committed to gaol for 7 days.—Richard Myerhouse and Martin Mitchell, tramp's, were charged with a similar offence, and were each sentenced to T days' imprirommnt—P.C. Anderson proved the calm.

FRlDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gasket!, jun. ALLEGED ROBBERY FROM A WAREHOUSE.--Elizibeth Glascheen and Elizabeth Taylor were charged with breaking and entering the warehouse lately occupied by Mr. Norbury, in Anne-street West. and stealing therefrom a dolly tub, a clothes line, a maiden, and a book case. Ellis Sankey holds a bill of sale on the warehouse, which was left in care of a boy named James Lyons, residing in Penn-street. On Satur- day morning the _ boy locked the premises, anti ou Thursday morning the door was eppn .oa the things were missed—P.S. MeCtzegor receiving information of the rob- bery made inquiries, in consequence of which he went to the house of the prisoner Glascheen. In a bedroom there he iound the clothes maiden (produced), and he asked Glas- cheen who it belonged to. She replied her children had brought it for firewood. Afterwards the officer found the dolly tub, and informed the prisoner the articles had been stolen from Norbury's warehouse. She then stated that she did not know who had stolen them, but she had taken them in from the back door for safety. The sergeant then visited Taylor's house, into which he had some difficulty in ob- taining an entrance, and found the bookcase in the back yard. Taylor said she " did not think there was any harm in having it, as she had known many people have things from the warehouse."—The prisoners were remanded until Monday, the Bench refusing to admit them to bail.

ALLEGED THEFT OF IRON—Martin O'Neil, a --boy nine years of age, was charged with stealing a quantity of scrap iron belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Company. The prisoner whilst walking through the streets with the iron was met by a constable, who took him into custody.—Remanded to Monday.

ley, which bears the name of Jas. Cross late chairman, the of a most .„ of the Board, was at work, and with the exceptio.l disagreeably loud noise from the valves, appeareia, to !lo it well. The imperfection in the valves, however, :111 be remedied. The works at this station have been in progrC's since 1875, and consist of an oval well 12 feet by 9 feet sunk through the red sandstone to a depth of a hundred feet, witn a 24 inch bore hole below it, making a total depth of about three hundred or four hundred feet below the surface. At the last meeting of the Board, the Chairman said he was under the impression the water at Netherley was depreciat- ing, and again Mr. Carey made an experiment. To the untrained eye there was no difference in the result of the test than was obtained at Stock'swell. It was understood, however, that the water was of a slightly inferior quality. In the neighbourhood of the gathering ground at Netherley is a sewage farm belonging to the Huyton-with-Roby Local Board, and doubts are entertained that the sewage may percolate-through the soil, and eeete—;....tet orne extent the we.te, in the well. Mr. Carey, accompanied with one or two members, and Mr. Dixon, visited a stream which flows past the works. Although iao specific indication of the presence of sewage in the stream, the suspicion was not entirely refuted, and Mr. Carey intends, we were informed, to convey two samples to his laboratory, where he will make an analysis. The probability is that,:even if the sewage does percolate through the soil, it will be purified before reaching the depth of the well. The inspection was now over, and orders were given to drive to Childwall Abbey. Fine weather had so far favoured the inspection, and the sun began to make feeble but ineffectual struggles to break through the clouds, but the atmosphere bri4htened suffici- ently-to make the drive through a most beautiful country very enjoyable. The route taken was through Gateacre, and having passed through that village, with its handsome church the companrwere driven along the "quiet peace- ful" lanes, and avenues of fine tall trees rich with foliage, their umbrageous branches gracefully stretching far across the road. Splendid mansions were passed in rapid succession, until there broke upon the view of the party Childwall Abbey in all its beauties—the ivy clad castellated walls of the ancient hall, the picturesquely situated church, with that peaceful solemnity born only of antiquity, and the old abbey itself, mantled in a green covering, and with curiously shaped heads looking upon us from its walls as the conveyances drew up at the door, for the abbey, or what remains of it, is new converted into an hotel, and here the company were to have tea. While this desirable adjunct to the afternoon's drive was being prepared, an opportunity was afforded of viewing the beauties of the locality, which was fully taken advantage of. The curious inscriptions on the old gravestones were full of interest, many of the stones bearing the date of the 17th century, one it was stated being discovered which went so far back as the 11th century. The landscape, as seen from the church yard, was exceedingly fine, the dark luxuriant foliage of the many plantations which dotted the ground, forming a pleasant contrast to the bright green of the grass, while in a coppice distant as far as the eye could discern, nested the mansion of, probably, a rich merchant prince. Tea was partaken of about half-past six; afterwards the time was " whiled " away in many ways until 9-15, when the homeward journey was commenced, the Board offices being reached about 10-20.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAT.—Before Messrs. John Brundrit (chairman) and Charles Reynolds. AN UNLAWFUL SETTLEMENT.—Peter Leather was sum- moned by Mr. Thomas Moore, landlord of the Vine Hotel, for being disorderly on his premises and refusing to leave. —The complainant said he was under the impression that he coul I settle the case out of court, and had accepted the payment of costs from the defendant in settlement.—lt appeared the defendant had previously been before their worships, and the Chairmen said they could not allow the case to be settled out of court in that manner. The case would consequently be adjourned to next Monday. STONE THROWING.—MichaeI Mannion, a boy 14 years of age, was charged with having, on the 11th instant, thrown stones in Brilge-street.—P.C. Bossons stated that on the day named he saw the defendant throw a stone under the bars of Delf Bridge at a passing flat, which was struck on the forecastle.—Defendant had no defence, and he was fined is and 9s dcl c ,sts, with the alternative of seven days' im- pris,mment, the Chairman expressing the hope that this would impress upon him the danger of such practices. If he committed a second offence be would be severely punished.

DISORDERLY WOMEN.—Catherine M'Cann was fined 10,s and 9s 6d costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, for being drunk and disorderly in Mersey-street on the 10th Jane.—P.C. Morris proved, the case.—Sarah Percival, for using obscene and profane language in Zion-place, on the 12th June. was mulcted in the sum of 5s and 9s 61 costs. BREACHES OF THE EDUCATION ACT.—Mr. Bowyer, school attendance inspector, summoned, on behalf of the School Board, the following persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school, and they were dealt with as follows :—Sarah Stannard, Brunswick-street, fined 55.; John Abbot,Mill-street, 55.; James Chambers Wellington-street, ss; Wm. Brown, Duke-street, 55.; John Filkin, Percivals- lane, warrant issued; Ellen Johnston, Stone Hills, 55.; Joseph Wilson, Mill Brow, 55.; John McDonald, King- street, 55.; Wm. Brazendale, Mill 8r0w,55.; Robert Massey, Jackson's-lane, 55.; John Henry Molyneux, Cemetery Field, ss.

THErr BY • 5E127115T Gpm.—Fanny Hopkins, 16 years of age, whose parents lice at Frodsham, was charged wi h stealing 14s. 11d, and a gold necklet, the property of Mrs. E. Stall.—The prosecutrix is a tobacconist in High-street, and a fortnight ago tool: the prisoner in her service. Last week she suspected some money bad been taken from the till, and on Friday she missed 6s. 61 from a cash box which was placed in a bedroom. Next morning she also missed a gold necklet. She called the prisoner to her, and asked her if she had seen it, as it was safe when she was cleaning the room on the previous day. The prisoner commenced a search for the necklet, and in about five minutes said she had found it in the "next drawer." Mrs Stall then accused her of stealing the money horn the cash box, which she admitted, and further stated she had thrown half-a-crown in the ashpit, which was subsequently found by PS. Walley, and had abstracted some money from the drawer with which to buy the boots she then wore. Mrs. Stall then found 6s 5d hidden in an old carpet, and 63. in copper in another piece. —P.S. Walley apprehended the prisoner on Saturday at noon, and, when charged with the robbery, she answered "Yes." —The prisoner was fined 20s. and costs, or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. James Reynolds and S. B. Chadwick.

THE EXTRAVAGANCES OF A BOAT LAD.—Job Longson, a lad 11 years of age, was brought up on remand from War- rington charged with having feloniously stolen £3, the monies of his father.—lt appeared the prosecutor is a boat- man for Mr. George Horsefield, and on Friday the boats of which he has charge were lying in the anal near Sprinch. At that time a purse containing £3 was safe in a cupboard in the cabin, but next morning abont six o'clock the prisoner and the money wer3 missing. Shortly after that hour the prisoner gave a boy named Thomas Williamson, of Pennington's-row, a sovereign, which he afterwards gave to Mr. Horsefield. The prisoner then made his way to Warrington, where, from the statement of Superintendent Williamson, he went into all kinds of youthful extra- vagances, purchasing in the market there a bird cage, a rabbit, three or four small boats, and other things. Mr. Hunt, the Chief Constable of Warrington, hearing of this, had the boy apprehended, and then communicated with the police at Runcorn. The boy was subsequently given in charge of P.S. Bossons.—ln reply to interrogation from the Bench, the boy's father said he had a house at Bugsworth Derbyshire, but the boy lived on board one of the' boats, and had never been to school.—ln sentencing the boy to six strokes with the birch rod, the Chairman said he was not all sorry the father had lost the money; he ought to have educated his child better.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell, Ben., and Holbrook Gaskel I, junr.
rNEBRIATES.—Catherine Kenny, Michael Gormley and David Ankers were each charged with being drunk at Widnes on :•_aturday night, and a fine of ss. and costs was imposed in each case.

Assarm's ON TNE Poracm—Patrick Riley, who made his sth appearance, was charged with having on Saturday, assaulted P.C. Irvine. That officer was on duty in Waterloo- road, and hearing a disturbance in an adjacent chemical works, lie proceeded there. When he arrived the prisoner struck him on the face with his fist and then ran away. He was subsequently captured, and be again assaulted the officer.—Prisoner was fined 20s. and costs.—James O'Hara was brought up on a charge of assaulting P.C. Barker. This officer stated he found two men fighting in Well ington- street on Saturday night, and he took one of them into cus- tody. 'Phe prisoner then walked up to him and assaulted him, kicking him several times. He also struck another constable on the face, and the prisoner who had been apprehended made his escape.—Mr. T. J. Peters, who appeared for the prisoner, having addressed the Bench, the Chairman said they considered this a bad case, and committed the prisoner to gaol for a month with hard labour.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun, (chair-
man), and Mr. John Brock.

A DEFAULTING RATEPAYER.—AIfred Dutton, publican, of the Marsh, Widnes, was summoned by the Local Board for £5 5s lid, the amount of a gas and water rate due from him.—The defendant, who did not appear, was ordered to pay the morky in seven days, or in default serve a month's imprisonment.

IntIINIEEWNRSS.—Thomas Glynn and Patrick McDonald were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness. BREACHES OF THE PEACE, &c.—Elizabeth Ann Hill, a married woman, was summoned by Rachael Johnson for using language calculated to provoke a breach of the peace on the 13th June, and she was bound over to keep the peace, or in default 14 days' imprisonment.—Peter Riley and Michael Malone were etch charged with committing a breach of the peace on the 10th June. The defendants, it appeared, were fighting tog_ther in Waterloo-road. Riley was bound over to keep the peace for three months in the usual sureties. Malone did not appear, and a warrant was issued for his apprehension.—For committing a breach of the peace in Pepper-street, on the 10th inst., John 'McCleary was biind over to keep the peace for three months, himself in .£lO and two sureties of .£5 each.—Ann Greaves was bound over for_t he same period for a like offence.

Pero AND Toss.—John Delaney, Wm. Wymm, and John Hinchky, boys, were summoned on a charge of play- ing pitch and toss at Widnes, on the 10th instant, to which they all pleaded not guilty.—An officer said he saw the boys playing pitch and toss in Travis-street, on the day in ques- tion, when they ran away. He, however, eventually caught them. The father of one of the defendant's appured in .court, and alleged that some other boys were playing pitch and toss, and that the constable not bring able to catch them, reported the defendants.—The magistrates itnpsed a fine of Is. and costs on each defendant.

A TRUMPERY Cass.—John Henry Edwardaon, a youth, who described himself as a printer, sun-anoned another youth, named Thomas Davies, for an assault.—The com- plainant stated that on Saturday last he was playing with a soft bill when it went into the defendant's yard. He went to recov.r it, and the defendant struck him on the face._ The defendant exprained that his younger brother had a•-isoal the ball, and that the complainant was ia consequence ill-

div.head: STOCK AND SHOE MARKET.
div.p: STOCK AND SHOE MARKET.

Messrs. Joseph R. and P. Baines, sharebrokers, 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (June 22) : The weather during the past few days has been very wet, and this, coupled with the disturbed state of political affairs, has had a depressing effect on the share markets. Specu- lative stocks, the most pro nineet of which have recorded numerous fluctuations, have mostly tended downwards, fol- lowing the lead of Consols, which on the week show a decline of 1. Egyptian Stocks have jumped about quickly, the highest and lowest prices on some days being very wide. Canadian Railways have!also marked some quickly-changing prices, leaving off to-day with a decline on the week. In the other classes a moderate number of transactions are reported, prices realised, except in a few instances, compar- ing favourably with those ruling a week ago.—Coal, #c., Mining: The business done in this class has been mainly in Bolckows fully paid and Ebbw Vales, the former of which have passed at or near last week's figures, whilst the latter have fallen away. The dealings in others have been solitary and at prices calling for no special mentton. On Friday last the Indian Gold Mines quoted here were done at an ad- vance, but have receded since, and now only Indian Phcenix exhibit any change. Quotations show a great majority of changes for the worse, but only a few severe ones. Bolckows £l2 paid remain almost stationary, the buyers' figure stand- ing unchanged, whilst the sellers' price is down a fraction. Ebbws have slipped during the past two days, having shown only fractional change up to Tuesday last inclusive: Canadian Coppers, little doing, and the turn easier. Llynoi and Tendw Coal, drc., lower, the ordinary especially. Nanty, Glo, and Blaina with no business recorded shew a fall from 49-50 to 48 49}. Rio Tiritos of both issues also are lower. Higher India Phcenix gold /. United States Rolling Stock Lower Stavely Coal, clic. A. 1. Thareis Sulphur, ezc. Rio Tinto -If. Llynoi and Tendw ordinary -1, ditto, preferred 1-16, Ebbw Vale Steel and Iron g. A. Knowles and Sons, ±. Cammello, Nantyglo and Blaina preferred Chillington iron, 13-- and Canadian copper 6d. Cotton Spinning and Mann.factur- ing : Notwithstanding a fair amount of activity in the cotton market these shares have gone very flat and though quotations are not much altered owing to sellers not pressing lots on the market to any large extent, buyers are scarce except at is. or 2s. lower than last week's prices, and in some cases more reduction is asked to bring about business. Some few concerns, however, maintain their figures very steadily, and for these buyers still meet with little response from sellers. The present case points to the late rise, being to a large extent a speculative movement, but the fact that prices shew so little change or realizations tends to prove that holders view the future with confidence.—Telegraphs: The changes are all adverse and Anglos of all issues are prominent in the movement. Ordinary and deferred being each and preferred 2 lower.—ln Telephones Lancashire and Cheshire have changed hands a few times at steady figures. Uniteds after being done once (Saturday last) mark a fall of i.—Corporation Stocks, #c.: Quite firm what lots are passing, being chiefly "odd lots," and for these full prices generally are realized. Manchester Corporation Consolidated Stock are again marked better.—Railways: The Egyptain difficulty has caused numerous fluctuations and changes, and the result on the week is a heavy decline all round. Heavy lines shew a distinct fall although traffics are well supported. Most attention has been devoted to Canadians in which variations have been extreme and rapid, the question of "fusion having been stated as broken down, and then once more arranged causing the wide changes which are marked. In Americans, Philadelphia and Readings have shewn most activity, but prices have relapsed since the lower (potations from 'New York.

div.head: ANNUAL INSPECrIoN OF WIDNES
div.p: ANNUAL INSPECrIoN OF WIDNES
WATERWORKS.

Conforming to their annual custom, the members of the Widnes Local Board on Thursday held an inspection of the waterworks, at Stockswell and Netherly. Whether on a business or a pleasure excursion, the weather, on all oc- casions uncertain, has aa important effect on its success; and in this instance as the time fixed for the start, two o'clock, drew nigh, the members could be seen wending their way to the Board's offices, Alforde Chambers, through mud and pools of water, with upturned trousers, and clad in over- coats. Truly not a pleasant augury for a drive into the country. Owing to certain late arrivals, it was balf-past two before the members had commenced their journey, and the rain had then ceased thouwh dark clouds still hovered over- head. A waggeinette, drawn by three fine grey horses from the stables of Mr. Lea, of Widnes, took the lead followed by a cab to which were harnessed two black hacks. 'rise com- pany bad to regret the absence of the Chairman of the Board, Mr. F. H. Gossage, Dr. Booth, Mr. Kershaw, and Mr. Forster, while in addition to the other members present whose names are Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. F. H. Pankhurst, E. Carey, T. Handley, E. Martley, J. Midwood, J. E. Johnson, D. Wright, and H. Webster, there were Messrs. J. r. Allen (clerk), Roberts (water engineer), Higginson (surveyor), and Dickson (nuisance inspector). Stockswell pumping station was the place to be first visited, and for there the conveyances directed their course. They ran along ap- parently all right, but when a short distance past the Congre- gational chapel in Milton-road, a crash, which sounded like the snapping of an axle, ems heard in the waggonette. The vehicle at the same titne gave an alarming lurch_to one side, and its occupants jumped to their feet. Soon recovering, however, from any alarm they may have felt, they again seated themselves, and were laughingly informed that the driver's whip had got entangled in a wheel and broken. This admitted of an easy remedy, and the carriages were quickly moving towards their destination. Entering Stuart's- lane, a view of smoke-begrimed Widnes, with a portion of the viaduct, was seen, its many chimneys belching forth volumes of fumes. Evidences of their deleterious qualities were only too palpable. To the right, and to the left, the country was studded with what had once been trees; once, we say, for now they are shorn of all foliage, and are merely upright poles; less painful, indeed, to see than when, as in some instances, the tree, making a last faint effort for life, put forth a few scorched brown leaves on its lower branches. Passing Hough Green station a glimpse of Pex Hill was caught, and having increased our distance from Widnes, the vegetation had a much improved appearance, more and more noticeable as the conveyances approached Stockswell, which was reached shortly after three o'clock. Although previously described, we may state the works here were commenced during the early part of 1868, and the _year fol- lowing were completed. Originally they consisted of a 10 feet circular well sunk to a depth of 60 feet from the surface, from which the water is pumped by a pair of 50 horse-power, double-acting beam, connensing engines, and delivered into the reservoir at Pex Hill by a 16-inch rising mEn of about two miles in length. Subsequently extensions were made, a second well of nine feet diameter, sunk to a depth of 62 feet, and having a 24-inch borehole below it to an additional depth of rather over 238 feet. This well is surmounted by an engine of the ball Cornish type of about 120 horse-power. The two engines over the old well are named " Virginia " land "Mars'," so called after the wives of Mr. John Knight, formerly Chairman of the Gas Committee, and Mr. McLellan, a former Chairman of the Board, respectively. The engine which works the other well is named "Frederick H. Gos- sage," and it is this which performs most of the work at Stockswell. At each stroke it raises 130 gallons, and nearly a million gallons per day of 24 hours. On Thursday this engine was at work, and its smooth action, and the scrupulous cleaniinees of the machinery, which had the highest degree of polish possible, was universally admired. Descending from the engine room the members were much interested in a test Mr. Carey applied to a glass of the drinking water he had obtained in order to ascertain if it contained any impurities, but especially decayed vege- tation, and the result was very satiefactory, no perceptible teace being discovered. Being now about half-past three,l the company again seated themselves in the vehicles and were quickly driven through Tarhock to the prettAy situated works at Netherley. For a short period only have these works been used, and additional interest was lent to the visit by the fact that the engine at work was on its trial for a month, a fortnight of which time has elapsed. it is a very powerful one of the some type as No. 2 at S:ockawell. It has the power of 130 horses, and delivers into the reservoir about 1} co 1?-; millions of gallons per day of 24 hours. The consumption of water per day at Widnes is about 11 mil- lions of gallons, and it will thus be seen that from Nether- icy alone the town could receive an almost sufficient supply of water. Indeed, the supply is almost solely received from Netherlev, the engines at Stockswell lazing but occasionally used. Al tin time of Ike inspection, the engine at Nether-

div.head: RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.

PROPOSED DEMONSTRATION. . As previously intimated, the inauguration of the Free Library will he celebrated on the 6th proximo, when Sir J. A. Picton, r.s.A., will visit Runcorn for the purpose of declaring it open; and we think our readers will be pleased to hear of the arrangements which are either made or con- templated, to give eclat to the event. The ceremony is fixed to take place at the public offices at six o'clock, and shortly before that hour Sir J. A. Picton is expected to arrive. Immediately afterwards a procession will be formed, and we have been informed that circular notes have been sent to several Friendly Societies inviting them to join in the procession. Other bodies have also had similar intimations conveyed to them; and Captain Hazlehurst has kindly con- sented to allow the excellent band of the Rifle Volunteers to head the procession, Dr. Steele, the chairman of the Com- missioners, also intends asking the tradesmen to close their establishments at four o'clock in the afternoon, so that the shop assistants and others employed may take part in the demonstration. The procession will leave Fountain Square about a quarter-past six, and by a circuitous route arrive at the Public Hall shortly afterwards. A monstre tea is being arranged, to be followed by a public meeting, presided over by the chairman of the Free Library Committee, the Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A. At this meeting an address is ex- pected to be delivered by Sir J. A. Picton, which we have no doubt will be looked forward to with pleasurable antici- pations. Other gentlemen, including J. Simpson, Esq., C. Wigg, Esq., G. S. Hazlehurst, Esq., and Dr. Steele will also take part in the subsequent proceedings. We also under- stand that the leading gentlmen of the district will be in- vited to give countenance to the proceedings by their presence. Arrangements are also being made for the decoration of the Public Offices, Public Hall, and other places by the hoisting of fltgs and banners, and we doubt not if the day prove fine the town will have a holiday appearance. The Committee seem to be doing all in their power to make the inaugural ceremony a complete success, and to anticipate every possible contingency.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF CoMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF CoMMISSIONERS.

The annual meeting of this Board was held at the Board- room, on Wednesday morning, Dr. Steel presiding. There were also present Dr. McDougall, Messrs. T. Norman, J. J. Speakman. W. Whittaker, W. Lake, W. Handley, D. E. Taylor, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), and Brooks (secretary).
ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN. DR. STEEL ON THE FREE LIBRARY.
The CHAIRMAN intimated that the business of the meet- ing was the election of some member to fill the chair, which he vacated.

The LAW CLERIC then took the chair, and Mr. NORMAN rose and eaid it behoved him, in the first place, to move a vote of thanks to Dr. Steel fcr presiding over the Board for the past year. He thought, Dr. Steel had been the right man in the right place; be did not know that there had been anything that any member of the Board could find fault with during the past year; and he (Mr. Norman) was sure they could not do better than to again appoint Dr. Steel chairman for another year. (Hear, hear.) If that met with the wishes of the Board he would at once move that their best thanks be given to Dr. Steel for his services during the past year, and that he be re-appointed chairman for the ensuing year. (Hear, hear.) Dr. McDoulatar, said he thought the thanks of the Board were due to Dr. Steel for the manner in which he had con- ducted the business of the Board for the past year. There ' had been a goad many knotty questions discussed at the Board during that period. Some of them were not yet solved, and would require time before they were brought to an issue; and he thought it extremely desirable, from that point of view, that the ehairman who had had all these matters under his supervision, should continue to supervise them until they were brought to an issue in some way or other. He (Dr. McDougall) was himself largely indebted to Dr. Steel for privileges accorded himself on more than one occa- sion. They had differed on different public matters, and were "agreed to differ." Suffer him, however, to give his cordial concurrence with Dr. Steel's appointment for another year. He thought the Board could not do better than re- appoint him, and thus show that they felt generally indebted to him for the courteous and gentlemanly manner in which the business of the Board had been con- dected during the past 12 months. He concluded by second- ing the motion proposed by Mr. Norman. The resolution wis carried unanimously, ard Dr. STEEL was applauded on taking the chair. He said he had to thank them for the confidence they had placed in him in again bestowing upon him the office of chairman. He had alsa to thank the members for the uniform kindness and courtesy he had received from them during the past year. Although he should have been glad to have laid aside the cares of the chairmanship, yet he should have had some feelings of regret in doing so. (Hear, hear.) He thought no event of movement had taken place in the history of Runcorn during the past year, except the adoption of the Free Libraries Act by the ratepayers. This was a thing which would be a great boon to the public generally,—(hear, hear)—and especially to the working classes. At the same time, he did not think the working classes generally appre- ciated the movement, but no doubt in time they would be brought to see the use of the library, and, if they did not read learned works, they would at any rate read novels, which was better than spending their time in public houses, and such places. (Hear, hear ) He had pleasure in inform- ing them that Sir James Picton had consented to open the library on the 6th July. it was intended to make some demonstration in order to bring the library before the notice of the public generally, and also to have a public tea party in the Public Hall, which they hoped would be largely at- tended. The shopkeepers were to be asked to close their shops at four o'clock on that day, to allow of their young men to attend tea and take part in the demonstration. (Hear, hear, and applause) This concluded the public business of the Board.

div.head: FAILING TO PAY THE POOR RATE:
div.p: FAILING TO PAY THE POOR RATE:
A HARD CASE.

At the Warrington Petty Sessions, on Wednesday—he7ore Messrs. George Artingstall (chairman), S. Rigby, and P. Stubbs—William Wright, a farmer at Arpley, was. sum- moned for non-payment of two poor rates, amounting La the aggregate to £3 9s. ad. It was stated that two rates had been levied, both of which the defendant had failed to pay. The first was £1 us. al and be second LI Is. Mr. Moore (who appeared for the defence) said that for the last two or three seasons the. defendant had suffered very much through floods, and he had lost all his crops. Last year he was com- pelled to file a petition, and the creditors had accepted a com- position of 2s. 6d. in the Z. He had paid his landNrd, and. through the kindness of friends, who had lent him money, he continued on the farm. He was unable to pay the rats, , and he (Mr. Moore) askcd their worships to excuse him en the ground of poverty. He was really unable to pay it, and. would hate no means of doing so until he had got his crops in.—Mr. J. Fairhurst (the collector) stated that the defen- dant had paid his creditors as required under the-Bankruptcy Act. He opposed the application i of Mr. ffloore.—Mr. Moore: The first composition is payable n about a week, mud if the rate collector would accept the composition in 'part payment of the rates it will be paid. He really has no means of payir.g the whole until he gets his crops in this rair.—Mr. Fairhurst : I would ask your worships t(t grant me a distress warrant.—

The Bench: Why won't you give him time? Mr. Fair- hurst : We should do so if you would grant me a warrant. —The Bench : What did you say the first rate was ? Mr. Fairhurst : LI Hs. 81., and the second Li 185.—The Chair- man: Well, if you get an order for £1 lie. Bd. you will be sat'sfied. Mr. Fairhurst: I don't want an order for payment; I apply for a warrant.--The Deputy Clerk (Mr. Nicholson): ;yants a distress warrant—The Chairman : For the whole Mr. Fairhurst : Yes, sir. We will take care that it is not i,ed at once. This is the only legal way of pro- ceeding.—Tht: Chairman: There appears to be no alterna- tive, and we TMI3: grant the warrant.—Mr. Moore asked if the case could not be adjourned, so as to give time for the defendant to pay the rai.ses. If a warrant was issued now it might be put in force at once.—Mr. Fairhurst: They can trust us for that—Mr. Rigby, J.P. : They will accept a recommendation from the Bench not to put it in force at once.

div.head: ELECTION OF MEMBEIti OF THE
div.p: ELECTION OF MEMBEIti OF THE

RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. A public meeting of the ratepayers of Runcorn was held in Bethesda school, Vicar-street, on Thursday evening, for the purpose of appointing three members of the Burial Board, in place of Messrs. Samuel Collier, Peter Briscoe,and Wm. Whittaker, who retired by rotation, but who were eligible for re-appointment. There was a fair attendance, and the Rev. Canon Barclay presided. After the notice convening the meeting had been read, The REV. CtIAIRMAN remarked that after looking back at the first meeting held for the election of the Burial Board, where they had the advantage and advice of a very efficient, law clerk, he thought it would be better if they proceeded on the sames lines, viz.,that when a gentleman was proposed, either have him elected or discarded. Mr. H. CoLsBuRN proposed the re-election of Mr. Peter Briscoe. Mr. TEtos. RILEY seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. On the motion of Mr. Wm. DYER seconded by Mr. SEFTON, Mr. Whittaker was also re-elected. Mr. HOUGHTON then nominated Mr. James Dobson, who was seconded by Mr. T. STRINGFELLOW. Mr. LITTLER proposed the name of Mr. Wm. Mellor, and the motion was seconded by _Mr. ADAMS.

A RATEPAYER asked if he would be in order in nominating another gentleman, and the CHAIRMAN replied that he thought it would be better if they bad one amendment alt once.—The names of Mr. Dobson and Mr. Mellor were then submitted to the meeting, and the result was: Mellor 17 votes, Dobson 2.—A Ratepayer then nominated Mr. Handley as a member of the Burial Board.

Mr. HANDLEY : I may as well save you the trouble of voting. I have so many public offices that I can not add another to the ones I already bold. I thank you all the same but I really must withdraw my name. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN remarked that many of the ratepayers would be sorry to hear the declaration of Mr. Handley. With Mr. Handley's retirement, he had to declare that Messrs. Peter Briscoe, Wm. Whittaker, and Win. Mellor had been elected.

div.head: NOMINATION OF fIIARDIINS.
div.p: NOMINATION OF fIIARDIINS.

The Rev. CHAIRMAN observed- there was another point which the Overseers had suggested, and which they wished to introduce to their notice. They would be aware that only two out of five were elected at the last election of Guardians, and a public meeting was afterwards held, at which it was decided to apply to the Local Government Bcard for an order to hold a special election. That order had been received. In olden time Guardians were elected at towns' meetings like that, which saved a great deal of the trouble, inconve- nience, and expense arising out of the present system. He thought they might have three candidates proposed at that meeting, although they would not be legally elected, and any one not present would not ha prevented, if he thoagtit necessary, from nominating others. He scarcely thought, however, that any ratepayer would take upon himself the responsibility of having a contested election, which would involve an expenditure of between £4O and £so.—lt was ultimately decided that the late members, Messrs. William Whittaker, William Fisher, and William Handley, should be nominated.—Mr. WM. HANDLEY then proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman, which was seconded by Dr. McDouctem,, and carried unanimously.

div.head: CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE. MR. G. W. LATHAM AND HIS CRITICS.
div.p: THE CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE. MR. G. W. LATHAM AND HIS CRITICS.

"A Cheshire Landlord," writing to the editor of the Standard, says:—"Sir,—No significance at all is attached in Cheshire to the revolutionary resolutions lately passed by the so-called Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture, and noticed in your impression of to-day. The Cheshire farmers are, for the most part, contented, and, as times go, prosperous, and thoroughly loyal to their landlords. But an unsuccess- ful candidate for Parliament in the Liberal interest at the lest election has lately been trying to persuade the tenant- farmers of Cheshire that they have grievances against their landlords, though the county has been ransacked in vain to discover them. He formulated (as he expressed it to the meeting) these resolutions, and he tells the farmers that if they will only send to Parliament some one who will keep up a constant agitation on the subject, he will, in that truly liberal spirit which lavishly gives away what belongs to others, enrich them with spoil taken from their landlords. It is hardly to be expected that all tenant-farmers will be virtuous enough to refuse the prize which this Prcesens Mercurius ' thus offers them. Still it must be remembered that the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture is not a repre- sentative body, but comprises anyone who fancies he has a grievance to ventilate, and who is willing to pay five shillings a year, and that out of ten thousand tenant-farmers in Cheshire not one in ten is a member of the Chrmber at all, and not one in a hundred was present at the meeting at which these resolutions were passed." Mr. G. W. Latham replied as follows:—Sir,—l am so pointedly alluded to in your columns of to-day in a letter from "A Cheshire Landlord," that Lbelieve myself to have a claim on you for the insertion of a few lines in reply. "A Cheshire Landlord" brings the charge against me that, being a defeated candidate for a seat in Parliament at the last election, I have since that time, and in consequence of that defeat, been stirring up teriant farmers against landlords, and offering in return for their support on some future occa- sion to enrich them with the property of their landlords. I began to agitate some 15 years ago for the legislative altera- tion of certain lawaand legal presumptions which I believed injured landowners, producers, and consumers. Since the general election of 1880 I have, in Cheshire at least, said less, rather than more, on this subject, and I challenge "A Cheshire Landlord" to produce a single word of mine, either spoken or written, whieta advocates any spoliation of the landlords. As a landowner myself I am hardly likely to have suggested such a course, though lam proud that I have never ceased, and hope never to cease, to protest against laws and presumptions which enable a grasping landlord to appropriate another man's pro- perty either by annexing what is left unexhausted by the outgoing tenant without payment, or by raising the rent of a tenant on improvements made by himself. All honest men are now agreed as to the wickedness of such procedure, and the qucstion among them is merely how this act of honesty may be most effectually carried out. There were five resolutions, which "A Cheshire Landlord " is pleased to call revolutionary, carried at the meeting and the adjourned meeting of the Chamber. The first related to unexhausted improvements, to be at the wish of either party assessed by arbitrators; the second to an enlarged notice to .quit—a change which had Lord Betconsfield's approval; the third to the necessity of a good and cheap Court, prin- cipally as a remedy against injury by tenants to property in their hands, which Court it was suggested might be found in the County Court Judge; the fourth, to freedom of culti- vation and of sale; and the fifth to the abolition of the Law of Distress. For my part, I attach little significance to the carrying of these resolutions, for I believe that no gathering of honest men could refuse to pass them; but I do attach significance to the fact that a select club of a few landlords spoke and voted against all measures of justice, and tried by proposals of adjournment and quibbles of every kind to pre- vent an honest expressions of the opinions of the tenants. No one claims that the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture is representative, but it is at all events as much so as the Central Chamber of Agriculture, whose vote on this question "A Cheshire Landlord" has probably seen. I hardly know to which of the diverse characters of " Mercurius," or to which of the many dictionary meanings of "Prcesens" " A Cheshire Landlord" means to refer, when he calls me by the name of that heathen deity. lam afraid that he uses a dead language to assert that I am a capable thief. If lam this, at all events lam a more disinterested thief than even Robin Hood was. He stole from the rich , and gave to the poor. I, should the measures which I advo- cate turn out to be acts of spoliation, shall be robbing myself, as a landowner, to enrich those who are tenants on this estate. On the contrary, I believe that landlords would benefit by the proposed changes more than tenants would, and I have at least given proof of my solid belief in this opinion by giving agreements which, as far as Possible, place those who occupy my land in, exactly the same position as all tenants would be should these resolutions become the law of Great Britain.

div.p: FRODSHAM.

VOLUNTEER PARADE. - On Saturday the Frodsham Yolunteer Corps paraded in full uniform. and marched to the residence of Captain Robert Ashton, of Newton. It bad been intended to go through various movements and a sup- ply of blank ammunition had been served out, but owing to the very unfavourable weather the manosavres had to be dispensed with. Substantial refreshments were plentifully provided by Captain Ashton and were done full justice to. This is the fourth. occasion on which. the volunteers have received invitations, and credit is due to Sergeant-Instruc- tor Flannagan for the interest which he has enlisted in or lscal volunteer corps.

ROYAL COU.NTIES AGRICULTURAL SHOW.—The Royal Counties Agricultural Show opened at Preston Park, Brighton, on Thursday. The weather was wet till late in the afternoon, but there was a largo attendance. The ex- clusion of cattle somewhat detracted from the general interest. In addition to horses, sheep, pigs, and imple !lents) there was a capital rose, poultry, and bee show,. for which prizes were offered. In the afternoon the annual dinner was held, the Duke of Norfolk presiding. There was a numerous attendance, including the boroned) and county members. POLITICAL ITEMS. Lord John Moaners, to whom leave of absence from the House of Commons was granted, on Tuesday, for five weeks' is suffering from a renewal of gout, and will spend a month at Hamburg. Mr. R. W. Duff was, on Saturday, nominated and re- elected without opposition for Banffshire, the vacancy having been caused by the honourable gentlearan's appoint- ment as Junior Lord of the Treaauiy. In the division, on Tuesday evening, upon Mr. Glad- stone's motion that the Arrears Bill should have precedence over all other business in Parliament except the Crime Pre- vention Bill, the Liberal majority of 253 inclecre,i of - • LIM 11,110V17 mash seetia, whilst the minority of 97 con- sisted entirely of Conservative members. bir Wilfrid Lawson has by ballot secured the first place in the motions of the 18th July for the following resolution : —" That, in view of the great and grievous evils which the nation suffers from the liquor traffic, this house is of opinion that the power of removing the cause of these evils by some efficient measure of local option, as recommended by resolu- tions of the House on the 18th of Juin, 1880, and 14th June, 1881, should be entrusted to local committees at the earliest practicable opportunity." The Standard believes that an effort will be made to arrive at an understanding between the two sides of the House on the procedure question, with the view of avoiding an autumn session. The Government, it is understood, will accept a two-thirds majority, and probably defer the con- sideration of the question of grand committees until next year. The Daily Noes understands that up to the present date the question of finding a means of progression with the procedure rules has not formally come before the Cabinet. Mr. Gladstone's statement of Tuesday; afternoon, is not, therefore, anything more than it professed to be—namely, a doclaration that the proceduae rules must be passed before next session. Whether this shall be done by an extension of the session or an autumn session is a matter which yet remains for the consideration of the Cabinetai The Select Committee on the Artisans' and Labourers' Dwellings Act on Monday afternoon agreed upon their re- port. They make various suggestions for atating the enormous expense in the way of erecting cheap dwellings for artisans, or cleared areas in urban localities, and for re- moving technical difficulties to the working of the Acts. The committee strongly recommended that both Sir R. Cross's and Mr. Torrens's amendments of the Acts should be worked irrari passu, and that the obligation placed upon the Eastern Counties system otrailways out of London to provide trains for artisans at the rate of id. per course of seven orcight miles should be extended to other suburban railways as opportunities arise. No step has yet been taken to 'carry out Mr. Gladstene's suggestion that the three bills dealing with English agri- cultural holdings should be allowed to pass the second read- inuaro forma, in order to be referred to a Grand Committee. The more active promoters of the bills introduced by Mr. Chaplin and Sir T. D. Acland demur to the more advanced proposals in Mr. J. Howard's bill being placed on the same level as their own for future consideration. There is also considerable hesitation about venturing upon The untried experiment of a Grand Committee, which might not hasten legislation, although it is -thought possible that Mr. Chap- lin's and Sir T. D. Adana's might be to some extent amal- gamated if both were referred to a Select Committee.
